Borderlands 2 is both a great improvement over the first one and a great game on its own. It maintains the structure of the first game, but adds new and improved characters with much better-structured classes and skill trees, a proper story and impressive graphics.
Borderlands 2 starts off a bunch of years after the first one. The vault has opened and there was nothing of value there...Just kidding! The opening of the vault actually released a powerful alien power which has drawn the attention of Hyperion Corporation's president: Handsome Jack, who is also an as*hole. That should be his name. As*hole Jack. So, this Jack guy completely enslaves the population of Pandora. His greed is almost as big as the number of guns in this game. Seriously, did I already mention it? The number of guns in this game is just amazing. I don't even know how much is 'bazillions', but that probably doesn't even exist and had to be made up just to count the amount of weapons generated in this game.
Again, you are a vault hunter. But Handsome Jack does not want anyone else going for the vault. He wants it all for himself, so one of his goals is to kill you, and one of your goals is to kill him. Throughout the game you'll meet Borderlands 1's main characters, such as Lilith and Roland, and you will help them achieve some of their goals. Roland is the leader of a resistance who is fighting against Hyperion forces but is pretty much losing, as far as you can tell. Without getting any further on the story, it basically just ties the loose ends that the disappointing Borderlands 1 ending had and develops beyong that with a good, solid story. All that without taking away from the gameplay and, of course, the humour.
Borderlands 2 can be played solo, but it is harder to do so than it was on the original game. This game is made to be played in coop, and it is SO much better. Of course the game is really fun solo too, but there's just no denial that the real fun is on playing with friends, selecting different classes and learning how to play with them to properly cooperate with others and create a great team.
I am trying really hard to search for a let down in this game, because there isn't. Maybe some quests are kind of repetitive and/or irritating, but those are mostly sidequests and should not be bothered with. So, Borderlands 2 is a wonderful experience and you should definitely buy it, ESPECIALLY if you have a couple of friends who also play it or want to play it.
+Good gameplay mechanics
+Beautiful graphics
+Way more variety in the game's world than the first one
+Infinite amount of weapons
+Well-written story
-Most of the side-quests are repetitive
SCORE: 94/100

When a game only has a couple of faults, generally you are in for a good time.
That's definately the case here but I think the drawbacks need pointing out for those who enjoyed the original.  It is worth noting that this is much more multiplayer focused than the first title and that large parts of the game are hidden behind a DLC paywall.
The game plays well despite this, only those determined to max out their characters will experience the grind required to do so in single player.  Gathering a few friends to play with helps this aspect and character abilities combine nicely to make teamwork worthwhile.  DLC is integrated well, so it never feels like your progression is hampered, but 2 playable characters, maximum character levels and large chunks of gameplay are unavailable unless further cash is forthcoming.
That said, core gameplay is fun, weapon collecting is compulsive and the sense of humour is pitched nicely.  All in all, this is an improvement on the original only in areas outside of the gameplay, which is essentially unchanged.  A solid eight out of ten; drop a point if you find the DLC distasteful and add a point if multiplayer is important to you.

At first, I kind of didn't want to get Undertale. Mainly because the internet
talked about it, so a decent number of plot points were spoiled for me. I figured I wouldn't be able to enjoy the game with a fresh experience. But a friend bought it for me on a sale, so I decided to play it anyway.
I'm happy to say that it was still a very enjoyable experience.
Without getting into significant detail (don't want anyone to feel like I did), the story does a great job at making you care about the characters and making you feel awful for trying to kill them. It uses some surprisingly strong narrative techniques that can really touch your heart.
The gameplay is also pretty good. Combat works by controlling a heart around a box, avoiding a variety of enemy attacks. Bosses shake up this formula in very cool ways and are easily the most memorable parts of the entire game.
But, Undertale is a not a perfect game. Fighting bosses is a lot of fun, but that's because they don't have a chance to wear out their welcome, unlike the regular enemies. It's neat the first time you fight an enemy, trying to figure out how to spare them (if you're trying to, that is). But after fighting the same enemy for the fourth time or so, it becomes tedious. It gets even worse when you're fighting multiple enemies of differing types. You have to go though their specific song and dance to spare them one at a time. It feels really slow. Mercifully, the random encounter rate is rather low, so as long as you move forward with purpose, you shouldn't have too bad a time.
The game also sadly has very little replay value. I can't see people playing this game more than three times, so if you're looking for a game to keep pulling you in, Undertale won't be it.
But even with these two issues, Undertale is a still a fantastic game and an experience that anyone with even a passing interest in RPGs should try out.

When a game only has a couple of faults, generally you are in for a good time.
That's definately the case here but I think the drawbacks need pointing out for those who enjoyed the original.  It is worth noting that this is much more multiplayer focused than the first title and that large parts of the game are hidden behind a DLC paywall.
The game plays well despite this, only those determined to max out their characters will experience the grind required to do so in single player.  Gathering a few friends to play with helps this aspect and character abilities combine nicely to make teamwork worthwhile.  DLC is integrated well, so it never feels like your progression is hampered, but 2 playable characters, maximum character levels and large chunks of gameplay are unavailable unless further cash is forthcoming.
That said, core gameplay is fun, weapon collecting is compulsive and the sense of humour is pitched nicely.  All in all, this is an improvement on the original only in areas outside of the gameplay, which is essentially unchanged.  A solid eight out of ten; drop a point if you find the DLC distasteful and add a point if multiplayer is important to you.

A very well done game. Borderlands 2 (in my opinion), sets the standard for what it means to be a great co-op, hybrid shooter. While I can go on and on for hours and days about all of the interesting things that makes this a great game, I'd rather just touch on a few subjects that I felt could use improvement in the game.
Single-player mode in the game, while fun, ceases to be so once you get about 60% of the way through your second playthrough. Even with the addition of more expansions and content the game runs you into the ground as a solo player trying to hit the level cap. With more than one person though this feeling is diminished as you can chit-chat about the days happenings while you murder bandits what-not, but still, the solo aspect of the game is missing something that would make this game go from near perfect, to perfect.
In my experience I feel that this game could use an option to skip cinematic videos after the 1st playthrough was completed. This would dramatically enhance the multiple playthroughs you have to do in order to reach the level caps that are in place. I can't tell you how bored I became after I ran through True Vault Hunter Mode on a character having to sit and watch all of the same cutscenes over again, not to mention the fact that I've done what feels like a hundred more times since then, on the next highest difficulty with other characters, and my friends characters.
More random weapons!
I can't tell you how much I want a sniper rifle that shoots a singularity style bullet!
In all seriousness though, I understand game balancing and such being a major issue when it comes to how these things are introduced into the game, but in terms of "true" variety of weapons in the game...there just really isn't any. It's a recycling and relabling of the same twenty or so standard weapon styles which gives you a staggering number of extremely similar weapons...which is great for filler gear until you stumble upon a pre-designed weapon and then the hunt begins to find more of them. Which is ultimately just boring and wasteful.
More varied gun types, like a shotgun that has nuke pellets, or a pistol that shoots splat-gun style projectiles, or an assault rifle that fired independently firing bullet spheres, or grenades that operated like landmines or claymores, or sniper rifles that shot proximity bombs...the list is literally endless. So I understand that there are programming restraints and such, but in the future, things like this on even the most common of weapons would make them worth possessing simply for the varied effect, with rarity impacting on how useful or uncommon that type of function actually is.
Keep the additional Vault Hunter's coming!
More character types to choose from in the game is great and the synergy of certain character combinations (Maya and Kreig) make these new characters or even old characters, extremely fun to play and refresh the replay value of the game itself.
Another thing that would make this game amazing is to play character oriented story expansions. A short series of missions with each character that takes place in the present time that could reveal more about that characters personality and history. This would add a tremendous amount of value to the gameplay and content of Borderlands 2 and allow players to experience things with their favorite characters on a more personal level, since the main story and the expansions are more of a general experience.
Aside from those things I feel that this game is amazing and that any future sequels for this game (if any) will be just as good, if not better. Just don't go the MMO route or let money be the sole reason you make future games. Quality above quantity.

Similar to its predecessor Borderlands, Borderlands 2 has a great storyline and brilliant writing/humor, but it's been polished further. It also features the worlds best antagonist. Think of it as a sci-fi/western, but painstakingly well written and freaking hilarious. This game can be enjoyed equally with friends or solo.
I give this game a 9/10. It's easily in my top 10 most played with over 100hrs so far.

First things first, to everyone that loved the first game: buy this. That is all.
Now to everyone else:
Borderlands 2 is a FPS-RPG (of sorts), a lootshooter basically with great art design, a proper story this time around with bigger, more colourful environments and a lot more interaction with NPCs.  Very quite literally is a bazillion items in the game, varying from pistols that shoot out multiple rockets, shotguns that lob corrosive globs and shields that absorb enemy rounds.  Gun variety does not seem to be quite as vast as in the first game, but the amount of weapons that are extremely similar (alot were in the first game) is extremely low.  The storyline is quite an upgrade from the previous game's rather disappointing story and is filled with some great voice acting and humour.  Each playable character has their own skilltree and specific action ability (like the Gunzerker's dual wielding of ANY two weapons).  There is also 4 player co-op.
So just very quick rundown of the game:
Pros
- Great visuals
- Awesome weapon variety and animations
- Great enemy variety and inter-enemy interaction
- Co op is fun
- The DLC packs are rather good
Cons (mostly related with the difficulty that the DLC adds)
- Third playthrough mode (added with the purchas of one of the vault hunter DLC packs) can get frustratingly tough, seeing     as enemies have 4x health now
- DLC, especially the Sir Hammerlock and Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep are almost impossible to play solo in the third playthrough, the enemies are ridiculously buffed even in the second playthrough
Conclusion:
The DLC, even though they add a rather unpleasant level of difficulty in the 3rd and 4th DLC packs, are all rather excellent.
If you love loot intensive games, shooting, explosions, cool weapons, witty dialogue and things that go boom, get this.

The problem I have with the game is that it is a nightmare to try and be helpful to the community.  Whenever you enter a CQB situation if you try to defuse the situation with words, you are inevitably going to die.  Then ofcourse, said individual will come and gloatover your body because he wasted you.  Nevermind the fact that you attempted to be un hostile so he had first shot. In the end it forces you to play one way... shoot first, and if everyone is doing that, what makes it any different from any other shooter?  And in those, you dont waste hours trying to find gear and battle the elements.  Without some sort of incentive to have people work together, i see no reason to put in the time this game should really deserve.  And before fan boys go, "you're just angry because you got killed" please understand that the mentality of shoot first forces everyone to play like that.  And in a sandbox game that is supposedly free to multiple play styles, having a forced go to option of kill on sight negates the choice.  In the end... if you do decide to play the game, If something moves that is not you... Shoot it until you have no ammo... then reload and shoot it in the head.  Then and only then should you attempt to talk to it.  Also, please note my time played... i have attempted to be a friendly survivor many times.  I have repeatedly tried not to murder everything, and the only time i am really enjoying myself, because i dont die, is when I slaughter people without question.  So take my review how you will, but it is benificial both for bandits, and for survivors if there are incentives to working together.  Who are you going to bandit, if everyone is dead?  The senseless killing will drive away players and when the community population drops, it is bad for everyone.  Maybe it will change outside of alpha, but for now... unless you can handle the constant hostile nature of those you are playing with, and dont mind spending hours finding gear you have little chance of maintaining for long periods, I would wait.

People like to bring up Earthbound in relation to this game for good reason.  It's clearly a game that was made by someone influenced by Earthbound in some big ways.  But it doesn't rely on that game as a crutch, through it's humor, music, characters, and gameplay Undertale is it's own game in every way.
If you like games that are funny, if you like games that let your choices matter, if you like games that have strong characters with backstories that exist for you to find but aren't shoved down your throat, play Undertale.  But most of all, if you like games that actually earn their emotional impact instead of just telling you when you're supposed to be angry, sad, disgusted, or excited, play Undertale.
But the gameplay delivers as well.  While the 'bullet hell' portions of combat can sometimes be a little too randomized to feel fair (your mileage may vary), they're a great mechanic for keeping turn-based combat interesting in a genre where it's become pretty routine.  The different weapons all working a little differently for attacks is fun too.  And of course if you prefer solving problems instead of resorting to violence, the puzzles built into monster encounters are always interesting and usually really funny too.
Every part of the game feels genuine, fun, and touching.  And it's fun to play!  Undertale is packed to the brim with charm and content.  And it not only lets you play however you want, it rewards you for doing just that.
You don't need to know anything else about the game: play Undertale ASAP.
And buy the soundtrack.  Even if you don't get the game, do that.

Borderlands 2 was my favorite game of 2012. 2 warnings: I bought but have not finished Dishonored or Far Cry 3. But let's get into...
The humor. It is over the top at times but I (for the most part) enjoyed it.
The aesthetics. I loved the music, the graphics style, and the world.
The items were cool.
I loved the style of Mechromancer and always got a kick out of trying to snipe with anarchy charges.
The gun play was not the best but was not weak.
The DLC was fun and felt less like small addons and ALMOST like the expansions I grew up with (before we had DLC we had full fledged expansions to games that you'd have to buy in a box... on disc and everything!). I enjoyed both Scarlet and Crater.
The bad:
New game plus is fine to give replayability but eventually all ARPG style games with this mechanic eventually get repeatitive. It took plenty of time (I'm showing 84 hours) but I never did finish all of the DLC because I just got burned out. I'm not complaining. 84 hours of gameplay for the original price? Not bad! Just warning that if you've ever felt similar games got repeatitive, even the insanity of Borderlands 2 can get there eventually.
The bosses. 99% of the game. But bosses were not. Bullet sponges. Mechanics that were just not fun for single player. And multiplayer is not always possible unless you have friends actively playing the game. The final boss in the Badass Crater basically killed the game for me. Again I felt like I got PLENTY of gameplay for my buck. But the bosses were the only turn off.
Overall, great game. It feels less like an fps and more like an ARPG with guns. If you like that style and can catch this game on sale, go for it!

I love this game so much! I have played enough of this game to be able to review it.
Note: I have the Game of the Year edition which is different from the standalone game.  That means this review is on the improved version of the game, not the original game.
What are the good parts of Borderlands 2?
-This is a very awesome game with a very awesome story.
-Six characters!  Have some fun.
-Weapons! There are so many of them, I doubt there are billions of them, but there are so many you will lose count into how many weapons there actually are in this game. Weapons in this game are just completely unique, unlike other shooters where it just shoots bullets and only bullets.  You can get weapons that can shoot fire, green acid, blue shock waves.  Hell, you can even get a gun that shoots explosive swords that explode on contact, or a talking weapon!  Very unique and original, and this game excels at that.  There are six types of weapons: normal, explosives, fire, shock, slag, corrosive.  There are probably more types of weapons but since I played only up to Lv.50 out of 72 in this game, there may be more types that I never got to see or have forgotten about.  Also, branded weapons, there are brands of weapons like Torque, Dahl, Maliwan, Hyperion, etc... Many weapon variations and you get to try out many of them.
-The main story is amazing.  Very funny, very unique, very original. I won't describe the story here, but you can read or watch it elsewhere.
-Gambling in this game can get addicting! Go slot machines.
-Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep is also a really good post-game story.  Very funny side quests, very awesome story as the teenage girl makes up while keeping her players occupied.
-Mr. Torque's Badass Crater story was also amazing.  Very nice side story quest and makes you feel badass overall.
What are the bad parts of Borderlands 2?
-Captain Scarlett's story is boring at first and in the end, was slightly rewarding.  Overall a decent story, but not as good as everything else.  This side-quest was a letdown.
-The worst post-game quest I have ever played and is advertised in the game's description was Sir Hammerlock's Big Game Hunt (or whatever it's called).  The story was boring from the very beginning all the way to the end.  And in the end, it was not rewarding.  After all the hard work you have done to complete this main post side-quest, the rewards were just really bad.  There was basically little to no value in doing this post-game side-quest that was in the game's description.
-Small issue: if you change the source of your playback system, the game will cease to stop playing the sound, requiring a restart.  Let's say you want to wear your headset while the game's playing on speakers, once you plug the headphones in, the game sound just stops.

Rust is one of the number of survival games which have emerged on the market after the success of the original DayZ mod for Arma II. It has been in development since the late 2013 and is made by Facepunch studios lead by the well-known creator of Garry's Mod, Garry Newman. It is still advertised as alpha although the game is already pretty well fleshed out. Similar to other survival games, players are pitted against each other in harsh enviroment to fend for themselves and do their best to survive.
To survive in Rust you ought to fulfill your basic needs. If you do not eat or drink you will die really quickly. Finding food on a densily populated server may be hard for a new player but as in all survival games you are much less likely to die of hunger than by getting killed by other players. Indeed it is the fellow men you ought to be afraid of most. In Rust this is emphasized even further by the sparsity of other threats. There are no NPC zombies that would eat you like in DayZ, at least not anymore. You can ocasionally run into a wolf which you can easily beat with basic weapons. Be wary of bears though which are deadly to even well equipped players.
That should do for the introduction. Now the real question is what exactly do you do? Right now I would sum up the game with the words "Survive, gather, build and prosper, just to have everything taken from you by raiders." While you can just run around in the beautiful world of Rust, explore and die, the real fun lies in building your own sweet home. To do that though, you need to gather enough materials first. For starters you can work with wood and stones which are quite easy to get. From the very beginning you can craft a stone hatchet and pickaxe which will make gathering much easier. Once you have got enough materials you can get to building.
Rust has a pretty intuitive building system. First of all you create a a base for you new house. You do that by stacking square or triangular pieces together until you get a desired shape and size. After you have your base ready you can add walls, windows, doors and even a roof. The system is open to creativity, which is encouraged, because your house is going to be under the constant threat of being ransacked by other players.
So far we have gone through gathering and building part of the game but that is just a half of it. Second half is all about fighting. For your encounters with other players the game has a whole arsenal of weapons to have fun with ranging from basic weapons like swords and bows to semi-automatic pistols and assault rifles. The combat itself is pretty satisfying. There are no crosshairs but with guns one can look through the iron sights to aim precisely. Shots are affected by physics so arrows and even bullets lose velocity and drop down as they travel into distance. Everything in game is designed to look like a makeshift weapons, even the most advanced rifles and it does look awesome! Compared to ranged weapons, melee combat is very basic. Basically you just swing your weapon, eventually throw it at your foe but there is no blocking or alternative moves. Bringing a melee weapon into a ranged fight usually ends badly.
When you feel like you have already done everything you could, have a nice place of your own, plenty of weapons and resources you can always join other players (after making sure you can trust them) and go out raiding - attack other players bases and steal their stuff. This is basically Rust's end game content and requires one to be quite knowledgable about the game as it is necessary to know different base designs and their weaknesses as well as to be proficient in combat since blowing up walls makes a lot of noise which is sure to lure in other groups. This is probably the reason why most of the raids happen during the night (in the real world) since the owners of the base are likely to sleep and there is much less players lurking around waiting for their opportunity to rob you which is kind of a shame since I believe that base defense and fights tied with raiding are when the real fun starts.
As I have mentioned before, from a technical standpoint Rust looks pretty good and not at all like an Alpha. Running on a Unity engine the game looks pretty slick, I would even go as far as to compliment the looks as amazing when you set the settings on high; However it is important to say that it is insanely demanding on hardware. If you are looking for a fluid experience with stable 60 fps on decent settings you will need a high end machine so optimalization definitely still leaves a room for improvement. Apart from that the game looks finished although Facepunch is still working on improvevements with regular updates to the game.
In its current state I would certainly recommend Rust to everyone who likes survival games as well as to people who would like to find out what is all the surival ruckus about. Not only does everything work properly despite it still being an early access but devs also keep bringing in new content into the game quite often which keeps the game interesting in a long run. Rust is definitely worth the asked price!

Basically if you die you lose pretty much everything. You can store a strongbox in a hut, but they're destructable too, and good luck appearing anywhere near them when you die, unless you also have sleeping bags...
...which require animal skins...
which require weapons to kill animals...
which require staying alive for long enough to build tools, collect resources, build a hut, a strongbox, weapons, kill 3-6 animals and fashion a sleeping bag before dying.
GLWT.
Took me a day to make a pair of pants and they were stolen within five minutes.
Took me a week to build a hut, and someone bashed the door in 30 seconds later, killed me, and looted my strongbox.
Took me a month to build a stone hut, with a wooden hut some distance away for backup, and two sleeping bags.
When I logged in the next day my wooden hut was gone, and someone had beaten their way in and changed the locks on my stone hut.
Who could have done such a thing? Someone with the kind of high level weapons you will never ever get, in a world as hostile as rust.
Back to the very beginning of the game - by which I mean I went back to the point before it had been installed on my computer - and I've never looked back since.
It was definitely an interesting experience, but I didn't learn much that I liked about myself or other people.

Super fun shoot and loot. I like how the RPG mechanics fuse with the FPS element. Great variety of weapons and enemies. This game also drastically improved on the visual element over Borderlands. The GUI looks cleaner, it plays easier, and the storyline is more concrete. A noticeable fix in game mechanics comes with how your character picks up loot. In the original, you could hold down a key to pick up money and such, but it would only pick up the loot in your immediate area. In this game, you automatically pick up money if you travel over it, which is especially nice when you are in a vehicle. That's the other thing. There are some very fun additions for the vehicles. Gearbox really trcked out customization in Borderlands 2. Not only do you have many different unlockable skins for your character, your vehicle can also have many different looks. Also, the buying interface is much cleaner. Instead of asking for confirmation when you buy ammo (like in the original), in this game, you just buy it. It saves time and hassle. Overall a very well-developed game with great replay value. I haven't personally tried any DLCs yet (waiting for the season pass to go on sale), but this provides loads of content. I would highly recommend getting the GOTY edition, now that it's out. That way, once you finish the main game, you won't be lacking DLCs.

Do not sleep on Undertale.
This game has an incredible story, beautiful and mesmerizing writing and extremely unique combat (or non-combat) style.
There are constantly new enemies being introduced and the gamepay and puzzles continue to stay fresh. It actually gets better as you go along. If you've been thinking about getting Undertale, DO IT!!!

Gameplay:
RPGs and Bullet Hell should not mix. It makes the game utterly frustrating when I'd rather focus on paying attention to the plot and characters. Though, more on plot and characters later... Given the methods, I suppose it may have been necessary for the intended purpose. Oh, and backtracking to GET the story and some needed friendships, despite a few things helping, is way too tedious. Actions having consequences is good. 6/10
Graphics:
Below what I desire, but for the price, they were actuallly good. The final area was nice, too. 6/10
Story
Okay, the backstory is very good, especially for the length of the game. No complaints from me about that. The gameplay story, however, struck me as way too shallow. It can basically be summarized as "A bunch of people want to get free and disagree about who and how, but become friends." Given the game's length, it could stand to have a bit more complex of a plot, and maybe have the player do more than just go through a bunch of areas and briefly meet people along the way. I want the ability to take more alternative options than are presented. 6/10
Characterization:
A lot of the characters are only met a few times, and are thus basically flat characters. This hinders the intended way to play it, of getting the player to care for every character (moreso than they would for any random stranger, that is), and the boss monsters, who are met multiple times, ... okay, they have meaningful development, but I'd really like if there were more interactions with them to get to truly understand them, not just get to know them. (I'm aware that definitions on what I just said may vary from person to person.) 6/10
Meta
I'm fine with it encouraging more peaceful RPGs, and with it brutally punishing anyone who goes for a No Mercy route. However, the deconstruction of
Frankly, all it did was make me like the things it's deconstructing more, and, despite the intent to make the player reconsider their gameplay, made me want to NOT reconsider it. 3/10
Controls/Interface
The controls are simple, but only displayed once. The format for dialogue, as well as the slow scroll speed, made pressing "X" to skip the scrolling a habit, which in turn leads to occasionally answering questions from the characters too quickly, before understanding what they mean. The interface-adjusting enemies are fine, and have good instructions leading up to the adjustments, but after using "X" to skip scrolling, it's hard to remember which button, "X" or "Z," has the desired effect. 9/10
Summary:
In short, the game wasn't for me. I can see why it would appeal to someone else, but ... well, not to me, maybe because I already look for peaceful solutions when/where feasible in games? 36/60 (= 6/10)
It passes, but... I wouldn't want to play another of it. (Maybe another issue is that
)
I give it 6/10

Undertale's Message to Humanity
The 1st fallen human, the said player is actually Chara. At the true pacifist ending when the ruins open up once again, those who are patient enough to travel back to the beginning of all, will find Flowey in its true form, the young Asriel Dremurr. When talking to Asriel over and over you realize the player, the 1st human, is (emphasis on is and not was) not a kind soul. Harboring hatred for humanity with such DETERMINATION, the human travelled to Mt Ebbot on the year 201x, the mountain legend says no traveler can return from. The player is "us" the humans with souls that does not need compassion, forgiveness or mercy. It is true that we humans can live without such things. The story goes when the human dies. With Asriel and the human's soul, they passed the barrier to the over world. The human absorbed the soul and shared the true form with Asriel. The human picked up the body to the surface. The human wished to use the divine power to wipe out humanity. Chara came to Mt Ebott to get the soul of the monsters. It is said a being with a human and monster soul can become GOD. With it, Chara gains the power to wipe out humanity. That said human over the course of time became Frisk if the player has found redemption at the judgement hall. Note we have taught and brainwashed ourselves to kill without mercy. Everything has been without a choice. Over time, we have grown distant, the more we are distant, the less we will be hurt. The less we get hurt, the more we can come to hurt others. EXP or execution point is a variable measuring the capacity of humans to hurt others. Every time you kill, your EXP increases. When you gain enough EXP, your LVL (LOVE) increases. LOVE or level of violence is Chara. Chara is pure evil, the darkness and the feeling that we get when we gain LOVE and EXP. Having earned no LOVE does not mean we are innocent. We have all been through the darkness and the cruelty. It only means that somewhere deep down, we still have a certain tenderness with us. With no LOVE we gained love. Of course, this is to say no matter what happened, no matter how frustrating, we held onto hope. We showed mercy to all and even when running away, we did so with a smile. So.... What is Chara? We, as humans are very conflicting beings. We are both Frisk&Chara. Chara is the pure evil  and Frisk is the innocent, the child that many has lost. Chara is Character. The symbol of all games or characters that we have created. Each and every character kills to gain exp to gain LOVE. We did not care, we did not stop but to slay all with a smile. WE ARE CHARA, the SOULLESS. Those who tread the path of no return will have to sell their souls to reset, to be reborn again... but it will never be the same. You hands will never be clean. Despite it all, Flowey is the symbol of the ugly nature of mankind. There are many Floweys in the over world and not everything can be solved by mercy. Will you be Frisk or Chara?
Chara: "IT'S KILL OR BE KILLED"
Frisk: "DON' KILL AND DON'T GET KILLED"

Borderlands 2 was my favorite game of 2012. 2 warnings: I bought but have not finished Dishonored or Far Cry 3. But let's get into...
The humor. It is over the top at times but I (for the most part) enjoyed it.
The aesthetics. I loved the music, the graphics style, and the world.
The items were cool.
I loved the style of Mechromancer and always got a kick out of trying to snipe with anarchy charges.
The gun play was not the best but was not weak.
The DLC was fun and felt less like small addons and ALMOST like the expansions I grew up with (before we had DLC we had full fledged expansions to games that you'd have to buy in a box... on disc and everything!). I enjoyed both Scarlet and Crater.
The bad:
New game plus is fine to give replayability but eventually all ARPG style games with this mechanic eventually get repeatitive. It took plenty of time (I'm showing 84 hours) but I never did finish all of the DLC because I just got burned out. I'm not complaining. 84 hours of gameplay for the original price? Not bad! Just warning that if you've ever felt similar games got repeatitive, even the insanity of Borderlands 2 can get there eventually.
The bosses. 99% of the game. But bosses were not. Bullet sponges. Mechanics that were just not fun for single player. And multiplayer is not always possible unless you have friends actively playing the game. The final boss in the Badass Crater basically killed the game for me. Again I felt like I got PLENTY of gameplay for my buck. But the bosses were the only turn off.
Overall, great game. It feels less like an fps and more like an ARPG with guns. If you like that style and can catch this game on sale, go for it!

I love this game so much! I have played enough of this game to be able to review it.
Note: I have the Game of the Year edition which is different from the standalone game.  That means this review is on the improved version of the game, not the original game.
What are the good parts of Borderlands 2?
-This is a very awesome game with a very awesome story.
-Six characters!  Have some fun.
-Weapons! There are so many of them, I doubt there are billions of them, but there are so many you will lose count into how many weapons there actually are in this game. Weapons in this game are just completely unique, unlike other shooters where it just shoots bullets and only bullets.  You can get weapons that can shoot fire, green acid, blue shock waves.  Hell, you can even get a gun that shoots explosive swords that explode on contact, or a talking weapon!  Very unique and original, and this game excels at that.  There are six types of weapons: normal, explosives, fire, shock, slag, corrosive.  There are probably more types of weapons but since I played only up to Lv.50 out of 72 in this game, there may be more types that I never got to see or have forgotten about.  Also, branded weapons, there are brands of weapons like Torque, Dahl, Maliwan, Hyperion, etc... Many weapon variations and you get to try out many of them.
-The main story is amazing.  Very funny, very unique, very original. I won't describe the story here, but you can read or watch it elsewhere.
-Gambling in this game can get addicting! Go slot machines.
-Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep is also a really good post-game story.  Very funny side quests, very awesome story as the teenage girl makes up while keeping her players occupied.
-Mr. Torque's Badass Crater story was also amazing.  Very nice side story quest and makes you feel badass overall.
What are the bad parts of Borderlands 2?
-Captain Scarlett's story is boring at first and in the end, was slightly rewarding.  Overall a decent story, but not as good as everything else.  This side-quest was a letdown.
-The worst post-game quest I have ever played and is advertised in the game's description was Sir Hammerlock's Big Game Hunt (or whatever it's called).  The story was boring from the very beginning all the way to the end.  And in the end, it was not rewarding.  After all the hard work you have done to complete this main post side-quest, the rewards were just really bad. SPOILER ALERT- SCROLL PAST IF YOU WANT TO SEE THE STORY YOURSELF
I played through the true pacifist run and literally can't find it in me to run the genocide route. I felt the game was a chore to play, with cheap difficulty spikes, shallow characters who you never really get to really KNOW, and a depth that you need to look and search for rather than experience. Although this game is definitely 2 things: Nowhere near as bad as I thought, and nowhere near as good as everyone says it is.
Lets start with what I liked. First, what I legitimately did like was the soundtrack. Albeit a few choice tracks for me, it is undeniably pleasant to listen to. The characters, while not very developed, are still lovable and quirky with their own unique personalities. The game's story is actually very deep, but it needs to be found rather than experienced, but the depth is still impressive. The enemies have some good variety, but none of them are very interesting, and many have asinine ways of appeasing them, although there is good variety.
Now for the story it's pretty simple. Your character has fallen to the underground world where monsters reside, and your character simply wants to return home. The first major character you meet is the game's antagonist, Flowey, a 2-dimensional villian who wants to claim your soul, as well as steal the other six human souls in this world to essentially become god. After encountering him, you meet the infamous Goat Mom, or Toriel. Only for her to leave and pretty much never be seen again until the end of the true pacifist ending, who you also cannot call on your in game phone. Then you meet the skeleton brothers Papyrus and Sans, honestly the 2 characters I hated the most. Their humor grated on me and made it a chore to read their dialogue, dialogue I opted into skipping early on unless it was essential to the story. Along your journey you meet the whole crazy cast of characters. Obnoxious weeaboo Alphys, overzealous Undyne, narcississtic Mettaton, head artist cameo Temmie, duty bound Asgore (probably my most liked character), Flowey again, then finally Asriel (most pitiful character in the game). You never really get attached to these characters as you only interact with them for such a short amount of time, especially Asgore, who dies pretty much right after you meet him for the first time.
As for gameplay, it's a mix of turn based RPG with a bullet hell-esque dodge system. While for anything but bosses it is fairly easy, many bosses have sudden difficulty spikes which will make you rack up double digit attempts. Especially Sans, whose sole reason for being a boss battle brings me to my biggest problem with the game.
Undertale prides itself on a game that can be completed without killing anyone. Although it tries to let that be the thing to carry it to greatness. No, it's not the first game like this which can be completed without violence, and it is not the best example of pacifism in games. There's Mirror's Edge, Dishonored, MGS2, even ♥♥♥♥ing Postal can all be completed without killing anyone, along with many other titles. Undertale relies too much on its cutesy and familiar characters to ride on its accolade of being pacifist friendly, while punishing players who play the way they want with permanent game tainting, and an extremely difficult boss battle which is literally a punishment for running the genocide route. It makes the game feel very disingenuous and encourages players to only take the easy pacifist route as any other is much more difficult.
This game is the most critically acclaimed game of 2015 and I don't see why, because the depth that's there needs to be searched for, and requires multiple playthroughs in a specific order in order to attain the perfect ending. This game is nowhere near as good as critics and players make it out to be, people are assigning profoundness where there is none. Stanley Parable deconstructed game mechanics in a much more meaningful way, Spec Ops: The Line had more to say about senseless violence than a genocide run of Undertale, To The Moon actually explored themes of love and loss, Braid deeply explored themes of philosophy and tropes in video games. This game tries to be a jack of all trades, but ultimately ends up not really excelling much at anything, except at having a fanbase that rabidly downvotes any review or opinion that doesn't suck the game's metaphorical♥♥♥♥♥♥

TL;DR: Great game with many flaws. It's Alpha after all!
I received this as a gift from a friend over a year ago now. I never got around to installing it and trying it out, sadly, but recently I decided to do so at the recommendation of another friend. Luckily it came at a time when my interest in the Survival-Sandbox-Crafting 'genre' had been piqued. I decided to give RUST a good try after having tried ARK for the first time a few days prior.
... I became addicted...
123.4 of my 123.5 total hours played have been in the last two weeks alone. I can't get enough of this game and it's quite clear that I have a problem... and my friends have had no aversion to telling me so. ;< RUST is unique to me as it's the first game to truly take my virginity to the genre. Although I had played ARK once before, it was for no longer than an hour and it had failed to fully engross me (not bashing it, I admit I haven't played it very much at all). As high of praise as it may seem I'm giving RUST, there are definitely issues... So enough meandering personal bs, let's get into it.
The Good:
- Fantastic Graphics for Alpha (Sun shafts, water and environments look particularly gorgeous).
- Great Sound Design. Footfalls, wildlife, explosions and gunshots all come from the direction of origin and decrease in volume with distance, making it easy to orientate yourself and roughly estimate enemy locations.
- Good Models/Textures. Character models are surprisingly well designed and relatively realistic, proportionally. Textures, of course, vary depending on your settings but for the most part they're on par with even some of the newest games.
- Procedurally Generated Maps. This is a double edged sword but I'll get into the negatives down below. These are fantastic in theory and make for a unique experience between servers and wipes; making it so that no one person can gain a mastery of a certain map which lends itself to an equal playing field... literally... and encourages exploration.
- Fun and Engrossing Base Building. Nothing is more satisfying than building a good base and RUST's system is rather entertaining and indepth... The problem is grinding for enough resources to build it all.
- Immersive. I wouldn't have been able to stomach 124 hours if the game wasn't immersive. There's nothing quite like being out in the world with an inventory full of stuff, on edge that a player or bear could come by at any second and ♥♥♥♥ your♥♥♥♥♥♥up. The adrenaline is real.
- Weapons/Gear. Weapons are punchy and feedback is solid. Gear is relatively bland at the moment but it serves its purpose. Ingame models look great for an indie title and mechanics are passable. Nothing too special here but nothing bad either.
- Development Progress. The team has made some amazing strides when it comes to fidelity and gameplay. They've updated graphics, character models, game models/mechanics, and even the game engine such to the extent that Legacy RUST looks like an entirely different game from New RUST. Just go look at some videos, you'll see what I mean. Hopefully this is one that will continue through Alpha and into Beta and ultimately release. I feel that many of my grievances below will be addressed in the future.
- Ingame Progression. The progression is actually quite good and it can be done at your own pace. You're forced to go into Radtowns or Landmark areas (pre-built structures. Air Fields, Military Bases, Power Plants, etc...) in order to collect Blueprint Fragments which are used to discover new items to craft. It's an RNG system so good luck... The problem with these areas is that they're usually highly contested and very hostile, whether by other players in the area farming Blueprints, snipers or radiation. The process is obviously much faster if you team up with friends to share resources and to have someone watch your back in sticky situations.
The Bad:
- ♥♥♥♥ING BEARS! Seriously. Bears are way too fast, have way too much health and deal way too much damage. The primary cause of death for me has been bears, secondary being players, tertiary being falls and lastly, wolves.
-♥♥♥♥♥♥Optimization. The game is very poorly optimized and eats up WAY too much RAM. My average is around 6gb on medium settings and tabbing out is basically a no-go for me. Load times are excruciating and I've been told it's because of the procedurally generated maps. Why the game can't just cache this information on your HDD? No idea... Alpha is alpha though, I guess.
- CRASHES. To expand on optimization, the game is almost unplayable as of the latest patch, for me and a lot of other players it seems. Though sadly this isn't anything new as the issues I've been having have been occuring on and off throughout the development cycle. Two weeks ago I was running the game for hours on end without a single problem. Ever since the latest patch, however, I've been crashing every 15-20 minutes or so which is incredibly discouraging.
- Animations. Character/NPC animations aren't necessarily all that bad--in fact, some are good--but they definitely seem a bit jenky and/or floaty, depending. First person animations are actually quite good, save for what looks like some weight-painting issues, wrists contorting in odd ways and certain mesh vertexes not adapting to the animation rig well.
- Character Design/Gender Randomization and Lock. The developer's philanthropic view of giving each Steam ID a unique, permanent randomized character appearance is, quite frankly, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t as many have aptly pointed out. I'm personally of the belief that this is some copout/consolation. A way to give players variety but also dodge the bullet of implementing a character creator. Give us the ability to create our own characters and stop being an SJWtard. Whether or not this is due to laziness or a lack of skill/ability, I can't tell, but the fact remains that it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and you know it, Garry! Hire some more devs or get your♥♥♥♥♥into gear! ALSO GIVE US HAIRSTYLES FFS! I'm tired of being bald...
- A.I... A.I. Is literally braindead, it's absolutely awful, just terrible. Bears, Chickens, Deer and Wolves (all the wildlife, really) often just walk in circles forever. The pathing and waypoints are terrible and the only time they appear to have any brains is if you get close. Predator animals will attack you on sight and prey animals will run from you.
- Collision/Object Detection. This goes in tandem with the A.I. NPC's literally have no detection of hills, rocks, cliffs, buildings, etc. A creature will run straight up a cliffside, denying all laws of physics, or whatever it encounters. Luckily, this is not the case for player structures. You can stand on top of your house and snipe creatures without them being able to reach you. However, this is not the case for player structures that do not require placing a foundation, wildlife completely ignore those as if they have noclip enabled. Items such as large wood/stone walls, barricades, traps, etc... will be completely ignored by NPC's. They will receive no damage for walking over/near/through these objects, it's as if they're not even there. It's clear that these are only intended for enemy players, at least for now.
Here are just a few things that are not necessarily good or bad but are worth taking into consideration if you're thinking about buying:
- Players can be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Most will probably kill you on sight if they are in a position to. These are usually very progressed players with full armor, guns and a lot of ammo. This is common for the genre so be prepared.
- The game is tedious. Gathering and farming is real and can be a turn off for many players.
- You WILL die and you WILL lose many valuables! I can feel your anger...
- Wipes can make the game feel pointless sometimes as once or twice a month, all of your progress will be wiped.

Rust is one of the number of survival games which have emerged on the market after the success of the original DayZ mod for Arma II. It has been in development since the late 2013 and is made by Facepunch studios lead by the well-known creator of Garry's Mod, Garry Newman. It is still advertised as alpha although the game is already pretty well fleshed out. Similar to other survival games, players are pitted against each other in harsh enviroment to fend for themselves and do their best to survive.
To survive in Rust you ought to fulfill your basic needs. If you do not eat or drink you will die really quickly. Finding food on a densily populated server may be hard for a new player but as in all survival games you are much less likely to die of hunger than by getting killed by other players. Indeed it is the fellow men you ought to be afraid of most. In Rust this is emphasized even further by the sparsity of other threats. There are no NPC zombies that would eat you like in DayZ, at least not anymore. You can ocasionally run into a wolf which you can easily beat with basic weapons. Be wary of bears though which are deadly to even well equipped players.
That should do for the introduction. Now the real question is what exactly do you do? Right now I would sum up the game with the words "Survive, gather, build and prosper, just to have everything taken from you by raiders." While you can just run around in the beautiful world of Rust, explore and die, the real fun lies in building your own sweet home. To do that though, you need to gather enough materials first. For starters you can work with wood and stones which are quite easy to get. From the very beginning you can craft a stone hatchet and pickaxe which will make gathering much easier. Once you have got enough materials you can get to building.
Rust has a pretty intuitive building system. First of all you create a a base for you new house. You do that by stacking square or triangular pieces together until you get a desired shape and size. After you have your base ready you can add walls, windows, doors and even a roof. The system is open to creativity, which is encouraged, because your house is going to be under the constant threat of being ransacked by other players.
So far we have gone through gathering and building part of the game but that is just a half of it. Second half is all about fighting. For your encounters with other players the game has a whole arsenal of weapons to have fun with ranging from basic weapons like swords and bows to semi-automatic pistols and assault rifles. The combat itself is pretty satisfying. There are no crosshairs but with guns one can look through the iron sights to aim precisely. Shots are affected by physics so arrows and even bullets lose velocity and drop down as they travel into distance. Everything in game is designed to look like a makeshift weapons, even the most advanced rifles and it does look awesome! Compared to ranged weapons, melee combat is very basic. Basically you just swing your weapon, eventually throw it at your foe but there is no blocking or alternative moves. Bringing a melee weapon into a ranged fight usually ends badly.
When you feel like you have already done everything you could, have a nice place of your own, plenty of weapons and resources you can always join other players (after making sure you can trust them) and go out raiding - attack other players bases and steal their stuff. This is basically Rust's end game content and requires one to be quite knowledgable about the game as it is necessary to know different base designs and their weaknesses as well as to be proficient in combat since blowing up walls makes a lot of noise which is sure to lure in other groups. This is probably the reason why most of the raids happen during the night (in the real world) since the owners of the base are likely to sleep and there is much less players lurking around waiting for their opportunity to rob you which is kind of a shame since I believe that base defense and fights tied with raiding are when the real fun starts.
As I have mentioned before, from a technical standpoint Rust looks pretty good and not at all like an Alpha. Running on a Unity engine the game looks pretty slick, I would even go as far as to compliment the looks as amazing when you set the settings on high; However it is important to say that it is insanely demanding on hardware. If you are looking for a fluid experience with stable 60 fps on decent settings you will need a high end machine so optimalization definitely still leaves a room for improvement. Apart from that the game looks finished although Facepunch is still working on improvevements with regular updates to the game.
In its current state I would certainly recommend Rust to everyone who likes survival games as well as to people who would like to find out what is all the surival ruckus about. Not only does everything work properly despite it still being an early access but devs also keep bringing in new content into the game quite often which keeps the game interesting in a long run. Rust is definitely worth the asked price!

For my review, I'm going to tell a new player how to play solo.
Step 1 - Collect a small amount of stone and wood, make arrows.
Step 2 - Collect Hemp and Wood, make a bow.
Step 3 - Make more arrows. Congrats, you are now able to defend your loot. Do this before making tools.
Step 4 - Make a hatchet and a pick.
Step 5 - Kill animals to get fat and use it with your hemp to make fuel. Get stone and wood. Make a furnace.
Step 6 - Hide the furnace behind a cliff and only run during the day. Hide a sleeping bag in a bush nearby.
Step 7 - Burn metal ore in the furnace while you are chopping wood. Get 2-3k wood and spend 1k on a toolbox. Let the furnace make 250 metal frags.
Step 8 - Get stone by hitting nodes.
Step 9 - Make a tiny stone base, one level high, no more than 2x2 but maybe smaller. Put the toolbox inside and wall it off with stone. Use the metal frags to make another door.
Step 10 - Be careful leaving so no one runs inside your house. Do not open the door to your house again until you can make another furnace inside and have enough metal ore and wood to make a second door for the house before you leave again.
You must have two doors back to back, like an airlock, a furnace and a walled off tool box to block building authority, a storeage box and a sleeping bag inside this tiny, tiny building. Use this building to store materials to make a larger base.
For bonus points, build your base as far from other bases as possible while still building near a road or power lines. Do not put your base down unless you SEE hemp growing. Do not put your base down unless you see multiple nodes.
More bonus points for finding a small stone base with a tool box you can access and a prebuilt furnace. Putting doors on a raided and empty base is easier than building one.
Even more bonus points for using someone else's furnace to make a door before you kill animals.
Warnings - do not rely on wood walls, wood floors, or wood ceilings. They will be destroyed. Stone walls only. Wood doors only if you can put a metal door inside the wooden door while someone is destroying it. It can by time but you have to put a metal door deeper in the base.
Master level - build extra bases and fill them with doors and random loot boxes, each with stone, wood, hammers and building plans. If you log on and see you got raided, move inner doors out and patch the walls, make one supply run and get back on top in an hour.

Borderlands 2 attempts to step up from the first game, but in the end they don't deviate much from the original setup. There's guns, loot, ridiculous characters, and EXPLOSIONS.

The Challenge Accepted achievement takes more time to complete than the main campaign does, but man does it feel good to land it.
My biggest complaint with the Borderlands series continues to be with how stinkin' easy the game is. Yes, they added Ultimate Vault Hunter mode and made the baddies better (also the overleveling DLC), but I'm concerned with the original campaign. I want my first playthrough to be challenging. It took me all of a minute to defeat the final boss on my first playthrough, do you know how unsatisfying that is? Instead of building the game around a pre-set structure of levels for opponents, why not structure the first playthrough where all enemies level up with you? Nothing is worse than coasting through the final mission while shooting a gun that's ten levels above your worst enemy.
Overall, it's a game that's very fun to play and has reasonable replay value, but you won't find many surprises here if you played the first.

This is not the place to get too in-depth with a discussion of Undertale, so I'll be brief;
Undertale is a very important game. If you haven't played it yet, you probably should.
I do not mean to sing it's praises. It's not a perfect game by a long shot. In fact, I have some big issues with it, most notably with the way that the plot is structured. After my first playthrough, I was left dissappointed and unsatisfied.
But then I played it a little more. And then more after that. And by now, I've played it a lot. Even though I didn't enjoy it at first, I kept going. Hell, I'm probably going to keep playing even after I beat my current playthrough. Why?
Because Undertale may be one of the smartest games I have ever played. It is consistently surprising, even after 20 hours of gameplay. There is an absolutely absurd attention to detail, and I am not being hyperbolic. It is so, so clever. And more importantly, It is really, REALLY good at making you think about your choices. Undertale will hit you where it hurts; it will force you to act and then force you to confront the consequences of said actions. It is a tour de force of emotions. It may not be pretty, but from a design it is absolutely beautiful.
I love Undertale. I really, really do. It took me a while to realize it, but I love this game. Because for everythat it does, for all of it's failures and triumphs, it always succeeds in provoking thought. Even when it fumbles, you can pull something meaningful from it. Undertale will teach you about yourself just as much as it will teach you about the medium it exists in.

The 1st fallen human, the said player is actually Chara. At the true pacifist ending when the ruins open up once again, those who are patient enough to travel back to the beginning of all, will find Flowey in its true form, the young Asriel Dremurr. When talking to Asriel over and over you realize the player, the 1st human, is (emphasis on is and not was) not a kind soul. Harboring hatred for humanity with such DETERMINATION, the human travelled to Mt Ebbot on the year 201x, the mountain legend says no traveler can return from. The player is "us" the humans with souls that does not need compassion, forgiveness or mercy. It is true that we humans can live without such things. The story goes when the human dies. With Asriel and the human's soul, they passed the barrier to the over world. The human absorbed the soul and shared the true form with Asriel. The human picked up the body to the surface. The human wished to use the divine power to wipe out humanity. Chara came to Mt Ebott to get the soul of the monsters. It is said a being with a human and monster soul can become GOD. With it, Chara gains the power to wipe out humanity. That said human over the course of time became Frisk if the player has found redemption at the judgement hall. Note we have taught and brainwashed ourselves to kill without mercy. Everything has been without a choice. Over time, we have grown distant, the more we are distant, the less we will be hurt. The less we get hurt, the more we can come to hurt others. EXP or execution point is a variable measuring the capacity of humans to hurt others. Every time you kill, your EXP increases. When you gain enough EXP, your LVL (LOVE) increases. LOVE or level of violence is Chara. Chara is pure evil, the darkness and the feeling that we get when we gain LOVE and EXP. Having earned no LOVE does not mean we are innocent. We have all been through the darkness and the cruelty. It only means that somewhere deep down, we still have a certain tenderness with us. With no LOVE we gained love. Of course, this is to say no matter what happened, no matter how frustrating, we held onto hope. We showed mercy to all and even when running away, we did so with a smile. So.... What is Chara? We, as humans are very conflicting beings. We are both Frisk&Chara. Chara is the pure evil  and Frisk is the innocent, the child that many has lost. Chara is Character. The symbol of all games or characters that we have created. Each and every character kills to gain exp to gain LOVE. We did not care, we did not stop but to slay all with a smile. WE ARE CHARA, the SOULLESS. Those who tread the path of no return will have to sell their souls to reset, to be reborn again... but it will never be the same. You hands will never be clean. Despite it all, Flowey is the symbol of the ugly nature of mankind. There are many Floweys in the over world and not everything can be solved by mercy. Will you be Frisk or Chara?

TL;DR: Great game with many flaws. It's Alpha after all!
I received this as a gift from a friend over a year ago now. I never got around to installing it and trying it out, sadly, but recently I decided to do so at the recommendation of another friend. Luckily it came at a time when my interest in the Survival-Sandbox-Crafting 'genre' had been piqued. I decided to give RUST a good try after having tried ARK for the first time a few days prior.
... I became addicted...
123.4 of my 123.5 total hours played have been in the last two weeks alone. I can't get enough of this game and it's quite clear that I have a problem... and my friends have had no aversion to telling me so. ;< RUST is unique to me as it's the first game to truly take my virginity to the genre. Although I had played ARK once before, it was for no longer than an hour and it had failed to fully engross me (not bashing it, I admit I haven't played it very much at all). As high of praise as it may seem I'm giving RUST, there are definitely issues... So enough meandering personal bs, let's get into it.
The Good:
- Fantastic Graphics for Alpha (Sun shafts, water and environments look particularly gorgeous).
- Great Sound Design. Footfalls, wildlife, explosions and gunshots all come from the direction of origin and decrease in volume with distance, making it easy to orientate yourself and roughly estimate enemy locations.
- Good Models/Textures. Character models are surprisingly well designed and relatively realistic, proportionally. Textures, of course, vary depending on your settings but for the most part they're on par with even some of the newest games.
- Procedurally Generated Maps. This is a double edged sword but I'll get into the negatives down below. These are fantastic in theory and make for a unique experience between servers and wipes; making it so that no one person can gain a mastery of a certain map which lends itself to an equal playing field... literally... and encourages exploration.
- Fun and Engrossing Base Building. Nothing is more satisfying than building a good base and RUST's system is rather entertaining and indepth... The problem is grinding for enough resources to build it all.
- Immersive. I wouldn't have been able to stomach 124 hours if the game wasn't immersive. There's nothing quite like being out in the world with an inventory full of stuff, on edge that a player or bear could come by at any second and ♥♥♥♥ your♥♥♥♥♥♥up. The adrenaline is real.
- Weapons/Gear. Weapons are punchy and feedback is solid. Gear is relatively bland at the moment but it serves its purpose. Ingame models look great for an indie title and mechanics are passable. Nothing too special here but nothing bad either.
- Development Progress. The team has made some amazing strides when it comes to fidelity and gameplay. They've updated graphics, character models, game models/mechanics, and even the game engine such to the extent that Legacy RUST looks like an entirely different game from New RUST. Just go look at some videos, you'll see what I mean. Hopefully this is one that will continue through Alpha and into Beta and ultimately release. I feel that many of my grievances below will be addressed in the future.
- Ingame Progression. The progression is actually quite good and it can be done at your own pace. You're forced to go into Radtowns or Landmark areas (pre-built structures. Air Fields, Military Bases, Power Plants, etc...) in order to collect Blueprint Fragments which are used to discover new items to craft. It's an RNG system so good luck... The problem with these areas is that they're usually highly contested and very hostile, whether by other players in the area farming Blueprints, snipers or radiation. The process is obviously much faster if you team up with friends to share resources and to have someone watch your back in sticky situations.
The Bad:
- ♥♥♥♥ING BEARS! Seriously. Bears are way too fast, have way too much health and deal way too much damage. The primary cause of death for me has been bears, secondary being players, tertiary being falls and lastly, wolves.
-♥♥♥♥♥♥Optimization. The game is very poorly optimized and eats up WAY too much RAM. My average is around 6gb on medium settings and tabbing out is basically a no-go for me. Load times are excruciating and I've been told it's because of the procedurally generated maps. Why the game can't just cache this information on your HDD? No idea... Alpha is alpha though, I guess.
- CRASHES. To expand on optimization, the game is almost unplayable as of the latest patch, for me and a lot of other players it seems. Though sadly this isn't anything new as the issues I've been having have been occuring on and off throughout the development cycle. Two weeks ago I was running the game for hours on end without a single problem. Ever since the latest patch, however, I've been crashing every 15-20 minutes or so which is incredibly discouraging.
- Animations. Character/NPC animations aren't necessarily all that bad--in fact, some are good--but they definitely seem a bit jenky and/or floaty, depending. First person animations are actually quite good, save for what looks like some weight-painting issues, wrists contorting in odd ways and certain mesh vertexes not adapting to the animation rig well.
- Character Design/Gender Randomization and Lock. The developer's philanthropic view of giving each Steam ID a unique, permanent randomized character appearance is, quite frankly, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t as many have aptly pointed out. I'm personally of the belief that this is some copout/consolation. A way to give players variety but also dodge the bullet of implementing a character creator. Give us the ability to create our own characters and stop being an SJWtard. Whether or not this is due to laziness or a lack of skill/ability, I can't tell, but the fact remains that it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and you know it, Garry! Hire some more devs or get your♥♥♥♥♥into gear! ALSO GIVE US HAIRSTYLES FFS! I'm tired of being bald...
- A.I... A.I. Is literally braindead, it's absolutely awful, just terrible. Bears, Chickens, Deer and Wolves (all the wildlife, really) often just walk in circles forever. The pathing and waypoints are terrible and the only time they appear to have any brains is if you get close. Predator animals will attack you on sight and prey animals will run from you.
- Collision/Object Detection. This goes in tandem with the A.I. NPC's literally have no detection of hills, rocks, cliffs, buildings, etc. A creature will run straight up a cliffside, denying all laws of physics, or whatever it encounters. Luckily, this is not the case for player structures. You can stand on top of your house and snipe creatures without them being able to reach you. However, this is not the case for player structures that do not require placing a foundation, wildlife completely ignore those as if they have noclip enabled. Items such as large wood/stone walls, barricades, traps, etc... will be completely ignored by NPC's. They will receive no damage for walking over/near/through these objects, it's as if they're not even there. It's clear that these are only intended for enemy players, at least for now.
Here are just a few things that are not necessarily good or bad but are worth taking into consideration if you're thinking about buying:

The GUI looks cleaner, it plays easier, and the storyline is more concrete. A noticeable fix in game mechanics comes with how your character picks up loot. In the original, you could hold down a key to pick up money and such, but it would only pick up the loot in your immediate area. In this game, you automatically pick up money if you travel over it, which is especially nice when you are in a vehicle. That's the other thing. There are some very fun additions for the vehicles. Gearbox really trcked out customization in Borderlands 2. Not only do you have many different unlockable skins for your character, your vehicle can also have many different looks. Also, the buying interface is much cleaner. Instead of asking for confirmation when you buy ammo (like in the original), in this game, you just buy it. It saves time and hassle. Overall a very well-developed game with great replay value. I haven't personally tried any DLCs yet (waiting for the season pass to go on sale), but this provides loads of content. I would highly recommend getting the GOTY edition, now that it's out. That way, once you finish the main game, you won't be lacking DLCs.

I now run my own dedicated server available to anyone online (Name: [East] North Carolina. Wiped 5/5. No Decay). I have about 10 active players and everyone works together and gets along...for the most part. Occasionally we kill each other, but mostly its a collaborative experience. The game can be quite demanding on the computer, especially if you want to run it at max settings; however, they have many preset graphic settings from "fastest running" to "fantastic". I am running 2x 980ti's ftw model in SLI and get around 30-35fps at max settings at 4k. I am sure as they continue to optimize the game/improve NVIDIA and AMD support it will only get better. I am willing to bet they do not support SLI and that is part of the reason I cannot max out fps.
Take away:
I am 100% glad I purchased this game and am looking foward to what the future holds. When BL1 was released I was very excited, finally a game that mashed together MMO's, RPG's, and FPS's. It is very unfortunate that Gearbox was the source of this idea.
Borderlands 2, much like Borderlands 1, starts off brilliant. Engaging story and characters, great immersive eviroments, great pacing and balance throughout. It is not until that Playthrough 2 that Borderlands 2, much like Borderlands 1, starts to rear its true head. Starting on Playthrough 2 (which by the way is an incredibly lazy thing for ANY developer to do. Give me a full game, not the same thing 2-4 times.) Gearbox throws out all working concepts of the setting they've established for the game so far:
- You're super powerful.
- You have the best guns. Period.
- Enemies are psychotic, former scientists/miners. I.E, untrained with weapons, certainly less than a merc vault hunter.
- The enemies don't wear armor (most) and have guns that are duct taped together, literally.
These things lead to a very easy and very enjoyable Playthrough 1 to get acclimated to the game if you're a first time BL player. However, as I stated above, Gearbox ditches all of these established concepts on Playthrough 2 in favor of:
- You ain't♥♥♥♥♥♥
- You're best gun on the entire planet now shoots spitballls.
- Enemies are highly trained marine snipers capable of only hitting your head.
- The enemies still dont wear armor and still have duct taped guns, but now instead of HP/Gun Damage to refect this, they do exponentially more damage than your "Best Gun on the Planet" and have exponentially more health than your "Best Health/Sheild Kit" on the planet.
What does this lead to? A totally underwhelming experience, a ton of balance issues, and a game that turns from enjoyable mass-murderous fun to a tediuous, arguous experience that fights you to enjoy it every step of the way. Which is extrememly unfortunate because the story and characters are great, in fact they were the only reason I finished the game a second time. Even the DLC's in this game are great, but again are ruined by incompetent bullet sponging and balance issues.
TL/DR:
Try it if you want, but be warned the longer you play this game, the worse it becomes.
