Attention Deficit version: An excellent game that is essentially an FPS with some RPG elements. (Your recommendation is 1,402 characters too long. Please shorten it and try again.)!
...and now, a few brief caveats and addenda.
This is very much like "World of Warcraft" or "Diablo" but handles like an FPS with some very minor RPG elements.
The narrative isn't bad, however, the implementation is lacking in one way - I frequently had voiceovers trample previous ones, sometimes leading to narration that wasn't (to me) immediately important being squelched by a later one.
It can feel grindy, because, well - it is. See which games I referenced in #1? There are more sidequests and awards in the game than are needed to level, (even discounting challenge and exploration rewards or hidden sidequests) which will mean you will outlevel content regularly if you're a "do everything in the zone" sort.
It does mean you can often get by with (very) subpar FPS skills, and you can choose to retain or build up the challenge by tackling main quest missions and sidequests when they are at or above your current level. I recommend paying attention to the levels of quests and choose more enjoyable carnage.
Poor placement of RPG choices is a very minor issue for novices to the RPG genre, as the central locations have "respec" machines that can reset both skills and appearance for a nominal fee - often much less than dying, which has a somewhat less nominal monetary penalty.
Overall, an improvement on the first one. the acting can be a bit hammy and the references and tropes are pretty thick on the ground, but frankly, if you're still here, you're here to shoot things and take their stuff. This, you will find in Borderlands 2.
DLC deserves a mention for those of you considering the GotY edition or considering addons.
Story Packs
Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep is my pick of the litter. A great narrative and an enjoyable romp with aspirations to poingnant'. Can be a bit irreverent, and if you're 'touchy' about being a PnP gamer, this isn't for you. If you don't mind a bit of genre troping, you're probably in for a treat.
Captain Scarlett and Her Pirate's Booty: Average. Not bad, and an enjoyable shift in tone (arr) but expect much of the same. Plot here is fairly predictable, but it's got a fairly great exploitable treasure tomb, which is enjoyable for shortcutting the worst of the item-hunt grind somewhat before starting a new playthrough.
Mr. Torgue's Campaign of Carnage: Avoid. Trite. Plot twist just shy of completely and totally obvious. Gameplay mechanics include Torgue-brand vending machines that only run on "torguebux", which you will never see outside of the DLC. (Admitted: With orange loot... and prices to match.)
Sir Hammerlock's Big Game Hunt: No recommendation, because I haven't played it. (For folks who like fighting beasts, I'd suspect I know where this one is going.)
Class Packs
Mechromancer Pack: Played the "Ordered Chaos" tree. This one's about stacking Anarchy (less accuracy more damage) with low-clip weapons and then unleashing it with shotguns and SMG spray while balancing reloads. Very much like playing a Hellcat Siren from #1, with robot pet instead of "get out of jail free" card and bullets that ricochet at targets if they miss!
Psycho Pack: Takes a bit to get started, but Krieg is completely and totally lulz once you get down to the bottom of the Mania tree.  (Melee headshots! Melee bonus stacking! Roid shields! Nearly Infinite Axe Rampages! Kill-to-heal gameplay! Take damage to start the rage that heals you and maxes your pecs!)
He's also a metric ton of fun that plays like Brick only wished he had in the first game. Can be annoying if you don't like hearing about nipple salads, but I'll be honest: I almost never noticed, because bathing yourself in the blood of enemies using an axe and half-blind from the gore caking the camera is hilarious fun. I've considered levelling a second one, just for the sheer fun of pushing those rampages just a leeetle further...

Alright, this time I'm going deep. Why? Because this is number 2 on my 'MOST ♥♥♥♥ING BEST GAME LIST'. Like the prequel, this game combines the FPS and RPG genres. That's why this was such a sucessful game.

Let's take this one back to 2010 for a minute. First, they would come up with a (kind of) companion. Claptrap was soon made after. Claptrap is a kind of funny and idiotic robot who always messes up.

Last, the flaws. All right. The most OBVIOUS ONE EVER is the community. I think you know why.

So I bought this game on a whim. I was feeling pretty bad yesterday, and really down. I've been going through a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥lately and I've been hearing all over the place how great this game is that I decided what the hell. It's still on sale on Steam, I might as well get it before it's $10 again.
So I bought the game, booted it up, and started playing it. I did have to uninstall and re-install it to get it working properly, but I finally got it working. I ended up playing it for five hours straight. I'm about halfway through the game right now, and I have to say. If you're having just one of those bad days or you're going through a hard time in your life. Play this game.
The stupid puns made me life. The simple character arcs for each character was surprisingly sweet, and I loved it. The puzzles in this game are very simple, I doubt you'll spend more than ten minutes trying to solve one. The battles themselves (at least the boss battles) are surprisingly challenging too. Each one has it's own rythm and challenge, and if you're going the Pacifist route the game can get pretty challenging. (I highly recommend you go that route first, it's shockingly beautiful.)
It's a ridiculous amount of fun, and honeslty this game helped to pull me out of a rut. Does it deserve all the hype it's getting? Well, if you look at the game as more of just being about a story where you get to know the characters, deal with hilarious situations, and love stupid bad puns. Along with secret ways to get to the "true" happy ending of the game. Then yes. Buy it. I figure you'll probably get at least a good 10-15 hours of gameplay out of this game, and that's a pretty good deal for $10. Not to mention the replay value where you can just play the game to go back and see the story play out all over again. It's that sweet.

The most recent, which has been highly publicized, is the addition of genders. But a player's gender is permanently linked to Steam ID (and that doesn't mean it pulls gender from the Steam profile-- it is random and permanent).
Rust Legacy was great because players had a great many options available to them. The fact that every server had the same map meant that if you encountered hackers or players started harassing you, you could switch servers and starting over wasn't as bad because you already knew where you could pick up a few resources. Facepunch has reliably removed options for players since then, and when features are added, like unique avatars, Facepunch doesn't want to give players any power over it. When development began on the current incarnation of Rust, I thought I'd wait until it was somewhat more complete and start playing again. I tried to pick this game back up several times and each time, I was disappointed by how poorly it runs, how many hackers there are, and the massive map on which I was not only lost, but either very lonely or getting raided constantly.
Facepunch sold this game to me by saying that they valued player feedback and we, the players, would influence the direction the game took. That statement is still on the website for anyone to see. That was clearly a lie.
I have no interest in playing this game anymore, and I've already requested a refund, but I doubt that I'll get one since Facepunch  is obviously trolling its players and if they're willing to do that, why would they give me a refund?

Lets begin this review with a look at Borderlands 1 and how guns worked there.
In Borderlands 1 guns where randomly generated from a selection of parts such as barrels, clips, scopes and whatnot, then they were given a random modifier that effected its stats in some way, they also had a decent chance to have an elemental effect.
This resulted in there literally being millions of guns and the possibility of finding the same gun twice was astronomically small. Even two of the same named guns will be different.
In Borderlands 2 there is not a random selection of parts to attach to guns because all the parts are attached to specific(and much less varied) modifiers so there is never a chance of finding a torgue "juicy hulk" with more than two shots in it.  You may have asked yourself why they said there were "87 bajillion" guns in the game instead of giving an actual number and thats because there are depressingly few gun combinations that exist.  They even restricted one of the major selling points from the first game to pretty much one manufacturer because you will only very rarely find a weapon with an elemental effect unless its a toruge or maliwan.
And you will never find a non jakobs revolver, or a bandit weapon you can throw like a grenade, or a Vladof weapon that gets more accurate as you fire it. It wouldn't have been much more work to not have guns of one manufacturer have any trait they wanted. There could have been 87 BAJILLION MORE, CRAZIER, GUNS. There could have been a whole metagame revolving around finding the right gun, a torgue gun that reloades like a tediore does now, or a Bandit weapon with Hyperion characteristics.
Trying to find an exact replica of a gun in Borderlands 1 was seriously difficult but in Borderlands 2 its so easy to find a gun thats exactly the same as one you already have, to the point where the only difference is the level, I have at least three "juicy hulks". simply because the devs cut down on the randomness, to the point where you can't even get different scopes on weapons anymore because they are directly attached to the modifiers much like the actual parts on the gun.
Now lets talk about loot, the core of a shoot and loot game.
In Borderlands 1 every enemy in the entire game had at least a chance to drop a legendary weapon, every enemy in the game could drop a green quality or above weapon and also drop the weapon THAT THEY WERE USING.  Every enemy in the game had a chance to drop a weapon that was good enough for you to use.
There were also a lot of loot chests everywhere and even the vending machines could even have legendary quality weapons in them. This meant that rather than being a search for a good enough gun, borderlands 1 was more about the search for the perfect gun, that upgrade to your masher revolver or a better shield that regens health quickly.
In contrast is Borderlands 2 where normal enemies can never drop even green quality loot, every single one of them can only drop crappy quality vendor trash. I want you to think about the last time a normal enemy dropped something worth using, seriously think about that for a moment. How many psychos have you shot in the face and only got grenade mods, nothing but grenade mods?(other than face mcshooty he was pretty cool). They even stripped out most of the weapon chests from the game. Let me restate that, in fact I'm going to give it its own paragraph.
They removed loot sources from a "shoot and loot game". Let that sink in for a second. They actually wanted you to get the feeling of opening up a weapon chest and trying out new guns LESS.
Instead the only enemies that can have a chance to drop good loot are badass enemies or bosses which means that your time in borderlands 2 will be spent farming the same enemies or bosses over and over in order to find a decent enough gun to get by with.
Now lets talk about number scaling.
In Borderlands 1 numbers scaled very gradually such that a purple quality two shot masher revolver I found at lv. 12 was good enough for me to carry it through all the way to the end boss of the entire game 18 levels later.  Numbers went up but that weapon you got a couple levels earlier wasn't completely obsolete very quickly.
In Borderlands 2 number scaling is completely out of control, to the point that when I defeated the final boss of the game the legendary quality weapons it dropped did not even last me past the first vending machine in the starting area in True Vault Hunter Mode before I had to replace them because they did less damage than vendor trash, a rocket launcher two levels under in TVHM took more than a full clip to kill a normal enemy which could one shot me into "fight for your life" because I hadn't replaced my shield THAT LEVEL
Now lets talk about mechanics because those are fairly important as well. Take the badass rank system, it sounds cool, infinite improvement to whatever stats you like. In practice however its locked in so that you can only improve stats marginally because of serious diminishing returns and the system is rigged so you have no choices in it. Don't believe me? try putting all your points into weapon damage, just try. You CAN'T the system is designed to give you the illusion of choice without actually giving you any at all. the boosts are also really pathetic and nothing compared to weapon mastery in BL1 where you naturally get better with a gun the more you use it.
Lets look at ammo, in theory the game doesn't give you ammo you need so you'll use different weapons. In practice never getting ammo you need means you are forced to use different guns and most ammo drops are wastes of time. In Bl1 it will give you ammo you need.
Now lets talk about the still broken UI. I actually had four or five legendary guns in borderlands 2, but I don't have any of them anymore do you want to know why? The selling UI is easy to glitch up so that it sells the top item in your inventory... where the high quality guns are organized into. Its been almost two years now and they still haven't fixed that. I want you to try to listen to old audio logs like you could in BL1, you can't. I want you to try and use the UI without using an xbox controller, its clunky and horrible.
So in summary Borderlands 2 is like Borderlands 1 with better writing and massively stripped features, less gun variety, and less guns in general, less loot and more grinding the same boss over and over to find a half decent gun.
When I say I'm dissapointed in Borderlands 2 I'm not saying I'm dissapointed in the story(which is quite good) or the characters(which are undoubtably better than 1) or the gunplay(which the skill trees have seriously improved upon from the first game).  I'm dissapointed in the guns, I remember reading an article prior to the release of Borderlands 1 where they had a revolver that shot fire and used shotgun shells as ammo and whenever I look at Borderlands 2 I ask myself "What happened to that game? What happened to revolvers that fired like shotguns? What happened to shotguns with the flavor text 'Holy crap! it shoots rockets!'?"
Because I wanted Borderlands 2 to just drop all the restrictions, use that bigger budget to bury me in shotgun pistols and rocket shotguns which explode into electric grenades. I wanted borderlands 2 to be the game filled with the constant discovery of more and more absurd guns.
And then I reilze that Borderlands 2 was designed to be a flasher game with kickass reloading animations and ♥♥♥♥♥ier guns. Borderlands 2 favored more consistant easily balenceable guns over actual variety in the guns. Borderlands 2 is the big budget sequel to Borderlands 1 which was a game the developers didn't think would be popular so they tried making it fun instead. And what we're left with is Borderlands 2 a game thats prettier and better written but less fun, less varied, less random and above all less of a "shoot and loot" game that it tells us it is.

Definition of Overhyped : "make exaggerated claims about (a product, idea, or event); publicize or promote excessively." (by...google ? it's also an online dictionary now ? nice.)
This game might be overhyped. That's what fandoms do, overhyping the things they love. However, it doesn't mean the game is bad, just that it might not be as flawless as the average player says.
It has flaws, but it definitely takes you in a journey. You begin the game with the image of the character you will play during the whole game, which seems to be lying on some flowers, eyes closed and  inert. So you wait for something to happen, some kind of cutscene or an animation showing you the character you're observing waking up, opening its eyes or at least start to move a bit. But nothing. You can even stay a whole fifteen seconds if you're patient, but it won't do anything because the character is already awake and is actually standing on the flowers. It's waiting for you to make a move but you couldn't tell since the graphics don't have a coherent perspective. You might be confused on some of the designs you will see in game.
This start is the slowest bit in the whole game, and it's very likely done on purpose. There is no music, the background is just black and if you've been cautious you don't really know what to expect. So you move quickly to the next room and start what seems to be the tutorial. And then the game shatters your expectations for the second time in approximately a minute of gameplay. The whole game is like this, using the player's misinterpretations to surprise him and make the story go in ways no one could have possibly foreseen.
After this first tutorial, you remember what your first buddy told you in it and start applying it, thus changing your perception of the environment around you. Then you enter another longer tutorial with another buddy that learns you completely different things. Naturally, you will trust the character you first met and keep applying his words to the world that surrounds you, until you leave the second tutorial, while interrogating yourself on the "truth" of this game. "Have I done well this far ? Should I try another way ?" Either you erase your game to play a completely different way or you keep going to see what happens next.

No matter what choices you make, the game will remember them and let you know that everytime it can, while still shattering every base knowledge you thought having about it.
It starts with a silent stare at a lifeless pixelated character in a bland background and ends with the feeling it's actually the game that plays with you.

I'm not even kidding. My first paycheck will go for paying for the soundtrack and such.
Actual details of the game though:
Amazing soundtrack, tailored for each area or situation.
While the sprites are obviously meant to emulate retro games and so are fairly low-quality or pixelated, the sprites and faces and animations represent each of the characters very well. I was surprised how expressive the characters were.
The atmosphere for a given area is very strong, and changes based around the player's choices.
The game explores a lot of deeper subjects such as genocide, pacifism, redemption, antisocial personality disorder, depression, murder and mercy, companionship, etc. It's pretty intelligent for a game that will also change mood on a dime to tell a fart joke.
The characters are complex and fun... or not, depending on how you treat them and their friends.
It's minority-friendly, without taking itself too seriously either.
It has a lot of dogs.
...A lot of dogs.
The characters feel like they have agency in the story by doing things that normally only players can do, such as breaking off a relationship, saving and reloading, etc.
Overall a strong deconstruction of RPG's that likes to break the fourth wall, and has the full range of atmospheres from hilarious, creepy, to epic. If you want a good laugh, or the opportunity to think about some subjects from a different angle, or just murder lots of things, this game has what you want.

Attention Deficit version: An excellent game that is essentially an FPS with some RPG elements. (Your recommendation is 1,402 characters too long. Please shorten it and try again.)!
...and now, a few brief caveats and addenda.
This is very much like "World of Warcraft" or "Diablo" but handles like an FPS with some very minor RPG elements.
The narrative isn't bad, however, the implementation is lacking in one way - I frequently had voiceovers trample previous ones, sometimes leading to narration that wasn't (to me) immediately important being squelched by a later one.
It can feel grindy, because, well - it is. See which games I referenced in #1? There are more sidequests and awards in the game than are needed to level, (even discounting challenge and exploration rewards or hidden sidequests) which will mean you will outlevel content regularly if you're a "do everything in the zone" sort.
It does mean you can often get by with (very) subpar FPS skills, and you can choose to retain or build up the challenge by tackling main quest missions and sidequests when they are at or above your current level. I recommend paying attention to the levels of quests and choose more enjoyable carnage.
Poor placement of RPG choices is a very minor issue for novices to the RPG genre, as the central locations have "respec" machines that can reset both skills and appearance for a nominal fee - often much less than dying, which has a somewhat less nominal monetary penalty.
Overall, an improvement on the first one. the acting can be a bit hammy and the references and tropes are pretty thick on the ground, but frankly, if you're still here, you're here to shoot things and take their stuff. This, you will find in Borderlands 2.
DLC deserves a mention for those of you considering the GotY edition or considering addons.
Story Packs
Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep is my pick of the litter. A great narrative and an enjoyable romp with aspirations to poingnant'. Can be a bit irreverent, and if you're 'touchy' about being a PnP gamer, this isn't for you. If you don't mind a bit of genre troping, you're probably in for a treat.
Captain Scarlett and Her Pirate's Booty: Average. Not bad, and an enjoyable shift in tone (arr) but expect much of the same. Plot here is fairly predictable, but it's got a fairly great exploitable treasure tomb, which is enjoyable for shortcutting the worst of the item-hunt grind somewhat before starting a new playthrough.
Mr. Torgue's Campaign of Carnage: Avoid. Trite. Plot twist just shy of completely and totally obvious. Gameplay mechanics include Torgue-brand vending machines that only run on "torguebux", which you will never see outside of the DLC. (Admitted: With orange loot... and prices to match.)
Sir Hammerlock's Big Game Hunt: No recommendation, because I haven't played it. (For folks who like fighting beasts, I'd suspect I know where this one is going.)
Class Packs
Mechromancer Pack: Played the "Ordered Chaos" tree. This one's about stacking Anarchy (less accuracy more damage) with low-clip weapons and then unleashing it with shotguns and SMG spray while balancing reloads. Very much like playing a Hellcat Siren from #1, with robot pet instead of "get out of jail free" card and bullets that ricochet at targets if they miss!
Psycho Pack: Takes a bit to get started, but Krieg is completely and totally lulz once you get down to the bottom of the Mania tree.  (Melee headshots! Melee bonus stacking! Roid shields! Nearly Infinite Axe Rampages! Kill-to-heal gameplay! Take damage to start the rage that heals you and maxes your pecs!)
He's also a metric ton of fun that plays like Brick only wished he had in the first game. Can be annoying if you don't like hearing about nipple salads, but I'll be honest: I almost never noticed, because bathing yourself in the blood of enemies using an axe and half-blind from the gore caking the camera is hilarious fun. I've considered levelling a second one, just for the sheer fun of pushing those rampages just a leeetle further...

This is a game like many other survivor pvp games. You start with nothing and have to gather materials to make a base. The combat is decent, definitely has room to grow in terms of controls, hit reg, and balancing. You can make a decent base with the materials you gather in the world, as well as hunt to feed yourself, if you manage to live long enough. For higher leveled tools/weapons/armour you need to gather what are called blueprints to reveal the crafting recipe.
Here are the problems: You start with only a rock and a torch, the torch may as well be useless, the light is too low to be useful and you don't exactly want people to know where you are. There are many servers to play on, you DO NOT want to play on a populated server, you WILL DIE many times. People will not hesitate to gun you down, repeatedly. I have not had a situation where I saw someone with a gun, not kill someone, and 90% of the time, they know they get nothing from it. Players will camp the sites where blueprints spawn with the best gear, kill on the beaches where you spawn most of the time. The way the game sets it up requires you to play at the very start of a server, after the wipe, or have a clan. You cannot be successful on your own on a server with more than 50 people.
Do not expect a single person to help you. Even if you ask in the chat, in the many servers I asked new player questions to see the responses, most of the top players of the servers would rather insult and flame the new players, rather than help someone in the slightest way. The community has no dignity, they will kill you, trust means nothing, no one owes you anything for anything you do.
Developers if you are reading this your game needs to have something you can earn, preferrably crafting recipes, rather than having all comodities be able to be camped, hoarded and trolled. As well as guns are far too common, it simply makes it easier for people who know what they are doing to kill new players. This puts off anyone who has a small interest in the game, and for those who have higher interests in the game follow suit when they finally get a gun.

Definition of Overhyped : "make exaggerated claims about (a product, idea, or event); publicize or promote excessively." (by...google ? it's also an online dictionary now ? nice.)
This game might be overhyped. That's what fandoms do, overhyping the things they love. However, it doesn't mean the game is bad, just that it might not be as flawless as the average player says.
It has flaws, but it definitely takes you in a journey. You begin the game with the image of the character you will play during the whole game, which seems to be lying on some flowers, eyes closed and  inert. So you wait for something to happen, some kind of cutscene or an animation showing you the character you're observing waking up, opening its eyes or at least start to move a bit. But nothing. You can even stay a whole fifteen seconds if you're patient, but it won't do anything because the character is already awake and is actually standing on the flowers. It's waiting for you to make a move but you couldn't tell since the graphics don't have a coherent perspective. You might be confused on some of the designs you will see in game.
This start is the slowest bit in the whole game, and it's very likely done on purpose. There is no music, the background is just black and if you've been cautious you don't really know what to expect. So you move quickly to the next room and start what seems to be the tutorial. And then the game shatters your expectations for the second time in approximately a minute of gameplay. The whole game is like this, using the player's misinterpretations to surprise him and make the story go in ways no one could have possibly foreseen.
After this first tutorial, you remember what your first buddy told you in it and start applying it, thus changing your perception of the environment around you. Then you enter another longer tutorial with another buddy that learns you completely different things. Naturally, you will trust the character you first met and keep applying his words to the world that surrounds you, until you leave the second tutorial, while interrogating yourself on the "truth" of this game. "Have I done well this far ? Should I try another way ?" Either you erase your game to play a completely different way or you keep going to see what happens next.

No matter what choices you make, the game will remember them and let you know that everytime it can, while still shattering every base knowledge you thought having about it.
It starts with a silent stare at a lifeless pixelated character in a bland background and ends with the feeling it's actually the game that plays with you.

I'm not even kidding. My first paycheck will go for paying for the soundtrack and such.
Actual details of the game though:
Amazing soundtrack, tailored for each area or situation.
While the sprites are obviously meant to emulate retro games and so are fairly low-quality or pixelated, the sprites and faces and animations represent each of the characters very well. I was surprised how expressive the characters were.
The atmosphere for a given area is very strong, and changes based around the player's choices.
The game explores a lot of deeper subjects such as genocide, pacifism, redemption, antisocial personality disorder, depression, murder and mercy, companionship, etc. It's pretty intelligent for a game that will also change mood on a dime to tell a fart joke.
The characters are complex and fun... or not, depending on how you treat them and their friends.
It's minority-friendly, without taking itself too seriously either.
It has a lot of dogs.
...A lot of dogs.
The characters feel like they have agency in the story by doing things that normally only players can do, such as breaking off a relationship, saving and reloading, etc.
Overall a strong deconstruction of RPG's that likes to break the fourth wall, and has the full range of atmospheres from hilarious, creepy, to epic. If you want a good laugh, or the opportunity to think about some subjects from a different angle, or just murder lots of things, this game has what you want.

I've played through this game 3 times in the past week, completing the three significantly different endings that I am aware of at this time.  I have made every attempt to follow the lore and keep tabs on characters between playthroughs.  I take these things very seriously, and the game is incredibly rich in handing them to you.
I now have more unanswered questions than I started with, and that's incredible.
Undertale is a fantastic game by all the typical standards--the fighting system is intuitive in a brilliant way; the music (OH MY GOD THE MUSIC!) is phenomenal; the graphics are appropriate and they give an incredible emotion to the characters, and the writing is otherworldy.
Buy this game if you like unique games.
Buy this game if you like good soundtracks, good characters.
Buy this game if you like puzzle games, platformers, RPGs.
Buy this game if you hate RPGs, because it manages to be a fantastic criticism of the genre.
Just buy this game.
There are lively forums of intelligent conversation about this game's secrets (to illustrate--it's 2 AM and I have a class in 6 hours, but I'm still up reading forums trying to understand the fabulous depth of this game's secrets).
Also, for those feeling up for a little bit of murder in the digital realm, the game's kill-everything "genocide" run has the absolute best boss battle of any game I have ever played.
This is an incredible game.  It has a skeleton you can date, characters named after fonts, meaningful NPC interactions, dogs you can pet, one of the smartest combat systems I have ever seen in a game, and music I have already spent hours listening to (not to mention remixes, Sythesia tutorials, medleys, and so on).
There's no better way to say it than this:
If you like good games--if you're okay with an occasional quirk because it is more than made up for, get Undertale.  Play it, play it again, then play it again, and when you find yourself in my shoes--trying to get your point across on the reviews page fast enough for you to read a few more threads about what a fun value is, or the meaning of Entry 17 in the True Lab, or why that "DTE machine" means and why it's relevant--when you find yourself here, you'll know you've made the right choice.

Theres been times ive doubted Dayz, times ive hated it, times ive wished i didnt drop so much time into it, Yet i always come back to it. This is a First-person loot-centric post-apocalyptic shooting action game. Most character progression relies on passive stat boosts. It's got several proceedurally generated wacky, eccentric guns. Ultimately, the game is all about the guns.
Borderlands 2 is basically Borderlands 1 with a new spinoff story and more everything. If you have not played Borderlands 1, you'll be be fine starting with this one. If you have played Borderlands 1, your opinion of Borderlands 2 will probably be near identical.
Best played with 3 friends on multiplayer in a group.
Pros: Some dark and crass humor, much more colorful than Borderlands 1 (Yes, there's more than orange and brown in this one!),  really neat and weird weapons to play with, and lots of shiny bright glowy stuffs that are cool to look at. Great for goofing off with friends. The game is (somewhat) playable on minimum settings on lower end hardware.
Cons: Over-the-top graphic violence. Character progression is largely passive, and thus doesn't always feel very rewarding outside of milestones that change the way characters work. Repetitive.

By now anyone who has already heard of Undertale probably has a good idea of its main draw; you don't have to kill anyone. In fact, it is also likely that many people considering if they should play Undertale may have seen or heard spoilers regarding the plot, and characters.
Nothing you have read, heard, or seen, does it justice.
I went into it 'eyes open' and expected a fun, funny, sweet game. Well, I got it... and still cried like a baby at the end. The more emotionally invested I became with the characters, the more their struggles felt real to me. Soon I was playing in order to save them, not just to 'finish the game'. I will avoid giving any details (in case you have not had the game spoiled). I will end by reccomending it to EVERYONE.
Much like life, you will get out of it what you put in. Stay Determined!

Before I start, I have to say that I have NEVER written a review for ANY game before. Never thought any games were good enough for me to take my time and review them. Undertale, on the other hand, isn't any game.
This isn't going to be a 4 paragraph review explaining why this game is superior to others or anything like that, because, ultimately, all games are equal; and whether a game is good or not is whether you enjoy playing it or not.
I enjoy this game. My life is pretty boring... but... this game brought excitment to my life... vicarously...
Yes, that was an undertale reference shshhh.
The game is mostly played for the story. Some people will disagree, but I think the majority will agree. This is the best story I've seen in a game for a LONG time. I'll admit, if it was longer, there could've been more character development, and character relationships could've been even stronger.. nonetheless though, I found myself caring about these 8-bit characters that I barely knew, and laughing when they made jokes, even if I didnt find them funny at all.
Let me clarify... I REALLY cared about these characters. When they smiled, I smiled. When they showed signs of sadness, I felt sadness; and, the true ending made me cry, which says something (especially if you know what happens at the true ending), because I almost NEVER cry for video games.
The gameplay IS fun though. It is an rpg style game where you click the "fight" button and then try to hit the marker on the center as accurately as you can. If you don't end up destroying them in one hit, your SOUL, the very culmination of your being (Thanks Flowey!), appears, and you have to dodge a series of magic attacks using the arrow keys. It can get hard, trust me.
But, wait.. Why would you just go around killing everything? You monster... Why not just talk to them instead, and in the long run, spare them? In this game, you can kill monsters, or you can interact with them to get them out of the fighting mood, and spare them. Whether you flirt with them, or lie on the ground and think about life, there is a multitude of ways to spare monsters and ultimately befriend them. Sparing all monsters will give you one ending, the true ending. Killing every single monster in the game will give you another ending. Lastly, killing one or two monsters and sparing the rest will give you the neutral ending.
Here is the order of endings I highly recommend. Neutral -> Pacifist/True -> Genocide.
I wont keep dragging on, because, as you can see, this ended up being a 4 paragraph review.

By now anyone who has already heard of Undertale probably has a good idea of its main draw; you don't have to kill anyone. In fact, it is also likely that many people considering if they should play Undertale may have seen or heard spoilers regarding the plot, and characters.

Before I start, I have to say that I have NEVER written a review for ANY game before. Never thought any games were good enough for me to take my time and review them. Undertale, on the other hand, isn't any game.
This isn't going to be a 4 paragraph review explaining why this game is superior to others or anything like that, because, ultimately, all games are equal; and whether a game is good or not is whether you enjoy playing it or not.
I enjoy this game. My life is pretty boring... but... this game brought excitment to my life... vicarously...
Yes, that was an undertale reference shshhh.
The game is mostly played for the story. Some people will disagree, but I think the majority will agree. This is the best story I've seen in a game for a LONG time. I'll admit, if it was longer, there could've been more character development, and character relationships could've been even stronger.. nonetheless though, I found myself caring about these 8-bit characters that I barely knew, and laughing when they made jokes, even if I didnt find them funny at all.
Let me clarify... I REALLY cared about these characters. When they smiled, I smiled. When they showed signs of sadness, I felt sadness; and, the true ending made me cry, which says something (especially if you know what happens at the true ending), because I almost NEVER cry for video games.
The gameplay IS fun though. It is an rpg style game where you click the "fight" button and then try to hit the marker on the center as accurately as you can. If you don't end up destroying them in one hit, your SOUL, the very culmination of your being (Thanks Flowey!), appears, and you have to dodge a series of magic attacks using the arrow keys. It can get hard, trust me.
But, wait.. Why would you just go around killing everything? You monster... Why not just talk to them instead, and in the long run, spare them? In this game, you can kill monsters, or you can interact with them to get them out of the fighting mood, and spare them. Whether you flirt with them, or lie on the ground and think about life, there is a multitude of ways to spare monsters and ultimately befriend them. Sparing all monsters will give you one ending, the true ending. Killing every single monster in the game will give you another ending. Lastly, killing one or two monsters and sparing the rest will give you the neutral ending.
Here is the order of endings I highly recommend. Neutral -> Pacifist/True -> Genocide.
I wont keep dragging on, because, as you can see, this ended up being a 4 paragraph review.
Instead I will leave you distracted with this spaghetti! Nyeh heh heh heh heh heh!

Day-Z has its moments but for the most part, you'll be running around the outskirts of the map looking for supplies to make the agonzingly boring jog into the military bases where the "good" gear is.  I understand that it's very early on as far as development goes which is why I still play it from time to time, but it can range from supremely fun (rarely) to incredibly boring.  I am not really a devoted gamer but here is the average timeline for a bout in Day-Z for me:
Spawn. 2 minutes later my character is hungry, thirsty, wet/cold (if it is raining).  If you chose a server that has been active for a while, you're going to be hard pressed to find anything that will keep you alive.  If you can find food/drinks/clothing, you will quickly run out of space.  Or, you'll have tons of food but no can opener.  Or, you try to swap the pants you start with for cargo pants so you can carry more stuff, and everything you're carrying glitches away (this part doesn't really upset me-the game is under development so I assume things like that will be fixed if a final version is released).  Next, I spend 40 minutes running around the outskirts as my character slowly starves or dehydrates to death.  I don't know how many times I've died from dehydration or  I've had plenty of "fun" gear-guns, ammo, etc. but it's more than enough for me to definitively say this to the developers who will never read this: THE ENVIRONMENT NEEDS MORE SUPPLIES.  I understand it is about survival and realism, but it shouldn't be that you have to search 10 houses only to find 1 item, which most of the time is a useless bandana or broken flashlight.  If you want to have any players who aren't willing to spend 7 hours in a row playing, the first 4 hours of which they die 6 times from hypothermia, there just needs to be more supplies.
All in all, I like the game for its potential.  I plan on sticking with it until (if) it is fully developed.  My current hardware isn't  as robust as it should be to support the game but that's my fault not the developers.  However if it reaches full development and is still this ridiculously frustrating, I don't think I'll ever play again.  In-game, I recommend choosing a server that is new as opposed to one that has been open for a while- it's much easier to find stuff and stay alive longer.  I am a fan of open world games and games that take some time and commitment, but this is ridiculous.  Happy gaming.

Its a great game, and in almost every measurable way, it is on paper better than BL1, more missions, more weapons, more loot, more skills, more items, more everything... I can't help but feel a little bit tho that while in every measurable way it is better, there is some immeasurable thing that just seems like got left on the cutting room floor.
The weapons are bigger and badder with more effects, and fancier splosions and all... but they don't seem as randomized, which means pretty much theres just much less to 'aim' for.  Theres great pre-burned weapons, but they are all going to be almost identical. So, Undertale... It was indeed an experience, one way or another. While I had some pretty hair-pulling moments in the game, in the end I found the experience to be worth the investment in money and time.
I tried to avoid the buzz around this game as much as I could (to no avail), which did indeed color my expectation of the game I must admit. I have zero interest in the community, but the whole internet kept spamming "DONT DO X AND DO Y", which really, really annoyed me and controlled the way I experienced the game. However, I usually go for specific runs at first on games where that is possible (and indeed changes the experience, such as Fallout NV).
How to explain what Undertale is in few sentences? Well, that's a bit hard (IMHO), but comparisons to Mother series (ie. EarthBound) is well justified. SNES graphics, combined to the surreal world building and good atmosphere do wonders.
So, lets start with the bad; pacing seems to be a bit off. While I found the beginning interesting, it was followed by very long section of boredom, in association broken by few character interractions. The second problem is more "your mileage may vary" -situation; the bullet hell sections. You most likely have heard about this, if you know anything about Undertale. Primary form of action in the game manifests itself through bullet hell sections, broken between "turns" (your action, enemy action). As a person who has never, EVER been good at these things outside Ikaruga, my  experience of most battles was pretty dismal. Normal battles where just a chore, while several boss battles are ridiculously hard due to the way that the game in certain form expects you to play it.
Enough of the bad things.
This was one of the few games in years, where I didnt skip dialogue. It is well constructed, succinct and spot-on most of the times. While someone may complain certain childhish nature of the humorous parts (tons of terrible puns), they do fit the characters relatively well IMHO. Speaking of characters, this game has several easily memorable ones. While one of the final bosses was less spectacular than expected, the stories behind the characters and your interactions with them do bring out a lot of depth that any triple-A publisher would shiver to show. I was pleasantly surprised to find so many re-occurring characters, as well as few "I see what you did earlier" -moments. The soundtrack is absolutely fantastic and does bring the atmosphere up several points.
Integration of the game mechanics into the UI was jarring at first, but I got used to it very fast. I dont think I've ever seen such an interesting way of potraying the player (ie. you) in a certain "god" form, which the game itself would acknowledge. UI molds to the scenario according to its needs, rather than boxed into easy and comfortable checklist of mechanics and UI designs. Sometimes this does bring few minor annoyances, but to be honest, I cant even remember which ones, so I suppose they weren't big deals in the end.
While I dont consider Undetale to be the next messiah as many seem to, I did found it to be enjoyable experience with some very interesting ideas. I'll probably never forget Undertale, one way or another.

Day-Z has its moments but for the most part, you'll be running around the outskirts of the map looking for supplies to make the agonzingly boring jog into the military bases where the "good" gear is.  I understand that it's very early on as far as development goes which is why I still play it from time to time, but it can range from supremely fun (rarely) to incredibly boring.  I am not really a devoted gamer but here is the average timeline for a bout in Day-Z for me:
Spawn. 2 minutes later my character is hungry, thirsty, wet/cold (if it is raining).  If you chose a server that has been active for a while, you're going to be hard pressed to find anything that will keep you alive.  If you can find food/drinks/clothing, you will quickly run out of space.  Or, you'll have tons of food but no can opener.  Or, you try to swap the pants you start with for cargo pants so you can carry more stuff, and everything you're carrying glitches away (this part doesn't really upset me-the game is under development so I assume things like that will be fixed if a final version is released).  Next, I spend 40 minutes running around the outskirts as my character slowly starves or dehydrates to death.  I don't know how many times I've died from dehydration or  I've had plenty of "fun" gear-guns, ammo, etc. but it's more than enough for me to definitively say this to the developers who will never read this: THE ENVIRONMENT NEEDS MORE SUPPLIES.  I understand it is about survival and realism, but it shouldn't be that you have to search 10 houses only to find 1 item, which most of the time is a useless bandana or broken flashlight.  If you want to have any players who aren't willing to spend 7 hours in a row playing, the first 4 hours of which they die 6 times from hypothermia, there just needs to be more supplies.
All in all, I like the game for its potential.  I plan on sticking with it until (if) it is fully developed.  My current hardware isn't  as robust as it should be to support the game but that's my fault not the developers.  However if it reaches full development and is still this ridiculously frustrating, I don't think I'll ever play again.  In-game, I recommend choosing a server that is new as opposed to one that has been open for a while- it's much easier to find stuff and stay alive longer.  I am a fan of open world games and games that take some time and commitment, but this is ridiculous.  Happy gaming.

An incredibly flawed masterpiece, trading what made the series so unique and fun for a much more fleshed out and expansive story, and gorgeous visuals. A sequel in many ways superior and at the same time inferior to it's predecessor. Why?
GUNS, GUNS, GUNS.
What kept the game going in the first installment was how unique, variable and fair the loot system ways. Stinkers still dropped that you would only pick up to sell, but most other times, you picked up a really nice weapon that had good stats that made you want to use it, at least for a little. Legendaries often popped up from crates and even vendors, yet weren't dominant over purple loot, the strongest non-Orange/Pearlescent kinds of weapons.
Scaling wasn't a huge deal. Enemies went down how they should. The only real bullet sponges were Badasses and bosses, and that makes sense. Weapons you picked up weren't immediately inferior at the next level you reach.
In Borderlands 2, the manufacturer gimmicks and limitation of parts actually makes the gun variety worse off. Some guns actually suffer immensely from the gimmicks (Bandit, Hyperion, Dahl for example). There's no room for hybrid guns. Guns you pick up are immediately inferior once you go up a level. Normal old bandits are bullet sponges and can sometimes take multiple mags to kill. Legendaries almost NEVER appear. Bosses rarely drop them, enemies rarely drop them, and shops almost never have them. Purples are actually inferior to blues most of the time.
Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode is garbage.
I could go on and on and on, but these are enough points. Don't buy Borderlands 2 expecting more Borderlands. Play it as if it's an entirely different franchise.

This game could be great but it has a HUGE barrier to entry. Basically, if you need to read reviews to find out if this game is for you, it isn't. It likely means you don't have a group of friends that play it and you aren't playing it already.
I know it's a survival game, and that you have to expect to die, a lot. The issue is the massive imbalance inherent in this particular game.
To give you an idea:
In the 12 hours I have played, I was killed about 4 times. In the 3 hours I played before being killed, I ran around and hid, chopped down trees in the night, tried to find rocks and animals, finally built a rudimentary shelter. Put down a sleeping bag. Walked out of my "base" and was shot. That person then destroyed my sleeping bag (spawn point), took everything I had, then camped there for when I came back and kept killing me. I had a wooden axe on me and this person had an automatic rifle.
I was working towards the "having fun" part of the game where I would get to try and craft neat items and figure out how the game worked... but it was near impossible to get there.  I certainly am not going to continue to play the same part of the game over and over until, by chance, the 100 players that are 74 levels higher than me decide not to kill me. Everyone that wasn't naked that I ran into, killed me instantly... along with any other new player near me.
This isn't just one single case, it  happened 4 different times on 3 different servers. People chatting in game say the same thing and experienced players say "stop crying", "learn the hard way" etc... So, if you have a bunch of buddies that play the game, it is probably a lot of fun. For me, it ended up being basically a Call of Duty sniping clone, or a schoolyard bully simulator.
Until the devs put in some type of mechanic to allow the new players to advance, don't expect the community to give you a good game experience. Which is unfortunate because you would think that smart experienced players would realize that only by nurturing new players will the game make money and be able to grow.

So, Undertale... It was indeed an experience, one way or another. While I had some pretty hair-pulling moments in the game, in the end I found the experience to be worth the investment in money and time.
I tried to avoid the buzz around this game as much as I could (to no avail), which did indeed color my expectation of the game I must admit. I have zero interest in the community, but the whole internet kept spamming "DONT DO X AND DO Y", which really, really annoyed me and controlled the way I experienced the game. However, I usually go for specific runs at first on games where that is possible (and indeed changes the experience, such as Fallout NV).
How to explain what Undertale is in few sentences? Well, that's a bit hard (IMHO), but comparisons to Mother series (ie. EarthBound) is well justified. SNES graphics, combined to the surreal world building and good atmosphere do wonders.
So, lets start with the bad; pacing seems to be a bit off. While I found the beginning interesting, it was followed by very long section of boredom, in association broken by few character interractions. The second problem is more "your mileage may vary" -situation; the bullet hell sections. You most likely have heard about this, if you know anything about Undertale. Primary form of action in the game manifests itself through bullet hell sections, broken between "turns" (your action, enemy action). As a person who has never, EVER been good at these things outside Ikaruga, my  experience of most battles was pretty dismal. Normal battles where just a chore, while several boss battles are ridiculously hard due to the way that the game in certain form expects you to play it.
Enough of the bad things.
This was one of the few games in years, where I didnt skip dialogue. It is well constructed, succinct and spot-on most of the times. While someone may complain certain childhish nature of the humorous parts (tons of terrible puns), they do fit the characters relatively well IMHO. Speaking of characters, this game has several easily memorable ones. While one of the final bosses was less spectacular than expected, the stories behind the characters and your interactions with them do bring out a lot of depth that any triple-A publisher would shiver to show. I was pleasantly surprised to find so many re-occurring characters, as well as few "I see what you did earlier" -moments. The soundtrack is absolutely fantastic and does bring the atmosphere up several points.
Integration of the game mechanics into the UI was jarring at first, but I got used to it very fast. I dont think I've ever seen such an interesting way of potraying the player (ie. you) in a certain "god" form, which the game itself would acknowledge. UI molds to the scenario according to its needs, rather than boxed into easy and comfortable checklist of mechanics and UI designs. Sometimes this does bring few minor annoyances, but to be honest, I cant even remember which ones, so I suppose they weren't big deals in the end.
While I dont consider Undetale to be the next messiah as many seem to, I did found it to be enjoyable experience with some very interesting ideas. I'll probably never forget Undertale, one way or another.

Gameplay : Particular RPG where you can spare monsters, that aspect alone was interesting. I quite liked how you can dodge attacks while trapped in your box, it's really fun and challenging at times!
Soundtrack : Very beautiful soundtrack, a lot of great themes.
Design : Not going to lie, the first time I opened the game, I though "what the hell is this" and closed it. Though, after playing it, the design fits the mood REALLY well and the world is beautiful.
Characters : Another big part of the game, the characters are all unique and you grow to like all of them. They're all goofy in their own way, I found myself laughing almost at every interaction. I felt so conflicted at the end of the True Pacifist ending when I had to save someone, I thought I could only save one.
Overall this game goes into my GOTY list. If you're a fan of RPGs with humor and a very interesting twist, make yourself a favor and buy and play this game.

For the longest time I avoided Undertale like the plague, after the game being strongly praised for its optional pacifist route, winning GameFAQs' Greatest Game of All Time popularity contest despite only being out for a few months, and being compared to the MOTHER series, which is one of my favorite JRPG series, I was all but convinced that the game was nothing more than a fad. "It's just the latest craze in retro-style throwback gaming and yet another homage to EarthBound which will assuredly overdo it with the humor/pop-cultural references and just come off feeling like a soulless clone, and surely the whole Pacifist Route will amount to little more than the game's designer pimping his own agenda and hamfistedly preaching at the audience for the entirety of the game." I thought.
However, one day while I was bored I watched one of my favorite Youtubers do a blind playthrough of it, and my opinion of the game slowly changed as I watched. Upon watching him do a complete playthrough and playing it like a standard JRPG and killing every monster in his path, I saw that the game wasn't preaching at all, nor was it pushing some slanted agenda, and much to my surprise, the game actually did strongly remind me of the MOTHER series. So I went to Steam and bought a copy of the game for myself, eager to experience it.
I have since done a full playthrough of both the "Neutral Pacifist" & "True Pacifist" routes in which I killed no monsters, befriended as many monsters as I could, and generally tried to do what I felt was the right thing in every given situation according to my own moral compass. The playthrough lasted me approximately 12.1 hours according to Steam, which is quite a substantial amount of content for a game of its price, and I have only experienced roughly half of what this game has to offer.
Going in, I honestly didn't expect to enjoy an RPG in which you're encouraged not to fight, seeing as the fighting typically makes up much of the RPG experience, but upon playing the game for myself, I must admit that talking my way out of confrontations was overall a fresh and satisfactory experience which I'm not used to being in anything but WRPGs, and while Undertale is technically "Western" in origin, it was clearly inspired by classic Japanese RPGs, so I just didn't expect it to handle the concept of pacifism as well as WRPGs.
I expected a shallow, idealistic representation of pacifism which even Ghandi would think went too far and served no purpose but to pretentiously preach the developer's beliefs to the audience, but on the contrary, Undertale approaches the concept in a much more balanced manner by presenting the player with "enemies" who don't really want to hurt the player, but are doing so out of desperation by the order of their King whom is just trying to free his people, and said enemies will usually surrender after taking a certain amount of damage. Furthermore, some of the characters even acknowledge that it is a natural response to defend yourself from attackers with violence, and only really judge/condemn you for killing a foe who has surrendered rather than spreading the message that fighting back is always wrong, regardless of the circumstances.
Now before I start to sound too much like your garden variety gushing fan, I will say that Undertale is by no means perfect. It does a lot of things right and is highly entertaining as well as heartwarming, but there were a few things that I didn't like. Namely, and bear with me here, the seemingly forced homosexual relationship between two of the characters. Now before you get mad or start thinking that I'm a bigot, allow me to explain that I have nothing against homosexuality. However, I do have something against game developers putting in homosexual characters into their games for the mere sake of having homosexual characters, (it strikes me as disrespectful and disingenuous, like more of a sales gimmick meant to appeal to a wider demographic than a passionate effort to denounce discrimination by showing support for alternative lifestyles) and I sort of feel like that was done here. I won't name the characters because I don't want to spoil anything, but the two are completely incompatible, never exchange any on-screen dialog, hint towards being anything more than casual acquaintances, nor even appear in the same space together prior to a specific event which doesn't even occur during the first playthrough, and both either appear to or are otherwise explicitly stated to have a crush on another character of the opposite sex, so their whole relationship just sort of comes out of nowhere with absolutely no build-up, as though Toby Foxy shoehorned in a homosexual romance between them just for the sake of having one. I dunno, maybe I'm wrong and Toby Fox had this planned from the start but just didn't draw direct attention to either character's sexuality until late in the game because he didn't want it to be a defining characteristic of either character, which would be commendable, but I'm really not sure so I can only call it as I saw it, and to me it seemed forced, especially when no heterosexual characters have a romance subplot/sidequest. At the very least, it could have and should have been handled much better or otherwise been completely omitted.
That gripe aside, my overall experience with Undertale was a very positive one, and while I'd love to write out everything I like about the game in detail, this review has already dragged on long enough, so I'm just going to sum it all up with a simple list of PROs and CONs.
PROs:
+ Great story
+ Charming cast of characters
+ Fantastic soundtrack
+ Unique combat system (Standard turn-based combat meets Quick Time Events and a Bullet Hell-style dodging system)
+ Humorous dialog
+ Interesting spritework/character designs
+ Emotionally driven plot
+ Pacifist option with no preaching or pushing of agendas
CONs:
- Aforementioned homosexual romance feels forced (Comes off feeling like a cheap sales gimmick in attempt to appeal towards LGBs rather than an invested attempt by the creator to acknowledge and/or properly represent homosexuals)
- Color palette feels needlessly subdued at times, especially for a game inspired by the likes of EarthBound (A wider range of colors could have and should have been used, especially on battle screens in which the most prominent colors are black and white, which is needless to say, rather dull)
- Somewhat graphically inconsistent (Some character sprites are far less detailed than others, so much so that they look as though they are from separate hardware generations)
- Kind of a slow-starter (Don't expect the game to draw you in all at once)
- Overuse of Internet Memes (EarthBound had pop-cultural references, but most were centered around The Beatles, which were an international phenomenon and every bit as relevant today as they were in 1995 when EarthBound was released, whereas these memes will not age gracefully at all)
Overall: Undertale is an excellent game and I highly recommend it to anyone who is a fan of classic JRPGs and the MOTHER series.

This game could be great but it has a HUGE barrier to entry. Basically, if you need to read reviews to find out if this game is for you, it isn't. It likely means you don't have a group of friends that play it and you aren't playing it already.
I know it's a survival game, and that you have to expect to die, a lot. The issue is the massive imbalance inherent in this particular game.
To give you an idea:
In the 12 hours I have played, I was killed about 4 times. In the 3 hours I played before being killed, I ran around and hid, chopped down trees in the night, tried to find rocks and animals, finally built a rudimentary shelter. Put down a sleeping bag. Walked out of my "base" and was shot. That person then destroyed my sleeping bag (spawn point), took everything I had, then camped there for when I came back and kept killing me. I had a wooden axe on me and this person had an automatic rifle.
I was working towards the "having fun" part of the game where I would get to try and craft neat items and figure out how the game worked... but it was near impossible to get there.  I certainly am not going to continue to play the same part of the game over and over until, by chance, the 100 players that are 74 levels higher than me decide not to kill me. Everyone that wasn't naked that I ran into, killed me instantly... along with any other new player near me.
This isn't just one single case, it  happened 4 different times on 3 different servers. People chatting in game say the same thing and experienced players say "stop crying", "learn the hard way" etc... So, if you have a bunch of buddies that play the game, it is probably a lot of fun. For me, it ended up being basically a Call of Duty sniping clone, or a schoolyard bully simulator.
Until the devs put in some type of mechanic to allow the new players to advance, don't expect the community to give you a good game experience. Which is unfortunate because you would think that smart experienced players would realize that only by nurturing new players will the game make money and be able to grow.

I've tried Rust in legacy and now it's new format and I find both have the same fundamental problem. This game rewards stealing and griefing (destroyers) above gathering and building (creators), which inevitably leads to servers dying and there being a ridiculous number of abandoned buildings.
Why do I think this is inevitable with this game's model?
The only time the destroyers are having fun is by taking advantage of the creators who, by necessity, have to take more risks in the game (they have to be looking at a rock or tree and making noise while the destroyers just have to run around listening for the sounds of gathering or building). As a map matures, the creators stop having any chance at all of advancing far enough to compete with the destroyers as they have already compiled the resources of many other creators and all the supply drops they monopolize.
In the end, the only people left on the server are the destroyers who now can only fight the other destroyers, which is not the easy gains they are accustomed to, so they abandon ship and look for a server that wiped recently to restart the process.
Until they fix the broken game loop, this game will always be a pretty terrible experience for anyone who wants to roleplay and create instead of play deathmatch on a big map.

For the longest time I avoided Undertale like the plague, after the game being strongly praised for its optional pacifist route, winning GameFAQs' Greatest Game of All Time popularity contest despite only being out for a few months, and being compared to the MOTHER series, which is one of my favorite JRPG series, I was all but convinced that the game was nothing more than a fad. "It's just the latest craze in retro-style throwback gaming and yet another homage to EarthBound which will assuredly overdo it with the humor/pop-cultural references and just come off feeling like a soulless clone, and surely the whole Pacifist Route will amount to little more than the game's designer pimping his own agenda and hamfistedly preaching at the audience for the entirety of the game." I thought.
However, one day while I was bored I watched one of my favorite Youtubers do a blind playthrough of it, and my opinion of the game slowly changed as I watched. Upon watching him do a complete playthrough and playing it like a standard JRPG and killing every monster in his path, I saw that the game wasn't preaching at all, nor was it pushing some slanted agenda, and much to my surprise, the game actually did strongly remind me of the MOTHER series. So I went to Steam and bought a copy of the game for myself, eager to experience it.
I have since done a full playthrough of both the "Neutral Pacifist" & "True Pacifist" routes in which I killed no monsters, befriended as many monsters as I could, and generally tried to do what I felt was the right thing in every given situation according to my own moral compass. The playthrough lasted me approximately 12.1 hours according to Steam, which is quite a substantial amount of content for a game of its price, and I have only experienced roughly half of what this game has to offer.
Going in, I honestly didn't expect to enjoy an RPG in which you're encouraged not to fight, seeing as the fighting typically makes up much of the RPG experience, but upon playing the game for myself, I must admit that talking my way out of confrontations was overall a fresh and satisfactory experience which I'm not used to being in anything but WRPGs, and while Undertale is technically "Western" in origin, it was clearly inspired by classic Japanese RPGs, so I just didn't expect it to handle the concept of pacifism as well as WRPGs.
I expected a shallow, idealistic representation of pacifism which even Ghandi would think went too far and served no purpose but to pretentiously preach the developer's beliefs to the audience, but on the contrary, Undertale approaches the concept in a much more balanced manner by presenting the player with "enemies" who don't really want to hurt the player, but are doing so out of desperation by the order of their King whom is just trying to free his people, and said enemies will usually surrender after taking a certain amount of damage. Furthermore, some of the characters even acknowledge that it is a natural response to defend yourself from attackers with violence, and only really judge/condemn you for killing a foe who has surrendered rather than spreading the message that fighting back is always wrong, regardless of the circumstances.
Now before I start to sound too much like your garden variety gushing fan, I will say that Undertale is by no means perfect. It does a lot of things right and is highly entertaining as well as heartwarming, but there were a few things that I didn't like. Namely, and bear with me here, the seemingly forced homosexual relationship between two of the characters. Now before you get mad or start thinking that I'm a bigot, allow me to explain that I have nothing against homosexuality. However, I do have something against game developers putting in homosexual characters into their games for the mere sake of having homosexual characters, (it strikes me as disrespectful and disingenuous, like more of a sales gimmick meant to appeal to a wider demographic than a passionate effort to denounce discrimination by showing support for alternative lifestyles) and I sort of feel like that was done here. I won't name the characters because I don't want to spoil anything, but the two are completely incompatible, never exchange any on-screen dialog, hint towards being anything more than casual acquaintances, nor even appear in the same space together prior to a specific event which doesn't even occur during the first playthrough, and both either appear to or are otherwise explicitly stated to have a crush on another character of the opposite sex, so their whole relationship just sort of comes out of nowhere with absolutely no build-up, as though Toby Foxy shoehorned in a homosexual romance between them just for the sake of having one. I dunno, maybe I'm wrong and Toby Fox had this planned from the start but just didn't draw direct attention to either character's sexuality until late in the game because he didn't want it to be a defining characteristic of either character, which would be commendable, but I'm really not sure so I can only call it as I saw it, and to me it seemed forced, especially when no heterosexual characters have a romance subplot/sidequest. At the very least, it could have and should have been handled much better or otherwise been completely omitted.
That gripe aside, my overall experience with Undertale was a very positive one, and while I'd love to write out everything I like about the game in detail, this review has already dragged on long enough, so I'm just going to sum it all up with a simple list of PROs and CONs.
PROs:
+ Great story
+ Charming cast of characters
+ Fantastic soundtrack
+ Unique combat system (Standard turn-based combat meets Quick Time Events and a Bullet Hell-style dodging system)
+ Humorous dialog
+ Interesting spritework/character designs
+ Emotionally driven plot
+ Pacifist option with no preaching or pushing of agendas
CONs:
- Aforementioned homosexual romance feels forced (Comes off feeling like a cheap sales gimmick in attempt to appeal towards LGBs rather than an invested attempt by the creator to acknowledge and/or properly represent homosexuals)
- Color palette feels needlessly subdued at times, especially for a game inspired by the likes of EarthBound (A wider range of colors could have and should have been used, especially on battle screens in which the most prominent colors are black and white, which is needless to say, rather dull)
- Somewhat graphically inconsistent (Some character sprites are far less detailed than others, so much so that they look as though they are from separate hardware generations)
- Kind of a slow-starter (Don't expect the game to draw you in all at once)
- Overuse of Internet Memes (EarthBound had pop-cultural references, but most were centered around The Beatles, which were an international phenomenon and every bit as relevant today as they were in 1995 when EarthBound was released, whereas these memes will not age gracefully at all)
Overall: Undertale is an excellent game and I highly recommend it to anyone who is a fan of classic JRPGs and the MOTHER series.

If you aren't sure about the 20 bucks go play the game Unturned for free and get good at it. Then if you want a way better version of that you can buy Rust. Tämä peli ei ole mikään jeesuksen toinen tuleminen mitä jotkut antavat ymmärtää, gamemakerin takia pelissä on teknisiä ongelmia/rajoituksia ja pieniä juttuja siellä täällä jotka olisi voinut helposti korjata tai parantaa.
Mutta kaiken kaikkiaan suurin osa ongelmista on hyvin pieniä ja peli on niin hyvin tehty että loput ongelmat unohtuvat. Taidan muistaa joka ikisen hahmon jonka kohdalle osuin, muistan matkan jokaisen alueen läpi, pelissä ei tuntunut olevan yhtään huonoa kappaletta, minulla oli vähintään puolet peliajasta iso hymy naamalla ja joka kerta kun minulla on se hymy naamalla muistan miksi rakastan pelejä niin paljon. (ja sen lisäksi laaja skaala muitakin mielialoja siitä hymystä hermoromahdukseen asti...sillein hyvällä tavalla?)
Kuulin monenlaista juttua siitä minkälainen peli on ennen sen ostamista, suurin osa oli hyvin suuntaa antavia ettei paljastaisi pelistä mitään. Peli käyttää hyvin montaa lähestymistapaa ja mekaniikkaa, mutta ei ikinä tunnu oikein tarttuvan mihinkään yksittäiseen juttuun, joten yksinkertaisesti pelin pelaaminen antaa parhaan kokemuksen, sen sijaan että miettisi peliä visuaalinovellina, roolipelinä, pulmapelinä, metana tai minään muuna. Pelaa peli niinkuin se on olemassa ja koe se mukana, lämmin positiivinen fiilis jonka sen pelaamisesta saa.
Niin, ja muista saada täysi lopetus. Se on enemmän kuin sen arvoista.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

An emotionally powerful experience unlike any other, Undertale is one of the best examples of video games as a capable storytelling medium, able to tell a tale in a unique way unlike any other art form.
If a comparison is necessary to understand this game, the best I can offer is that of a love child between indie classic Cave Story and the cult-classic Nintendo series, Mother - especially Mother 3. Trying to describe the game too heavily, though, does it a disservice. The best thing I can suggest is that this is an RPG where you can save or kill any enemy. Anything more will simply make the game worse.
If you pick it up, do the best you can to keep yourself unspoiled. Avoid looking up hints online whenever possible, as usually the game gives you suggestions if you keep trying.
Above all, stay determined! You have the power to keep going.

After playing 75 hours of this game and experiencing all it has to offer, I feel inclined to post a review.
PROS:
- Fun and rewarding when working together with friends
- Very Easy to learn
- Base building is well developed and thought-out
- Can create Memorable moments/encounters
- Killing/looting/raiding feels satisfying
CONS
- Encourages vindictive gamer behaviour that defies all human morals
- Plagued with hackers and players using aimbots, toxic playerbase
- Very small mechanics that the game doesn't tell you about
- Focuses more on PVP/griefing rather than PVE/Survival
- Clipping issues with bears/wolves and other animals
- Hunger/thirst needs to be re-evaluated/rebalanced
Its a great game, and playing with friends can bring hours of enjoyment. Unfortunately, in some cases it can bring more disappointment and frustrating moments than enjoyment.
I feel there needs to be more of a focus on ACTUAL SURVIVAL rather than PVP/KILLING. You can go for days without eating or drinking.
The game has its technical issues being in early access, for example lag spikes, unoptimization and animals clipping though your base and killing you.
Bottom line is, the game encourages and rewards the wrong kind of player behaviour, which steers the game toward a very disastrous goal. They need to implement incentives for helping other players and working together.
If you're looking at buying this game, sweet, go for it. But be prepared to experience some VERY frustrating moments.
