DayZ is a good game. I played this when it was just a mod and it was good then and whilst the standalone is still in alpha and has many issues it is still a good game. I have had many many hours of fun playing DayZ, both alone and with a friend.
If you are looking to play this game do it, don't listen to all the people constantly criticising this game for it's slow development. Those people just want instant gratification, which you can't have if you want something different in a game. Those same people are the ones who complain about brands like Ubisoft constantly pumping out the same game over and over again with a different title. They want something new and perfect instantly, it's just unrealistic.
Also, when a game is in development if you don't participate in the development process and just complain constantly nothing improves. You get out what you put in. By allowing us access to their unfinished game the developers are saying; "This is our idea, help us get achieve this goal. So you have a game that's new and stimulating and we can say we developed it, with the help of the general public. Thus creating a more satisfying experience for people interested in the genre."
If you don't like hard games, you probably won't like DayZ, people are ruthless. Think of it as a social experiment. How would you act if this really happened? Would you haphazardly run across open fields, down main streets yelling out to every stranger you saw who was armed or unarmed, hoping that they won't kill you? Or would you be cautious? Sneak around them? Would you take them out from a distance? Remeber the aim of the game is to survive, and people are generally really♥♥♥♥♥♥at helping each other unless they know each other. So don't complain about kill on sight. There are plenty of times you won't be killed by people who see you when you don't see them.
A lot of people also complain about the loot economy and bugs that result in unexplained death and character resets. Yes these are all very frustrating when they happen to you or a friend you're playing with. However, these can be used to your advantage, think about how good you're going to be at going from newspawn on the beach, starving and dehydrating, to kitted out survivor, killing bandits, zombies and terrorizing newspawns. You're going to be a survival machine, you'll learn tricks on the way and perhaps make new friends. So it has it's advantages.
Also, with the loot situation, if everything awesome spawned all the time, in abudance, it would kind of defeat the whole nitty gritty survival aspect of the game. It's supposed to be a tooth and nail fight for survival not a mindless first person shooter, go play COD or any of those other hopelessly repeatative clones, if that's what you want.
After all the times i've been mercilessly killed by other players, zombies, killed by bugs and died by other means, such as starvation, dehydration, infected wounds, food poisoning, rejection of blood from a blood transfusion, blood loss, hyperthermia, hypothermia and countless others and respawned my experience has been different. New things have happened and i've discovered new things and places. I've been knocked out and kidnapped, imprisoned and interrogated and much more. So much♥♥♥♥♥♥has happened to my characters in this game, they'd all have some serious PTSD i'm sure. My point is this game is always interesting and entertaining. The sheer variety of scenarios you could find yourself in is limited only by your imagination, that's beauty of the level of detail the developers are trying to put into this game. They are trying to limit you as little as possible, Have you ever been playing another game and gone, "why the ♥♥♥♥ can't i go there?" or "Why can't i do that?" or "It would be real sweet if i could do x in this game." This game will, eventually, satisify some of those desires.
Remeber DayZ is revolutionary, no other game has anywhere near the amount of detail that the developers are trying put into this game, and while i don't know anything about the development of games, i'm sure it is a lot more difficult than most people realise. So support this game and it's developers, you patience will be rewarded with a game like none other in it's genre. Seriously, play this game, buy it, download it, install it and don't give up on it. Do it. Now.

After 600+ hours in-game playing vanilla solo, this is my take on Rust.
You start alone, naked and vulnerable in what is basically the wildest jungle (although animals could be much smarter). Danger is at every corner, and by danger I mean PEOPLE. Other players are your biggest threat and whoever complains about toxic players/community has not understood the heart of this game. Friends are a luxury in Rust.
You have to be as stealthy as possible until you have a decently safe base, and even then, you should keep playing smart. Audio plays a huge part in this. Noisy people are usually the first to go. You don't wanna be one of them. You wanna be a hunter, although you will feel as you are being hunted all the time.
Watching a fight from a distance hidden by a rock or a bush and then trying to sneak close to scavenge the corpses makes your heart pounding like you are on the brink of death (and in-game you actually are). You steal all the stuff you can as quick as possible and run away like crazy. You can only catch a breath when you are back to base, hoping that nobody saw you (and probably half of the time you'll get killed before that). Rust will give you adrenaline rushes like no other game. You will die A LOT.
The stunning visuals and audio effects help immensely to immerse oneself in the world of rust. These aren't just cosmetic features: gameplay is heavily affected by the weather (day/night/rain/fog) and by the landscape itself. The best way to understand if you are not alone in the area is using your ears. then you can decide if e.g. you want to join a gunfight, or run from it.
I also love the building mechanics. It's fun to try and engineer bases that are a pain to raid, as well as to try and figure out where other people's base weak points are.

After playing 75 hours of this game and experiencing all it has to offer, I feel inclined to post a review.
PROS:
- Fun and rewarding when working together with friends
- Very Easy to learn
- Base building is well developed and thought-out
- Can create Memorable moments/encounters
- Killing/looting/raiding feels satisfying
CONS
- Encourages vindictive gamer behaviour that defies all human morals
- Plagued with hackers and players using aimbots, toxic playerbase
- Very small mechanics that the game doesn't tell you about
- Focuses more on PVP/griefing rather than PVE/Survival
- Clipping issues with bears/wolves and other animals
- Hunger/thirst needs to be re-evaluated/rebalanced
Its a great game, and playing with friends can bring hours of enjoyment. Unfortunately, in some cases it can bring more disappointment and frustrating moments than enjoyment.
I feel there needs to be more of a focus on ACTUAL SURVIVAL rather than PVP/KILLING. You can go for days without eating or drinking.
The game has its technical issues being in early access, for example lag spikes, unoptimization and animals clipping though your base and killing you.
Bottom line is, the game encourages and rewards the wrong kind of player behaviour, which steers the game toward a very disastrous goal. They need to implement incentives for helping other players and working together.
If you're looking at buying this game, sweet, go for it. But be prepared to experience some VERY frustrating moments.

Wow.
Two things weren't in Undertale's favour when I first bought it:
1) The retro graphics art style. Sorry, I can't stand some of the colour palettes, like the ruin's hideous pink. Your mileage might vary.
2) It's combat system was twitch-based arcade, which is not a genre I enjoy much. My reflexes are not what it was in my youth; that alone gave me pause.
But Undertale simply won me over and I fell in love. Sublime music. Memorable characters. Excellent writing. Great gameplay. In many decades of playing games, this is one game that I think I'll remember many years on.
It took some time to win me over though. In the beginning I was thinking to myself - the jokes are funny, the gameplay is  quite good, but is that it? Why is this game so hyped?
No. It gets better. You don't see the consequences of what happened before till later in the game, all told through very smart writing. Few games make you ponder the actions of your choices.
For me the brilliance is how the story and characterization was done with the design of the game mechanics, where story and gameplay mesh organically.
For example (small spoiler) early on a NPC didn't want to harm you and you can tell simply by looking at the patterns of the attack. And I felt guilt at striking down this character (didn't know how else to proceed) which got even worse far later in the game.
All the main NPCs are memorable in their own right. Even side characters like the store owners have memorable personalities. Multiple endings depending on what you did (or didn't do).
All of this done in a reasonably short RPG that can be completed in about 7 hours for one playthrough.
A shoutout to the music, which is sublimely used. The music elevates the already great gameplay + storytelling into a work of art.
Undertale has more charm and gravitas than many bloated RPGs with 10x its length. It has all the makings of a classic, like Braid or FTL.

This is a blunt review from a solo vanilla player
(Who recently moved to lower population server for a change in pace)
I hardly ever write reviews, actually as a matter of fact, I don’t believe I have written a review before.
That being said I feel the mad urge to because this game… is something else.
It is rare and unique when a game can make the leap from having an effect on your virtual character to actually having an effect on you.
I know that sounds crazy but you will feel anxiety, fear and you will be creeped out.
Let me paint a picture for you, you just spent an hour or two gathering resources to build a base and you are out at night gathering more wood and rock when you hear footsteps and your inventory is full – the stuff of freaking nightmares.
The virtual environment this game has created is like no other, no matter what game you try unless you buy something that imitates rust - but you would be a fool to spend your money like that.
If you want to survive overnight in a vanilla server:
-crouch instead of walk
-do not run to gunfire/do not get smart to people with guns
-do not approach people most servers are Kill on sight - they want your meat and fat.
-Do not trust anyone unless you know them in person - they are less likely to betray you and if they do you can get some payback.
You can come across the strangest beings on the planet through this game.
From awful singing to descriptive abuse of your family members; to things you just never even thought another human being would think of doing/saying.
Thicker skin and quick wit is a must if you want to actually survive.
You will learn to hate and love this game.
For all those saying there is no end game; it’s what you make of it.
Content is always being added, the debs are killing it in the best way possible – think the state of alpha is more about the debs doing their jobs properly and not releasing half♥♥♥♥♥♥shit to the public and calling it a game,  hence weekly updates and the game has taken a form of its own.
My goal is to be able to make it through a server cycle without being raided – no shame in admitting I haven’t “clocked” the game…yet.
The grind is large but the feeling of achievement after finishing your project/mission or whatever you are doing is much larger.
There are problems that need to be addressed with cheating being one of the MAJOR problems.
No salt here but your 500m headshot that you managed to pull off while I was only able to see your head move up and down as a pixel doesn’t actually seem plausible at all.
Nope I actually truly simply can tell you
-You had an aimbot ohh and now you raided my entire base with your 6 boyfriends. Mint.
Insert.randymarsh&pc.jpeg
Other main issue is optimising- which I know I agreed to because it is Early Access but hardware requirements for the game are quite high if you want to run it at good FPS – which you do, FPS drops = cost resources. Average FPS ATM are around 30-40 on a GTX780ti plenty of ram, ssds and cpu.
-Crashes due to bugs – majorly annoying, especially if you play in a populated server which means – queuing and since you can’t always be on rust you become loot.
-Unsure if debs were trolling but unable to change what your character looks like seems like it shouldn’t bother me too much but the fact the fact I am now a female with no hair makes me feel a bit sad . I can’t frolic around the rust paddocks with this mean ginger mane.
TL;DR
Play it smart, get to know your guns do some research if you must.
Once you dive into this game you will fully comprehend what I meant, if you don’t like losing be prepared to rage quit and put your hardware away fast enough so you don’t smash it.

Two things weren't in Undertale's favour when I first bought it:
1) The retro graphics art style. Sorry, I can't stand some of the colour palettes, like the ruin's hideous pink. Your mileage might vary.
2) It's combat system was twitch-based arcade, which is not a genre I enjoy much. My reflexes are not what it was in my youth; that alone gave me pause.
But Undertale simply won me over and I fell in love. Sublime music. Memorable characters. Excellent writing. Great gameplay. In many decades of playing games, this is one game that I think I'll remember many years on.
It took some time to win me over though. In the beginning I was thinking to myself - the jokes are funny, the gameplay is  quite good, but is that it? Why is this game so hyped?
No. It gets better. You don't see the consequences of what happened before till later in the game, all told through very smart writing. Few games make you ponder the actions of your choices.
For me the brilliance is how the story and characterization was done with the design of the game mechanics, where story and gameplay mesh organically.
For example (small spoiler) early on a NPC didn't want to harm you and you can tell simply by looking at the patterns of the attack. And I felt guilt at striking down this character (didn't know how else to proceed) which got even worse far later in the game.
All the main NPCs are memorable in their own right. Even side characters like the store owners have memorable personalities. Multiple endings depending on what you did (or didn't do).
All of this done in a reasonably short RPG that can be completed in about 7 hours for one playthrough.
A shoutout to the music, which is sublimely used. The music elevates the already great gameplay + storytelling into a work of art.
Undertale has more charm and gravitas than many bloated RPGs with 10x its length. It has all the makings of a classic, like Braid or FTL.

Rust is a good game, one of those games you can have a really good time with, or... a pretty "meh" time with.
This game is in Alpha, so obviously performance issues would naturally be anticipated.
But Holy-Rusty-Naked's-Rocks, this game runs like absolute crap. I mean it's not like "ARK" Which is practically unplayable without only the most elite setup, and shouldn't even be bothered with if you're using a laptop, -even a high end ultrabook. But damn this game needs to be heavily optomized. Fortunately, for higher-end pc users, this game will run on roughly medium settings with an average of 40 FPS. Don't get this game if you are using a GPU that can't easily run most next gen games at least on medium to high settings, or Rust will look like crap with maybe 30 FPS if you're lucky.
As for the online experience, well, with the new addition of the "virtual waiting room" to join servers... you may need to try to convince your friend to leave their loot heavy base and join you on a less crowded server... Have to say, almost every server seems to start lagging sooner or later, sometimes leaving you jogging in place-spawning back and repeating for minutes at a time regardless of ping.
Alright so that's all stuff you can muscle your way past with a bit of effort and, well... cringing at times, but how's the actual Gameplay...?
Well for starters, I have never played a non-horror game that can pull off jump scares quite like this. Never. The actual sound of gunshots alone is enough to cause you to jump up and freak out. A gunfight is an all out adrenaline rush, that will leave you shaking for minutes after wether you lose, or win and try making off with all the gear your opponent has dropped. Facepunch has really done a good job capturing what a real threat might feel like. Unlike what the average FPS feels like. -I Easily think this one of the greatest things this game seems to pulls off so well.
Survival is obviously the main premise of the game and, well, it's not bad.
Scavenging basic materials such as wood and stone is tedious enough, but doing it alone? That's nearly a deathwish. Grab a friend if you wanna survive for more that a couple minutes much less have any fun doing so.
-This is because at the very heart of Rust, in the deep, deep, core of it all. one thing is certain.
PLAYERS ARE F---ING TOXIC. It is almost as if from the moment they are brought into this horribly optomized world, every breath they take is filled with bloodlust that can never be quenched no matter how many "Nakeds" they kill. It is as if the only thing they have ever wanted is to simply kill without question, and  to shoot without mercy.
Now, that isn't to say this is a bad thing, in fact, it is just one of those "things" that at the end of the day make Rust... well Rust.
As far as players go, they are almost always the usual "Trigger-Happy","Blood-Thirsty" Maniacs who want nothing more than to kill you, whether you have anything on you, or not. As a matter of fact, it is so uncommon to meet a friendly player on Rust, it is quite certain they will end up a regular friend you play with, solely because they are so uncommon.
I don't wan't put any of the above-mentioned out in a bad way, but merely as a tip. In Rust, Don't trust anyone.
If you are someone who thought it would be a good idea to create a "Pack" of players you meet in-game and start your own small gang, well, don't be disappointed if you end up playing as a lone survivor for hours and hours on the same server.
Servers are kept on a fixed "Wipe Date".
This means that players who build themselves massive fortresses, won't have 'em forever.
Some servers wipe every couple weeks, some once a month, and so on.
At the end of the day, if you are more of a casual gamer, rather than a competitive kinda player, I'd say try and go for a different game.
As for pricing, this game is relativley cheap and is worth buying if you have the specs for it, the patience and the time.

Overall, I would recommend this game for anyone who enjoys survival games, and can handle the toxicity of the common player. Not a game for the casual gamer, and not an FPS in particular if that's what you're hoping for. :)

It's very hard to describe Undertale at length without spoiling a large part of what makes it so effective, so here's some major points.
1. The Gameplay
The gameplay is honestly nothing special- it's a mashup of a turn based RPG and a bullet hell, both of which are somewhat niche genres (I like both, for what it's worth). Undertale isn't terribly difficult either outside of the final boss of one of the routes. You'll know it when you see it, assumed you haven't been spoiled as to who it is yet. Don't misunderstand this part: the gameplay is far from bad and remains fun throughout, but it's nothing I hadn't seen before (just the gameplay- the overall contextualized experience is something I've never seen before and will probably never see again)
2. Characters/Story
Again, nothing special at first glance. Both go MUCH deeper than they appear, however, as every character has their own motivations and despite Undertale's short length (6 hours or so per playthrough) most actually get some character development (Undyne especially!), it's quite interesting poking at the mechanics and seeing how their reactions change to your actions. This especially holds true in the most divergent path through the game: it almost doesn't feel like the same game any more, taking on a completely different tone. The best parts of Undertale definitely occur on the way to its best ending
3. The Gimmicks
The RPG where you don't have to kill anyone! This is true but it ends up being fairly tedious, especially during most bosses. Where Undertale really shines is just how it plays with RPG conventions, and even those of games in general. The characters even remember what you've done if you quit and reload a previous save, to varying degrees. One boss will even count how many times you've died, while another character revels in calling out the player character AND the player at various points. It's quite the surreal experience when it's not expected, and sometimes even a jarring experience even when it is!
4. The Choices
Technically this is another gimmick or story part, but it deserves to be talked about a bit on its own. The inevitable second playthrough reveals how shallow many of the choices are- Papyrus will come to the same conclusions regardless of your responses, Undyne challenges you for one of 3 reasons (killing Papyrus, killing anyone else, or if you've been a pacifist, because you're just going to die). However, the gameplay choices DO end up mattering, and ultimately this makes the player an active participant in the game: a fact that Undertale exploits to the fullest, and is the main reason why I would recommend this game.
5. Summary
With most games, you just play them. However, Undertale will play you right back. Even when you're expecting it to happen it will still catch you off guard with just how far it's willing to go. What you get out of Undertale is exactly what you put in, no more and no less. If you treat it like a typical RPG then it's a mediocre RPG. But when you push against it and really explore what it lets you do, there's a lot of depth and genuine emotional moments throughout. If you're a completionist like me then you'll go through the tearjerkers, give everyone their happy ending...and then feel like a terrible person for taking it away just to see the final path, which itself tries to make you abanadon it at all costs.
You looked for more words at the end of this review...
...but nobody came.

I'm not going to spend too many words on expressing my excitement for this game, because I don't think I could do better than to say that the hype is real. I'll save my words to try and explain what's so special about Undertale. If you're tired of hearing about this game, please excuse us, this game just has a lot going for it.
Undertale's storyline is one of the most emotionally gripping I've played through. It's hilarious, touching, dramatic, and more than a bit dark, just the way I like it. I've never related to so many characters in a game before, from the main cast to the minibosses to the shopkeepers. And Toby knows it too, he uses that connection to make the game that much more impactful.
This is the only game I can think of that really cares to approach social issues, and it does it so well. The game is on point with respect to gender and attraction. And while you could argue the interpretation, there are a few really positive instances of trans representation in Undertale as well, something that's virtually unheard of in other mainstream games. It's worth a whole discussion of its own, but I'd rather not spoil anything here. Nonetheless, Undertale has raised the bar on commentary in games.
Not to mention that it's just plain fun. The gameplay involves a minimalist RPG overworld with turn-based combat that involves dodging particles during your opponent's attacks. Its style is largely a pastiche of Earthbound (a game I've been inspired to pick up because of this one), but the battles are also reminiscent of the first two Paper Mario games, in that they combine dialogue and combat to great effect. And the Undertale soundtrack beautifully ties the whole game together.
If you made it to this page, odds are you already know how... enthusiastic... we fans can be. But there's a reason this game has stayed on my mind since I played it through for the first time four months ago. And no, it's not just the memes.
That said, I am SO hyped for the memes.

I hardly ever write reviews, actually as a matter of fact, I don’t believe I have written a review before.
That being said I feel the mad urge to because this game… is something else.
It is rare and unique when a game can make the leap from having an effect on your virtual character to actually having an effect on you.
I know that sounds crazy but you will feel anxiety, fear and you will be creeped out.
Let me paint a picture for you, you just spent an hour or two gathering resources to build a base and you are out at night gathering more wood and rock when you hear footsteps and your inventory is full – the stuff of freaking nightmares.
The virtual environment this game has created is like no other, no matter what game you try unless you buy something that imitates rust - but you would be a fool to spend your money like that.
If you want to survive overnight in a vanilla server:
-crouch instead of walk
-do not run to gunfire/do not get smart to people with guns
-do not approach people most servers are Kill on sight - they want your meat and fat.
-Do not trust anyone unless you know them in person - they are less likely to betray you and if they do you can get some payback.
You can come across the strangest beings on the planet through this game.
From awful singing to descriptive abuse of your family members; to things you just never even thought another human being would think of doing/saying.
Thicker skin and quick wit is a must if you want to actually survive.
You will learn to hate and love this game.
For all those saying there is no end game; it’s what you make of it.
Content is always being added, the debs are killing it in the best way possible – think the state of alpha is more about the debs doing their jobs properly and not releasing half♥♥♥♥♥♥shit to the public and calling it a game,  hence weekly updates and the game has taken a form of its own.
My goal is to be able to make it through a server cycle without being raided – no shame in admitting I haven’t “clocked” the game…yet.
The grind is large but the feeling of achievement after finishing your project/mission or whatever you are doing is much larger.
There are problems that need to be addressed with cheating being one of the MAJOR problems.

Rust has all of the mechanics you expect from a sandbox survival game, packaged into a neatly designed game with an immersive world. Whether or not you will enjoy the game depends not so much on the product, but the people who play it.
It feels wrong to describe Rust as a difficult game, but it is tiptoeing on the line of being tiresome at times. Rust is made addictive by offering you a seemingly simple challenge (gather materials, build a shelter, find food) only for your efforts to be hampered by other players in the game.
It can take time to build a secure shelter and place a sleep bag (the latter required for respawning at a familiar point) and it is hard to survive during this period. It is addictive to keep trying, but the frustration can set in, because it gets repititve if you can't progress beyond the early stage; you end up respawning far away from the area you were in, and losing your materials and food.
For some, Rust's mad-max style lawless world provides an incredibly fun challenge, where clans fight each other and the more passive of us hide and watch the chaos unfold. For others, it has been described as harboring a "toxic" community, spoiled by frustration, where snarky children can rule the roost and stop new players from establishing themselves at a server.
Games like Rust are only as good as the people who play it, and that changes moment to moment, server to server. Sometimes you'll find impressive structures, co-operative village builds, and friendly players who chat and share resources. Other times, you'll be hassled by advance players looking to kill for the sake of killing (the result of achieving a large base and a vast supply of resources, but ultimately nothing to do with them) or players smashing houses, killing people on sight even when unprovoked, and newbies running about naked and slamming people with rocks (okay, the last one is more like an essential Rust experience).
This game works for people who play in groups, but as a solo player, it can be a waste of time trying to get into the deeper aspectsof the game. Rust is as good as the people you play with.

Like many of these survival games the promise is there but it loses value the minute the melting pot joins in.  What was the original design purpose, what safeguards are in place to ensure that mission statement is intact, honestly I have no idea.
You start off with all the tools you need to survive asleep on the shores of some random beach on the server map you join.  There are up to 200 other players depending on where you're playing.  This is where you quickly discover how vulnerable you are.  In most servers, unless its reset day where everything is reset so it's a level playing field you will find a big disparity between yourself and most everyone else on the map.
You may go an hour or two proudly working on skill development but at some point you will encounter other humans, and they will most likely be hunting you.  There are wild animals in the game including bears but you can be sure nothing will be a bigger threat then your fellow humans.
The learning curve to actually craft and farm materials is pretty low, it's pretty easy to chop wood, mine minerals and craft basic items.  In order to progress further to build your first house in order to survive you need time and this is what adds to the challenge.
There are ruins and monuments scattered across the landscape along with old roads.  These areas have old oil barrels and scattered boxes of goods from before society fell apart.  It's in these boxes that you find blueprints to make modern things along with food and water items from before to aid in your survival.  Getting to these areas is an important part of the game which all of the experienced players are already aware so you need to plan smartly always scanning for others.
If I were to sum up the game, it's clearly a game of survival where even the most well armed person has the potential to die and start over.  Your best chances are to group with other people, and by that I mean people you know so if they kill you in game they know there are consequences for being unethical outside of game.  If your're on your own....trust noone.  There is nothing easier then hunting naked people who have no way of defending themselves and loading up on their resources.
Overall I would not recommend this game in it's present form because I feel it needs to do a more effective job at acclimating people into understanding the basics.  The premise is great and the risk is an important element but I feel like it exploits new players to pay based on this model only to scare them off.  Whether you have learning servers available where you can understand resources and crafting better before getting dumped into the Devil's playground to play Groundhog Day over and over again until you get all of the conditions right.

Like many of these survival games the promise is there but it loses value the minute the melting pot joins in.  What was the original design purpose, what safeguards are in place to ensure that mission statement is intact, honestly I have no idea.
You start off with all the tools you need to survive asleep on the shores of some random beach on the server map you join.  There are up to 200 other players depending on where you're playing.  This is where you quickly discover how vulnerable you are.  In most servers, unless its reset day where everything is reset so it's a level playing field you will find a big disparity between yourself and most everyone else on the map.
You may go an hour or two proudly working on skill development but at some point you will encounter other humans, and they will most likely be hunting you.  There are wild animals in the game including bears but you can be sure nothing will be a bigger threat then your fellow humans.
The learning curve to actually craft and farm materials is pretty low, it's pretty easy to chop wood, mine minerals and craft basic items.  In order to progress further to build your first house in order to survive you need time and this is what adds to the challenge.
There are ruins and monuments scattered across the landscape along with old roads.  These areas have old oil barrels and scattered boxes of goods from before society fell apart.  It's in these boxes that you find blueprints to make modern things along with food and water items from before to aid in your survival.  Getting to these areas is an important part of the game which all of the experienced players are already aware so you need to plan smartly always scanning for others.
If I were to sum up the game, it's clearly a game of survival where even the most well armed person has the potential to die and start over.  Your best chances are to group with other people, and by that I mean people you know so if they kill you in game they know there are consequences for being unethical outside of game.  If your're on your own....trust noone.  There is nothing easier then hunting naked people who have no way of defending themselves and loading up on their resources.
Overall I would not recommend this game in it's present form because I feel it needs to do a more effective job at acclimating people into understanding the basics.  The premise is great and the risk is an important element but I feel like it exploits new players to pay based on this model only to scare them off.  Whether you have learning servers available where you can understand resources and crafting better before getting dumped into the Devil's playground to play Groundhog Day over and over again until you get all of the conditions right.

Like the idiot that I am and despite all the warnings not to spoil it for myself, I read-up on Undertale beforehand so I basically knew what was going to happen (not details, but certainly the general gist). Yet, despite this, I found the game genuinely funny, challenging and uplifting but at the same time, sad and introspective.
The writing is perfect, the story and premise are excellent and truly turn the whole concept of what it means to be a game and a player up on their head. The music is awesome (and I, being British, do not use that word lightly) and fits the feel of the game, and of each individual part, exactly. If I had to name a gripe, it would be "simplistic graphics", but honestly, that's not a problem: They do the job they need to, and by being deliberately simple, they do not distract from the point the game is trying to make, and leave some things to your own imagination which again aids in the whole premise.
There are few games which can touch on a fundamental level. That say so little, and yet say so much. Say so much about issues large and small. About war and peace, about relationships and trust, about life, about you. Yes. You.
Do yourself a favour: Buy this game, play it, don't read any spoilers beforehand. At first you'll scoff at this game, but stick with it, it'll work its way into you and then tear at your core, you won't even realise its doing it until its too late. Nobody is perfect, and no-one ever will be, but this game will help you to make yourself a better person, by helping you to understand yourself. I know it has helped me.
Toby Fox: It is self-evident that this game is a profound expression of your own soul, and that makes it all the more meaningful. You have, without reservation, produced the best game I have ever played in my entire life, and improved and enriched it in the process. If I had a hat, I'd take it off to you.

The occupant opens the door and listens to me ask for food in exchange for wood.
He murders me with a sword.
I swear revenge.
I begin preparations.
I searched barrels, boxes, crates, anything that could give me the tools I needed to avenge myself.

A gracious barrel with a curious object.
A flamethrower.
I found just enough materials to repeair it and fuel it.
I made a few spears and found a grenade.
I found his house (again).
I waited until dawn to see if he would leave to forage the nearby ruins of an airfield.
He left.
With the door open.
The first mistake.
I began burning the wooden foundations with my fury and watched as it burned.
I entered the house after the first flames died down.
Bedrolls and beds in the open (respawn points).
I destroy them with my own sword.
I set the house aflame from within and watch.
It is the most beautiful sight my eyes will ever behold.
The owner returns.
The house is in shambles.
He fires a shell from his pipe shotgun.
He fails to kill me.
I throw my spear straight into his face.
He goes down.
"How does it feel to have your house burned down by the hands that you wronged?"
I strike the final blow.
13/10, would burn someone's house down in revengence again.

Rust has all of the mechanics you expect from a sandbox survival game, packaged into a neatly designed game with an immersive world. Whether or not you will enjoy the game depends not so much on the product, but the people who play it.
It feels wrong to describe Rust as a difficult game, but it is tiptoeing on the line of being tiresome at times. Rust is made addictive by offering you a seemingly simple challenge (gather materials, build a shelter, find food) only for your efforts to be hampered by other players in the game.
It can take time to build a secure shelter and place a sleep bag (the latter required for respawning at a familiar point) and it is hard to survive during this period. It is addictive to keep trying, but the frustration can set in, because it gets repititve if you can't progress beyond the early stage; you end up respawning far away from the area you were in, and losing your materials and food.
For some, Rust's mad-max style lawless world provides an incredibly fun challenge, where clans fight each other and the more passive of us hide and watch the chaos unfold. For others, it has been described as harboring a "toxic" community, spoiled by frustration, where snarky children can rule the roost and stop new players from establishing themselves at a server.
Games like Rust are only as good as the people who play it, and that changes moment to moment, server to server. Sometimes you'll find impressive structures, co-operative village builds, and friendly players who chat and share resources. Other times, you'll be hassled by advance players looking to kill for the sake of killing (the result of achieving a large base and a vast supply of resources, but ultimately nothing to do with them) or players smashing houses, killing people on sight even when unprovoked, and newbies running about naked and slamming people with rocks (okay, the last one is more like an essential Rust experience).
This game works for people who play in groups, but as a solo player, it can be a waste of time trying to get into the deeper aspectsof the game. Rust is as good as the people you play with.

Like many of these survival games the promise is there but it loses value the minute the melting pot joins in.  What was the original design purpose, what safeguards are in place to ensure that mission statement is intact, honestly I have no idea.
You start off with all the tools you need to survive asleep on the shores of some random beach on the server map you join.  There are up to 200 other players depending on where you're playing.  This is where you quickly discover how vulnerable you are.  In most servers, unless its reset day where everything is reset so it's a level playing field you will find a big disparity between yourself and most everyone else on the map.
You may go an hour or two proudly working on skill development but at some point you will encounter other humans, and they will most likely be hunting you.  There are wild animals in the game including bears but you can be sure nothing will be a bigger threat then your fellow humans.
The learning curve to actually craft and farm materials is pretty low, it's pretty easy to chop wood, mine minerals and craft basic items.  In order to progress further to build your first house in order to survive you need time and this is what adds to the challenge.
There are ruins and monuments scattered across the landscape along with old roads.  These areas have old oil barrels and scattered boxes of goods from before society fell apart.  It's in these boxes that you find blueprints to make modern things along with food and water items from before to aid in your survival.  Getting to these areas is an important part of the game which all of the experienced players are already aware so you need to plan smartly always scanning for others.
If I were to sum up the game, it's clearly a game of survival where even the most well armed person has the potential to die and start over.  Your best chances are to group with other people, and by that I mean people you know so if they kill you in game they know there are consequences for being unethical outside of game.  If your're on your own....trust noone.  There is nothing easier then hunting naked people who have no way of defending themselves and loading up on their resources.
Overall I would not recommend this game in it's present form because I feel it needs to do a more effective job at acclimating people into understanding the basics.  The premise is great and the risk is an important element but I feel like it exploits new players to pay based on this model only to scare them off.  Whether you have learning servers available where you can understand resources and crafting better before getting dumped into the Devil's playground to play Groundhog Day over and over again until you get all of the conditions right.

Now that I am nearing the 200 hour mark, I've decided to share my experiences and thoughts about DayZ.
I've been playing DayZ SA since version 0.45. I've read a lot of reviews, both negative and positive, and I've found that there are very good points to both arguments. For those of you with negative comments, I feel your pain. However, I do recommend this game to anyone that enjoys survival in a post-apocalyptic world. Note that I will only state my experiences and opinions as of version 0.58.
As of 0.58, I've seen a massive improvement on the way the game runs. I get a solid 50fps in the countryside and in the cities. However, prior to this update, I did make minor changes to my config files. You can google guides on how to increase performance, which I recommend. Prior to the update, I was only getting 30fps that was not consistent. I am running the game from an SSD. I do run the game at 1080p resolution.
DayZ is brutal. Despite the environment beating your character down, you will have to continue to nourish your character's health by eating, drinking, staying warm. and performing first aid. There are many youtube videos on these features. The real threat comes from other players.
I have 4 favorite servers that I play on, and they are quite popular. One of them is DayZ Underground, which normally sustains 50/50 players. In 200 hours, I have been killed 16 times. I have never killed another player. That's right. Never. Some of you veteran players may laugh at this, and that's fine. I have been in firefights, and tried to fight back. Normally I've been either overwhelmed by superior numbers or firepower, or, in several cases, it seems bohemia gave me blanks. It also seems that my character, even when healthy and wearing a plate carrier, is extremely allergic to lead. The weapons are loud or quiet as they should be, and the ricochet sounds when you're being shot at are alarming.
I normally travel alone, because most of the character I've met have tried to kill me on site or rob me. Although, that does not mean I haven't met good people. I'm very social and attempt to interact most of the time.
I enjoy hunting and fishing, although I would like to see more wild animals roaming around. I think it's great that you can craft the essential items needed to live away from civilization. I also like that the fireplaces in the buildings are useful now. There is a cabin in the mountains I visit often to cook my kills and hunt the surrounding area.
They seem to have removed the zombies (and it seems the bananas and zucchinis?!?!) from the game, and I am happy that they did. Prior to 0.58, the zombies were a broken mess, and I would rather them be completely removed until they are functioning properly. They should definitely be an enemy you fear just as much, or more, than other players. I think they should also grapple and try to infect you, rather than attempt to punch you to death. I guess this really depends on if you like traditional zombies, Day of the Dead zombies, or 28 Days Later zombies. I personally like the Day of the Dead zombies that run after you, but attempt to spread the virus. There should be an option to be able to inspect other players for bite marks as well, just in case you're not sure if you should let someone join your group.
The weapons, clothing, and gear in DayZ is vast and allows players to individualize their characters. I really like this, however, I agree that certain core aspects of the game need to be addressed prior to adding more stuff.
There is currently only 1 vehicle in the game. I have driven the military truck several times, but I haven't enjoyed it. The driving just doesnt feel right. Also, I don't care enough about it to attempt repairs or carry a battery across the map to use it again.
The animations in DayZ overall are really good, but could also use some improvements. In the future, I would like to see an item in my hangs when I wring out my clothes or start a friction fire, and I would also like to see the character grasp each individual rung when climbing a ladder. I would also like to be able to interact with objects in my environment. Most of the loot spawns on the floor or on tables now.
The game seems to have come a long way from when I started playing, but it does have a long way to go. The devs are keeping the players informed on the updates and seem to be supporting the game very well. They took extra time to release this last update, but for me it's the most stable one yet. I haven't experienced any issues that have annoyed me enough lately to comment on. I believe I will continue to play and enjoy DayZ for some time.
As always, I recommend everyone to read reviews and watch videos to assist them in deciding on making a purchase. I think $34.99 is a bit steep for a game in Alpha, but looking back over the experiences I've had, people I've met both good and bad, and the time I've put into this game, I feel pretty good.

Now that I am nearing the 200 hour mark, I've decided to share my experiences and thoughts about DayZ.
I've been playing DayZ SA since version 0.45. I've read a lot of reviews, both negative and positive, and I've found that there are very good points to both arguments. For those of you with negative comments, I feel your pain. However, I do recommend this game to anyone that enjoys survival in a post-apocalyptic world. Note that I will only state my experiences and opinions as of version 0.58.
As of 0.58, I've seen a massive improvement on the way the game runs. I get a solid 50fps in the countryside and in the cities. However, prior to this update, I did make minor changes to my config files. You can google guides on how to increase performance, which I recommend. Prior to the update, I was only getting 30fps that was not consistent. I am running the game from an SSD. I do run the game at 1080p resolution.
DayZ is brutal. Despite the environment beating your character down, you will have to continue to nourish your character's health by eating, drinking, staying warm. and performing first aid. There are many youtube videos on these features. The real threat comes from other players.
I have 4 favorite servers that I play on, and they are quite popular. One of them is DayZ Underground, which normally sustains 50/50 players. In 200 hours, I have been killed 16 times. I have never killed another player. That's right. Never. Some of you veteran players may laugh at this, and that's fine. I have been in firefights, and tried to fight back. Normally I've been either overwhelmed by superior numbers or firepower, or, in several cases, it seems bohemia gave me blanks. It also seems that my character, even when healthy and wearing a plate carrier, is extremely allergic to lead. The weapons are loud or quiet as they should be, and the ricochet sounds when you're being shot at are alarming.
I normally travel alone, because most of the character I've met have tried to kill me on site or rob me. Although, that does not mean I haven't met good people. I'm very social and attempt to interact most of the time.
I enjoy hunting and fishing, although I would like to see more wild animals roaming around. I think it's great that you can craft the essential items needed to live away from civilization. I also like that the fireplaces in the buildings are useful now. There is a cabin in the mountains I visit often to cook my kills and hunt the surrounding area.
They seem to have removed the zombies (and it seems the bananas and zucchinis?!?!) from the game, and I am happy that they did. Prior to 0.58, the zombies were a broken mess, and I would rather them be completely removed until they are functioning properly. They should definitely be an enemy you fear just as much, or more, than other players. I think they should also grapple and try to infect you, rather than attempt to punch you to death. I guess this really depends on if you like traditional zombies, Day of the Dead zombies, or 28 Days Later zombies. I personally like the Day of the Dead zombies that run after you, but attempt to spread the virus. There should be an option to be able to inspect other players for bite marks as well, just in case you're not sure if you should let someone join your group.
The weapons, clothing, and gear in DayZ is vast and allows players to individualize their characters. I really like this, however, I agree that certain core aspects of the game need to be addressed prior to adding more stuff.
There is currently only 1 vehicle in the game. I have driven the military truck several times, but I haven't enjoyed it. The driving just doesnt feel right. Also, I don't care enough about it to attempt repairs or carry a battery across the map to use it again.
The animations in DayZ overall are really good, but could also use some improvements. In the future, I would like to see an item in my hangs when I wring out my clothes or start a friction fire, and I would also like to see the character grasp each individual rung when climbing a ladder. I would also like to be able to interact with objects in my environment. Most of the loot spawns on the floor or on tables now.
The game seems to have come a long way from when I started playing, but it does have a long way to go. The devs are keeping the players informed on the updates and seem to be supporting the game very well. They took extra time to release this last update, but for me it's the most stable one yet. I haven't experienced any issues that have annoyed me enough lately to comment on. I believe I will continue to play and enjoy DayZ for some time.
As always, I recommend everyone to read reviews and watch videos to assist them in deciding on making a purchase. I think $34.99 is a bit steep for a game in Alpha, but looking back over the experiences I've had, people I've met both good and bad, and the time I've put into this game, I feel pretty good.

There are a number of things that Undertale does right, and they've all been expounded on plenty of times over. To try and contribute something a little different, I'd ask you to consider what "choice and consequence" games typically do when they attempt to leverage their claimed consequences on the player. By and large, you'll get some choice differences in dialogue or cutscene, right? Maybe a choice between the three primary colours? It still ends. You're probably happy enough you got it done. You get your ending, maybe call it a night and hit the sack, satisfied you've wrapped up another game.
Undertale leverages consequence far more successfully, via far more humble means. Depending on how things play out, it'll either guilt-trip you or leave you mildly horrified. It will do so in a way that will last. And all it takes is a simple implication that the tale never really ends.

Where to start...
A good start is: The Borderlands series is the greatest thing I have ever played on.
Borderlands 2 combines first person shooting with RPG and does it right for once.
You can play as a multitude of badass mercenaries, each with their own unique skills and powers which you can levelup, from throwing down turrets to magical powers to going invisible to.. setting yourself on fire and going on a rampage while screaming poetry across the battlefield.
Borderlands 2 features a huge variety of characters both friendly and enemy, such as a homocidal 13 year old with a passion for blowing things up, a teenage pirate girl, a half robotic british gamehunter and swathes of psychotic enemies.
The story writing is another great thing about this game. The jokes and gags in Borderlands 2 will keep you laughing thoughout the entire story, in particular the main antagonist Handsome Jack has some of the greatest lines since Oscar Wilde.
And then there's also when the game take on a darker tone, always keeping the humorous theme but with an underlying queeziness which makes you nervious to laugh and a severe case of 'feels' at the end of the scene.
And it's impossible to discuss Borderlands without mentioning the loot you can collect. The guns in this game are varied to make the biggest understatement of the century. Not only are there hundreds of unique named weaponary to collect, each of the common weapons you can collect are made up of parts, all of which cause some aspect of the gun to be drastically different.
No two weapons you will ever pickup in game will feel the same and NOT just because of the numbers being different. Some may have a different firing pattern, or may have elemental properties, or fire faster or slower, some turn into a grenade when you've emtied the clip to throw it at enemies, you can get assault rifles which shoot rapidfire missiles, or guns which get MORE accurate when you hold down the trigger. Not even the sky is the limit to the amount of variation you can find in Borderlands 2. (And not like the completely random nature of some games advertising 'billions of combinations for infinite viariety' like Diablo 3 or Minecraft or such, we're talking about this being reliably fun while still never experiencing the same thing twice, ever.)

BROLANDS TEW! (as I like to call it)
I think everyone and their mothers have played this game already. If you haven't, think of this as a first-person Diablo, but without the randomly-generated terrain and lack of Hardcore Mode. Basically, a first-person shooter with a bunch of randomly-generated loot, skilling, and many side quests.
What's different from the first Borderlands? Well, you play as four different classes this time: Gunzerker, Commando, Assassin, and another Siren. Pay more money, and you can play as Mechromancer and Psycho. What's also different is that you explore another area of Pandora; a larger area, if you ask me. You also get a new element for your guns: Slag, which amplifies damage on slagged units. Oh, and no fall damage this time. This is all aside from the bajillion more guns that Gearbox stuffed into the game.
The humor in this game, compared to the last game, is much better...but I feel like that the humor isn't going to age so well. Think of it as Gearbox taking a bunch of internet memes and references to current games, and built the basis of the humor on top of those. Sure, I had a good laugh, don't get me wrong. But I feel like people that pick this game up years from now may not get any of the humor. I guess time will tell.
Without spoiling anything, the story was definitely improved over the first game. When I played the first Borderlands, I barely was able to keep up with any of the story. I even forgot what I was on Pandora for until I reached the end. Here, I'm kept aware of my goal, but I guess that comes from Handsome Jack taunting at me from his multimillion headquarters in the sky.
With that, I'll get to characters: Handsome Jack is a ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. He does spurt out some comedic lines from time to time, but I was just glad to put a bullet in his head in the end (not spoilers if it's obvious, AMIRITE?!), as I pretty much just hated the character halfway through the game. I guess that's the point of creating a memorable villain, so I guess props to Gearbox for that. The new characters, I thought they were pretty nice. Claptrap's still the same goofball as before, which I didn't have much of a problem with. Even found myself laughing at him, from time to time.
The enemy dialogue is much more varied this time around, and is just hilarious to kill some of these enemies. Speaking of enemies, Gearbox definitely amped up the amount of enemies you can fight, and even incorprated types of enemies that are armor-based instead of health-based, meaning that the best way to kill them is with corrosive weaponry. One fun type of enemy I got to fight were the Goliaths, which got stronger each time they killed someone/something. But the stronger the Goliath is, the better the loot you can earn. But try not to go too far with letting them rank up, if you're not ready for the high-ranking Goliaths.
Oh yeah, the game is still drop-in/drop-out co-op with up to four players. But here's something to keep aware of: The loot dropped or found in chests are shared by everyone. This isn't a hassle with money and ammo, as everyone gets that when one person picks them up. But when it comes to guns and what not, everyone pretty much has to decide on who gets what. So choose wisely.
Alright, I think this recommendation's gone on long enough for some of you people. If you like RPGs and shooters, pick this game up, but try playing the game with friends. It's a fun and comical game, and a definite improvement over the first game. Enjoy your stay on Pandora.

I've always had mixed feelings about
. On one hand, the quirky humor and intricate plot made up for the fact that I'd always disliked turn-based RPGs. On the other hand, it didn't really innovate on the core gameplay and had a lot of forced grinding. And then along came this game. For me, hearing that it was basically
minus the things I disliked about
was enough to sell me on the idea, but in case you want to know more...
This is a game that not only discourages grinding, it discourages fighting at all. Monsters you encounter will still warp you into a battle screen, but very few of them are actually out for blood, and you can usually find clever ways to pacify them and send them on their merry way, and wind up a little richer in the process. (One of my favorites is that you can almost always just beat them to within an inch of their life and then spare them, turning the game into a school-bully simulator.) And you'll want that money for healing items and the occasional armor upgrade; the late-game enemies don't mess around. But you're not at the mercy of the Random Number Gods; every enemy has a unique graphical real-time attack to try to dodge, whether it's a visually-challenged dog who swipes at you with a sword or a depressed ghost who pelts you with tears.
If you're thorough about exploring, you should earn enough cash from regular encounters to stay stocked with items without having to wander around picking fights. And even so, you'll spend far more time solving puzzles and chatting with the Underground's wacky locals. The dialog would be worth the price of admission alone; there's a reason these characters have found their way into the hearts of players all over the Internet and inspired a tidal wave of fan art not seen since the
craze.

After playing through the game, I still think the game is somewhat overhyped.  It's a very very very good game, but I'm surprised so many people think it's one of the top games of 2015.  I think the best part of this game is it's story.  It's nothing short of excellent, and the way it's conveyed is brilliant.  I can't say the same for the battle system. If you played Earthbound and enjoyed it, you'll also probably enjoy this game.
I was going to try to avoid that comparison in this review, but when I realized that a lot of the things that I liked about it were things that were also present in Earthbound, or just reminded me of the times when I stayed up much later than I should have on a school night playing that game.
I've only played through the peaceful story arc, so I can't say anything about what my experience would have been had I played through the genocide route. What I can tell you, is that after playing through the peaceful route, I don't really want to play through the genocide route, because these characters touched my heart like a pixar movie. I think that is probably the biggest success of this game. They told me before I bought it that I wouldn't have to kill any of the monsters, and very quickly, I had absolutely no desire to do damage any of the monsters at all.
The story is excellently paced, with wacky comedy to keep you from getting bored, and some much darker moments sprinkled throughout. The world was one that I was very quickly invested in, and invested in completely.
The art-style is retro, and will fill you with memories of your old Nintendo console games, but will also impress you with how much they were able to do with an old pixle style.
When it really comes down to it, Undertale is a game with more heart and soul packed into it than I have seen in a game for a very long time, and if you're like me and were putting off the purchase because you didn't think it was going to live up to your standards, you should do yourself a favour and purchase this game.

Rust is a well made well thought out survival Sandbox game. However if you are not prepared to be distressed or have your hard work destroyed I would suggest another title.
People are constantly ranting on about the KOS behaviour and the unfriendly nature of the game. My suggestion to them would be to crouch when walking and don't build a base that can easilly be found.
Survival in this game relies soley upon your ability to utilize game mechanics and relationships you form. Having a few buddies to drop in the server with will give you a better game play but it does not stop someone from offline raiding you.
Griefing is normal, killing newspawns is overall an accepted strategy as new spawns can easilly hide weapons and people can imitate newspawns.
One thing that kindof bugs me is that someone with a bow or crossbow can easilly take down a fully geared armoured guy with an AK but again it comes down to skill, awareness and luck.
All in all rust is an excellent game, with an excellent focus. Most people who left bad reviews probably got raided and got salty IMO.

Ah, the game known as 'Diablo with Guns." There's some truth in that statement. At its core, you run around the huge vast land of Pandora, questing, killing anything that moves, while gathering sweet, delicious loot. I find the story to just be OK, but the witty, and often hilarious dialogues makes up for it. The game is a tad bit on the easy side though. Essentially, the REAL GAME starts in its New Game Plus mode with better loot and enemy level scaling. HOWEVER, to get the most out of this, you gotta get the DLC to increase the level cap (thus better lewt etc). *grumble grumble* JESUS, BL2!!

BROLANDS TEW! (as I like to call it)
I think everyone and their mothers have played this game already. If you haven't, think of this as a first-person Diablo, but without the randomly-generated terrain and lack of Hardcore Mode. Basically, a first-person shooter with a bunch of randomly-generated loot, skilling, and many side quests.
What's different from the first Borderlands? Well, you play as four different classes this time: Gunzerker, Commando, Assassin, and another Siren. Pay more money, and you can play as Mechromancer and Psycho. What's also different is that you explore another area of Pandora; a larger area, if you ask me. You also get a new element for your guns: Slag, which amplifies damage on slagged units. Oh, and no fall damage this time. This is all aside from the bajillion more guns that Gearbox stuffed into the game.
The humor in this game, compared to the last game, is much better...but I feel like that the humor isn't going to age so well. Think of it as Gearbox taking a bunch of internet memes and references to current games, and built the basis of the humor on top of those. Sure, I had a good laugh, don't get me wrong. But I feel like people that pick this game up years from now may not get any of the humor. I guess time will tell.
Without spoiling anything, the story was definitely improved over the first game. When I played the first Borderlands, I barely was able to keep up with any of the story. I even forgot what I was on Pandora for until I reached the end. Here, I'm kept aware of my goal, but I guess that comes from Handsome Jack taunting at me from his multimillion headquarters in the sky.
With that, I'll get to characters: Handsome Jack is a ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. He does spurt out some comedic lines from time to time, but I was just glad to put a bullet in his head in the end (not spoilers if it's obvious, AMIRITE?!), as I pretty much just hated the character halfway through the game. I guess that's the point of creating a memorable villain, so I guess props to Gearbox for that. The new characters, I thought they were pretty nice. Claptrap's still the same goofball as before, which I didn't have much of a problem with. Even found myself laughing at him, from time to time.
The enemy dialogue is much more varied this time around, and is just hilarious to kill some of these enemies. Speaking of enemies, Gearbox definitely amped up the amount of enemies you can fight, and even incorprated types of enemies that are armor-based instead of health-based, meaning that the best way to kill them is with corrosive weaponry. One fun type of enemy I got to fight were the Goliaths, which got stronger each time they killed someone/something. But the stronger the Goliath is, the better the loot you can earn. But try not to go too far with letting them rank up, if you're not ready for the high-ranking Goliaths.
Oh yeah, the game is still drop-in/drop-out co-op with up to four players. But here's something to keep aware of: The loot dropped or found in chests are shared by everyone. This isn't a hassle with money and ammo, as everyone gets that when one person picks them up. But when it comes to guns and what not, everyone pretty much has to decide on who gets what. So choose wisely.
Alright, I think this recommendation's gone on long enough for some of you people. If you like RPGs and shooters, pick this game up, but try playing the game with friends. It's a fun and comical game, and a definite improvement over the first game. Enjoy your stay on Pandora.

If you played Earthbound and enjoyed it, you'll also probably enjoy this game.
I was going to try to avoid that comparison in this review, but when I realized that a lot of the things that I liked about it were things that were also present in Earthbound, or just reminded me of the times when I stayed up much later than I should have on a school night playing that game.
I've only played through the peaceful story arc, so I can't say anything about what my experience would have been had I played through the genocide route. What I can tell you, is that after playing through the peaceful route, I don't really want to play through the genocide route, because these characters touched my heart like a pixar movie. I think that is probably the biggest success of this game. They told me before I bought it that I wouldn't have to kill any of the monsters, and very quickly, I had absolutely no desire to do damage any of the monsters at all.
The story is excellently paced, with wacky comedy to keep you from getting bored, and some much darker moments sprinkled throughout. The world was one that I was very quickly invested in, and invested in completely.
The art-style is retro, and will fill you with memories of your old Nintendo console games, but will also impress you with how much they were able to do with an old pixle style.
When it really comes down to it, Undertale is a game with more heart and soul packed into it than I have seen in a game for a very long time, and if you're like me and were putting off the purchase because you didn't think it was going to live up to your standards, you should do yourself a favour and purchase this game.

DayZ is like a box of chocolates, you never know what you're going to get.
One minute you find your fully geared character and fully geared buddy having a firefight in the middle of an airfield and go down guns blazing.
The next you find yourself wandering through the country side with your other mate, exploring, admireing the views and picking good gear at the same time.
The next you find you and the same buddy running through Berizeno with Chemlight man, make him fight other fresh spawns and kill them all when they take your buddy's gun. (Chemlight man survived to become Chem-bandana-boonie hat man)
The next you get knocked out by some scrub with an axe, wake up and go break his legs and leave him there and then you bleed out.
The next you chip your leg twice, starve to death twice. Spawn in Cherno and get knocked out by the invisible man, come back and kill 2 people in an axe duel as Arnold SchwarzenZagger. Then get killed by Legolas and his bow, along with his mate with the axe.
The next, you and your buddy head north after meeting up. You get geared and meet a man called Bill. While you looted, Bill disappered, he is still missing to this day. You later catch Hypothermia and both of you commit suicide.
The next you and your team of 3 are attacked in a police station. One of your mates is shot on the roof. You go outside to hunt them down while your other buddy covers the police station. After a 2 minutes of searching, automatic gunfire rings out from inside the station followed by your buddy saying: "I killed him!". You head back and while inside you get shot unconsious. You wake up to see your buddy get killed. You slowly crawl to the door and see a man. He opens fire and you shoot him in the stomach with your shotgun at the last second before you die.
The next you get your character fully geared up with an AUG, MP5 and FNX. And your mate kills someone who was stalking you.
The next your team of 4 get trapped inside a police station by another group. They order you to come out with your hands up and you will not be harmed. They shoot at you instead. They begin to throw flash bangs into the building. You pop out with your SKS and snipe some guy who was throwing the flash bangs. You eventually get shot through the floor and your whole team gets picked off one by one. Your last mate faces off the 2 enemies who rush inside with his MP5 and everyone dies.
The next your team comes back from Myshkino tents and your mate that went ahead of you gets sniped. 3 hostiles converge on your position, one rushes you and goes to fire. But his gun jammed, you kill him with your AK and he drops dead. Your other mate who survived shoots another enemy who was eating behind a rock. You spot another man from a distance closing in, you fire a couple of rounds into him and he retreats. You throw down some smoke to distract the sniper who's still shooting at you and you escape.
You later get your team of 3 together and fight 2 people with shotguns near VMC, as you're looking for new plate carriers to replace the ones that got destroyed, your mate gets snuck up on and is shot to death. The killer attempts to rush you with an SKS but is quickly dispatched, you get as much of your late friends gear as possible and run away.
DayZ is like a box of chocolates, you'd still eat those chocolates if they're stale right?

EDIT: Im changing my review to from positive to negative. This game has so much potential! But people liked it the way it was before! I miss the old Cherno! I miss the old Electro and campers in double red/green! I miss going up on triple yellow to cover my friends running though Cherno, and taking over cities like Kammy! I like the optimizations, but things have to change to bring people back to this game. The Tisy experiment isnt working. TALK ABOUT BECOMING DISCOURAGED!
Pitcure this: I spawn all the way across the map, loot up and make my way to tisy. Get solid gear, RULE Chernarus! Right?
WRONG! You'll most likey be eaten by wolves, shot by another player, starve to death, or become sick on your way up north because you had to drink dirty water. There is no worse feeling than loosing hours of your hard work trying to find good loot. This is what made old DayZ different.
I didnt have to run all the way to Tisy for good loot. I could go half way (myshkino), or even 1/3 the way (Pavlovo) and have decent loot to make it back down to my friends for urban warfare! This worked well, because if you wanted intense PVP you could go way up north (NWAF), or if you wanted some quick play, try to kill the sniper on apartments by using the CZ you found in the police station! If you die, no big deal! You can spawn right around the corner!
Like I said, im not a "WHEN WILL THIS GAME BE DONEEE" pleb, I understand it takes time to make a solid, complete game. I have no issues with game optimization, new items, or new player movements. I have no problem waiting for an optimized game. But when it doesnt become fun to play anymore, why try? This is why the game went from 40,000 + people playing it to just over 4,000 (max players per month). I log into a server and instantly want to log off, because I know its not worth running to tisy (or anywhere else).

I'd read plenty on Undertale before I played (as is the norm for me and games) and was pretty hyped once I got my hands on it. I already loved the characters and the story seemed fun. It seemed light and fluffy with a dark shadow cast over it, which only recieved a bad reputation due to the more rabid fans and people who just didn't focus on the right parts of the game (like those who've purposely fight to get a certain ending).
However, I then played the game.
To begin with, I was right. It was nice and fluffy and innocent and I enjoyed it. Then I got to
battle and lost several times. It annoyed me but I carried on and had a good laugh making him run back and forth between the living room and kitchen. Then
battle was a bigger pain... Then
... Before you knew it, I was suddenly no longer having fun and just spent my time googling ways to get past any and all scenes quickly. By the time I hit
battle, I'd resorted to file editing just so I could beat him (I was LV1 with 0EXP and 20HP and all boss attacks effectively violate your health bar in general). It wasn't until that last bloody fight that I found out I'd wasted my time avoiding conflict as I could only get the best ending by beating the game once... Then the final boss came along... Don't get me wrong, beat him second time around, but I honest to god had lost all will to game by this point.
Now I'm replaying to get the best ending and then intend to avoid the game for a while. Honestly, I like the story and love (most) of the characters, but the battle system is as fun as having your beanbag ran over by a steamroller. Regular battles you can live with the annoyance, but boss battles are like having a hacker on a PvP server... You just want to kill them so very badly but know you can't without one hell of a run around beforehand.
For the story, characters and bad jokes, I recommend this game. But, for the combat system, I recommend you get it on sale. A fun and fluffy game spoilt by ugly jagged battles. 7/10, will end up challenging my DETERMINATION again.
(Note: Haven't gone into detail about most things, so this should be spoiler free for the most part. Will leave the "had to beat the game once" here anyone who doesn't know that will be driven insane like I was.)

Ranging from tabletop adventures like Dungeons and Dragons to video games like Fallout and Shin Megami Tensei, I've been a fan of RPGs for a long time now, but I've always wanted something more.  Aside from more choices that matter, I wanted a critique.  I wanted to know that people aside from me were getting increasingly dissatisfied with the idea of level grinding, with the idea of "adventurer" being a euphemism for "murder-hobo."  I wanted to see my enemies have more texture to them than their stat blocks and attack patterns, in a way that matters more than just a few lines of background information I can look up in a codex.  I wanted to be questioned.  I wanted pacifism to be more than just "not killing people."  I wanted violence to be shown unglorified.  I wanted a game that took violence and peace and showed how the former can give way to the latter.  I wanted a game that made that transition seem possible.
It's true that all the games I mentioned above offer this in some fashion: Fallout lets you talk things out with important NPCs or sneak around enemies, and the wasteland changes with your actions.  Shin Megami Tensei hinges its outcomes on your declared morality and offers a universe where good and evil are not monolithic.  Dungeons and Dragons, of course, lets the DM decide what to do with the party, with imagination as the only limit.  At the same time, there was always something missing, whether a meaningfully nonviolent path, or richly textured characters, or simply less moral absolutism.  Despite how much I love the experiences I've had with each series, I was hoping to see something that would engage me on a different level.
As it turns out, I was hoping for Undertale.
