I've decided to finally give this a full reccomendation. This is because this is my favorite game ever made, so therefore I'd like to explain why it is that. If you're looking for a realistic shooter, this isn't going to be your game. However, if you're looking for mindless fun, mixed with the perfect balance of humor but also badassness and some seriousness, an interesting and fun storyline, and tons of replay value, this IS your game. There are just a million different things about this game that could be considered a reason why it'smy favorite, I'll name some important few. One being the endless (literally) amount of different and diverse guns that can be found or aquired in this game. From pistols to RPGs to Shotguns to Snipers and Assault rifles and more, there are so many and so many different of each one. And I'm not joking when I say endless. Next, there are so many areas to explore, and they're all so cool and different from eachother. They're huge, and Borderlands 2 really gives you such a cool sense of scale at how small you are in this huge crazy planet. Such a diverse amount of enemies, whether it's cannibalistic psychos, to hyperion powered robots, to devastating monsters. It mixes in the characters of the previous game in such a great way, even when they arn't playable. The new characters all have really awsome abilities. They are all planned out so well, and each characters ability can help out so much. I love how you can customize them much more as well. The DLC characters also add a nice touch and they fit right in. Your skill tree is so in depth and can make your character play out so much differently than a different skill tree set up (and you can always change it at any time too). The non playable characters (the good ones) are extremely lovable and hilarious. And of course the bad ones are well made to be hated by you. As if this game wasn't complete enough without any DLC, the 4 DLC's that have come out so far are all AMAZING. They are so much different and add such a large more amount of fun to it. The only downside I could possibly think of is playing with people that spend their time in a menu alot, that can sometimes slow down the pace. But besides that, it's highly reccomended to play with friends. And to maintain around the same level with eachother to keep balance. Even with this wall of text, I still havn't fully explained even a quarter of how much fun this game is or the fun stuff within it. The only way is for you to buy it if you havn't already. You don't really even need to have experience from the past one. Just give it a try, I can almost guarantee you'll get into it and love it.

Scone Recipe
Ingredients
225g/8oz self raising flour
pinch of salt
55g/2oz butter
25g/1oz caster sugar
150ml/5fl oz milk
1 free-range egg, beaten, to glaze (alternatively use a little milk)
Method
1. Heat the oven to 220C/425F/Gas 7. Lightly grease a baking sheet.
2. Mix together the flour and salt and rub in the butter.
3. Stir in the sugar and then the milk to get a soft dough.
4. Turn on to a floured work surface and knead very lightly. Pat out to a round 2cm/¾in thick. Use a 5cm/2in cutter to stamp out rounds and place on a baking sheet. Lightly knead together the rest of the dough and stamp out more scones to use it all up.
5. Brush the tops of the scones with the beaten egg. Bake for 12-15 minutes until well risen and golden.
6. Cool on a wire rack and serve with butter and good jam and maybe some clotted cream.

Let's keep this short so you can get to play this game as fast as possible:
Undertale is a bullet hell game. If you don't like that, watch a playthrough on your prefered online video platform, because the story is still really intense and worth just to experience. If you happen to NOT be disgusted by bullet hell games or are up for new challenges (to which I sort myself in) you should give this game a shot. The worst thing that could happen is that you look up a wiki on the internet helping you on your way.
Because: I really like Undertale as a story, as a RPG and as a innovation. It deserves the 10/10 scores in my opinion even if I don't happen to be a reviewer that fixates his opinions in numbers and scores. Yes, the graphics are somewhat old school and not the most beautiful, but you'll grow to like it soon enough finding yourself in a beautiful world full of unexpected changes, turns, twists and jokes that even break into your comfort zone.
There are three ways to bring this story to an end based on your decisions and each of it's own is worth like 4-5 hours of playtime. There are even many many more secrets to the game that frighten me to uncover and yes, I just happen to say that about an RPG game where being frightened of the outcome out of your choices is something strange to say.
As I said, it's innovations are awesome, groundbreaking and truely what I would like to see more of. I personly happen to end the experience in the best possible state of outcome and continued to educate myself about the other ways this story could take on the internet. Why you might ask? Simple: I've just grown to like what I've accomplished and I really like to keep what I achieved in the best possible scenario. It touched my heart through simple pixels but with a strong bond and determination of myself and the characters that I encountered.
So yes, this game is one of the rare gems that you maybe won't find again in this decade of video game history and if it does happen again, then we can all agree on this game being the first of it's kind charming our hearts with loveable characters, quirkiness and determination, which only you have the control over.

When I first saw Borderlands 2, I was a bit disappointed. There seemed to be little change since the graphics looked more or less the same as in the first title, and the playable characters seemed like modified versions of the original cast.
Boy, was I wrong. BL2 offers an interesting story and awesome characters, combined with great gameplay. I espsecially liked the love for detail within this game: the levels are filled with lots of easter eggs, silly stuff and even some (albeit slight) spoilers. Combat feels very alive (ironic, considering the outcome of those), as enemies react to your actions and character. When placing a turret, raiders might shout out that they're gonna shove your turret up your *censored*. Same goes for coop play, your character will automatically warn your allies when a badass enemy shows up, they'll thank you when you revive them and so forth. The game truly shines during coop play.
All in all, Gearbox managed to remove most of the flaws of Borderlands, however, it ain't all sunshine and rainbows. The menu can be somewhat unresponsive, and they removed the option to replay old dialogs. Which is bad, since dialogs can and will get canceled when you trigger a new one.
The biggest flaw however is still present, and for a coop game, it's a truly devastitng one. Connecting to other players via internet still sucks horribly, even with steam. Timeouts during connections happen randomly and far too often, and seems that Gearbox isn't fixing this.
Long story short, if you liked Borderlands, you will love Borderlands 2. If you like RPGs and FPS with a solid coop mode, you can't go wrong with this game.

I went in to Undertale with very, very high hopes. All I saw on the internet were people with profile pictures and names of the Undertale characters, perfect reviews, talk about the emotional endings, how amazing the OST is, the innovative bosses. However, no amount of hype could prepare me for the beautiful experience of Undertale.
Undertale is, in essence, an RPG/Bullet Hell game. You fight enemies and bosses, and dodge their variety of bullet-hell style attacks. You can increase your character's LV by killing foes and gaining EXP. However, although the comabt is incredibly fun and rewarding, where the game really shines is with the story, freedom and characters. Many years ago, there was a war between humans and monsters in which the humans won. Upon their victory, they pushed the monsters into a pit underground and sealed them in. In Undertale, you play as a small child who has fallen into the underground. That is it. However the story branches off into a much, much richer tale that you quickly become engrossed in and grow attatched to the quirky, lovable and often hilarious characters.
During battle in Undertale, you have three options. To kill, to spare, or to flee. This seems simple, right? However, in this game, death means death for good. You kill a boss that's also a major character? Gone for good, and the storyline is affected by this too. However, if you choose to spare them, they will stay in the game, affecting the story once again. The game offers a lot of freedom in that sense, allowing you to choose who lives in the game, and not just using the old cliched "You killed me? I'll be back!" method, and it really makes you think.
However, what really brings the amazing story, freedom, gameplay and characters together is the breathtaking OST. It consistently impresses right up until the epic final battle, whether it be with melancholy tunes, quirky jingles, tense drumbeats or epic compositions, it never fails to astound. Some of the tracks in it literally brought tears to my eyes, and many of them can easily be listened to over and over again.
In short: Undertale is perfect in every aspect, and you should play it. Yes I know it's mainstream to like Undertale, but if you haven't played it yet, I don't know what you're doing. Trust me,

Scone Recipe
Ingredients
225g/8oz self raising flour
pinch of salt
55g/2oz butter
25g/1oz caster sugar
150ml/5fl oz milk
1 free-range egg, beaten, to glaze (alternatively use a little milk)
Method
1. Heat the oven to 220C/425F/Gas 7. Lightly grease a baking sheet.
2. Mix together the flour and salt and rub in the butter.
3. Stir in the sugar and then the milk to get a soft dough.
4. Turn on to a floured work surface and knead very lightly. Pat out to a round 2cm/¾in thick. Use a 5cm/2in cutter to stamp out rounds and place on a baking sheet. Lightly knead together the rest of the dough and stamp out more scones to use it all up.
5. Brush the tops of the scones with the beaten egg. Bake for 12-15 minutes until well risen and golden.
6. Cool on a wire rack and serve with butter and good jam and maybe some clotted cream.

I've decided to finally give this a full reccomendation. This is because this is my favorite game ever made, so therefore I'd like to explain why it is that. If you're looking for a realistic shooter, this isn't going to be your game. However, if you're looking for mindless fun, mixed with the perfect balance of humor but also badassness and some seriousness, an interesting and fun storyline, and tons of replay value, this IS your game. There are just a million different things about this game that could be considered a reason why it'smy favorite, I'll name some important few. One being the endless (literally) amount of different and diverse guns that can be found or aquired in this game. From pistols to RPGs to Shotguns to Snipers and Assault rifles and more, there are so many and so many different of each one. And I'm not joking when I say endless. Next, there are so many areas to explore, and they're all so cool and different from eachother. They're huge, and Borderlands 2 really gives you such a cool sense of scale at how small you are in this huge crazy planet. Such a diverse amount of enemies, whether it's cannibalistic psychos, to hyperion powered robots, to devastating monsters. It mixes in the characters of the previous game in such a great way, even when they arn't playable. The new characters all have really awsome abilities. They are all planned out so well, and each characters ability can help out so much. I love how you can customize them much more as well. The DLC characters also add a nice touch and they fit right in. Your skill tree is so in depth and can make your character play out so much differently than a different skill tree set up (and you can always change it at any time too). The non playable characters (the good ones) are extremely lovable and hilarious. And of course the bad ones are well made to be hated by you. As if this game wasn't complete enough without any DLC, the 4 DLC's that have come out so far are all AMAZING. They are so much different and add such a large more amount of fun to it. The only downside I could possibly think of is playing with people that spend their time in a menu alot, that can sometimes slow down the pace. But besides that, it's highly reccomended to play with friends. And to maintain around the same level with eachother to keep balance. Even with this wall of text, I still havn't fully explained even a quarter of how much fun this game is or the fun stuff within it. The only way is for you to buy it if you havn't already. You don't really even need to have experience from the past one. Just give it a try, I can almost guarantee you'll get into it and love it.

If you came here looking for the standard RPG/Shooter hybrid look away, because Borderlands 2 (and 1) is everything BUT that. With great game mechanics and a story that will keep you in front of your computer for more than what you would want. And in case if you are wandering how is the game without any of the DLC let me tell you this: after 1 hour of playing this game you will want, but not only want, you will be obsesed on getting the Season Pack. Every new content pack is like a Christmas gift except that you know which is the one for you. So here is my advice: Buy the game (or first try the pirate version) and you will want to buy the Season Pack without hesitation.

Borderlands 2 is a vast improvement over the first Borderlands in multiple ways. The PC port itself doesn't feel like a port, instead fitting right in with some of the best PC releases out there. The story feels like there's less missing from it, and gives you reasons to both love AND hate everyone, a bit of a rarity for most stories. The classes and the characters representing them not only have a great degree of, well, character to them, but none of them feel truly lacking in any capacity. This can be said both about the default four classes, and the so far two DLC characters, where they even go into extensive detail to show how the new guys could be there without having shown up in the introductory cutscene. The graphics look amazing even on low quality, it's "gritty comic book" asthetic carrying a lot of weight in that regard. The only problem is that the writing can be a bit hit and miss. Some of the jokes work, but some are just plain terrible or unoriginal, at least one of them garnering a public appology from the writer for having stuck it in.
in short, definitely one of the better games of late 2012, let alone better port, but there are still a few issues.

Undertale is one of those games you wish wouldn’t end. You play through it, then replay it, maybe a couple of times. You devour the soundtrack. You lose hours exploring fan works. You watch blind Let’s Play videos to vicariously experience a bit of that first time, again.
At least, that’s the way it’s been for me!
Undertale isn’t perfect. The visuals range from memorable and expressive (most of the character sprites) through merely serviceable (environments like Waterfall) to downright janky (environments like the Ruins; some animations). There’s perhaps an overabundance of hand-holding, with several action sequences that ought to be intense undermined by the impossibility of actually failing at them. But those are remarkably minor gripes compared to the sheer brilliance of the game’s concept, writing, and emotional punch.
Undertale’s modest price tag buys you an unforgettable experience. I rank this game up there with the likes of Chrono Trigger and Super Metroid, a piece of gaming history that will influence the way I approach every game to follow it. It is not to be missed!

The first game,
, to actually, truly, and very genuinely tell a story through its gameplay.

I overlooked Undertale for the longest time, not expecting anything of interest from a Homestuck composer and the author of the notorious "EarthBound Halloween Hack." I intentionally avoided the Kickstarter of a young upstart named Toby "Radiation" Fox, truly believing that my time and money would be better spent elsewhere. Others encouraged me so strongly to participate that I actually became disgusted by the notion.
What I finally discovered after people left me alone long enough to give the game a chance for myself (a few years) is that Undertale's differences from its inspirations are deeply embedded into crucial game mechanics. Morality and choice are in every corner of the game, affecting its mechanics and story every step of the way. Where many modern game designers tinker away at meaningless dialogue trees and the illusion of control in a linear path that never changes, Toby Fox gives the player true control, true consequences, and truly branching paths instead.
Having become more attached to the game's characters than I expected, I experienced emotions from something I had thought was just a stupid game. Why was I crying when those characters were just a collection of pixels with some text and repeating split-second sound files? I had to study what other people thought of the game in order to find out. What I discovered is that you don't just play Undertale. Undertale plays you back, tracking your every move and toying with your emotions. Subtly at first, escalating in force until slamming them around mercilessly in the end.
And things may have gotten very serious then, but there were moments of genuine humor scattered throughout the game, begging to be understood until I finally gave in and laughed myself breathless a few times. And yet, there were also moments in which I experienced genuine horror and had to step away from the game briefly. It was an emotional roller coaster.
The soundtrack aesthetically improves upon every moment in this well-written and well-designed game even more. I still associate a few specific tracks with strong emotions I felt when I was playing the game the first time, and listening to them causes inspiration to strike. Writer's block is gone, and I feel like I'm really inside of whatever story I'm working on.
For me personally, Undertale sets a new standard that AAA game developers and producers have never met. I regret not supporting the game for the past few years, but I am grateful that I could still be a small part of it by buying and playing it after finally coming around. I would encourage you to play the game, too, if you haven't... But I won't. Only play this game if you want to. If you don't want to play it, you're not going to enjoy it as much as you could.

Undertale is one of those games you wish wouldn’t end. You play through it, then replay it, maybe a couple of times. You devour the soundtrack. You lose hours exploring fan works. You watch blind Let’s Play videos to vicariously experience a bit of that first time, again.
At least, that’s the way it’s been for me!
Undertale isn’t perfect. The visuals range from memorable and expressive (most of the character sprites) through merely serviceable (environments like Waterfall) to downright janky (environments like the Ruins; some animations). There’s perhaps an overabundance of hand-holding, with several action sequences that ought to be intense undermined by the impossibility of actually failing at them. But those are remarkably minor gripes compared to the sheer brilliance of the game’s concept, writing, and emotional punch.
Undertale’s modest price tag buys you an unforgettable experience. I rank this game up there with the likes of Chrono Trigger and Super Metroid, a piece of gaming history that will influence the way I approach every game to follow it. It is not to be missed!

While the game's progress has been extremely slow, the developers have been updating it at a constant rate for some time now. They've got a blog where they post spotlights on the development board almost every other week, and the updates have made the game better than it's starting state. While the updates that have come out haven't flipped the game on it's head from where it was, they have made considerable changes to the game, and the magnitude of the updates are starting to increase. The framework for the main systems are finally in, and in a bit of time the game will have a great deal more to it. Will the get the beta out by the end of this year? Doubtful. Do I trust Bohemia Interactive isn't just going to dump the game and move on? Yes. Now onto the actual present content of the game.
DayZ is, if you haven't already heard everything about it, a survival, post-apocalyptic, zombie game where you scavenge for food and resources and after a few hours of knowing where to search and a bit of luck, you can have yourself a pretty well gearded character. The current players in the game usually tend to lean towards banditry, and that is mostly due to the lack of long holding content in the game in its current state (i.e. base building), so people will get bored and decide they just want to use the guns they spent all this time looting for. At this point, it's just an element of the game, just like it is in real life. Do you want to go out there and try to talk to that person? Or will they just shoot you in the face? Should you just shoot them from where you're at? What if they're actually a good person? These are all questions you'll face as you go through your travels.
On a visual side the game looks absolutely splendid and runs far better now than it did at launch for my PC, which has rather average stats. It's an amazing thing to look out over a hill, spot a junk yard through your binoculars and say, "Hey, I'll go that direction," and after walking several miles actually find yourself at that spot. It just gives you this feeling of survival euphoria.
As for bugs, yes they are still very present and some of them are rather game breaking, I'll put a brief list here for new players to look out for:
-Falling
Do not jump down any ledge, ever. This is staple of the Arma 3 engine it seems, but if you go off a short ledge it's a complete toss up if you'll end up okay, with broken legs, or just straight dead.
-Zombies Glitching Through Wall/Doors
This one's finally fixed! (Hopefully stays that way)
-Lighting
Any light will phase through walls, so if you light that flare in a building, the light shines outside
-Persistence
This is supposed to be fixed with the next patch (Which should land within the week of this review) but at the time      tents, vehicles, items, etc. have no persistence. That means if you place them they will be gone after server restart
-Grabbing/ Holding Items
Ocassionally the game will refuse to let you pick up that gun you just dropped, it takes a bit of finagling but you can get it back
-And probably many more, they come and go with development
Once again, yes the development is slow, but the developers are still working on the game, if in a few months I see that the updates have stopped I will change this review accordingly, but as long as the game continues to be worked on, I reccomend this game for it's future, and not just its present content.

This legendary game was once just a mod on a game series called Arma, and is now a greatly detailed and amazingly fun 'standalone' game that has sold 2 MILLION copies in under 6 MONTHS. This game can be all confidence and heartwarming, but also dangerous and evil. That is what makes it beautiful, I recommend this game to anyone.

I got this game for 2 years or so, and the development has been over 2 years.
Playing the game from time to time to see if they finaly made a Stable version of the game (i might have to give up after 2 years i know)
This game is almost exactly the same way it was when it got released.
You might ask yourself is that bad?
Well if you take out the development process, it doesnt have to be bad, if the game of 2 years ago was good, but the game from 2 years ago wasnt stable, had tons of bugs, game crashing bugs, and the gameplay and controlls are realy bad.
A quick sumary of this game (since i dont want to waste too much time on games like this)
Pros;
+ Big World with a nice feel to it
+ Decent Grafics
Cons;
- Unstable game, crashes, bugs
- Horrible gameplay, moving as you want in this game is always a fight
- Rough arround the edges: grass comes true the floors of buildings, and things are misplaced or fly in the air, most buildings and the majority of doors cant be accessed.
- Unrealistic; Zombie game but barly any zombies, loot is all cluched together on spots where there normaly wouldend be any loot, while houses and other buildings that should have atleast something are completely empty
- No development at all, from what i can tell in 2 years time, they added trucks you can drive in, crossbows, maybe a building or 2, and new bugs, that wont get fixed.
- Hugely overpriced (its not worth more than 5 euro, max)
When should you get this game?
If you like survival games or zombie games, there are tons of others to choose from (like ''7 days to die'' that is also in early access and similair but better)
But if you dont care about a finished product or a game that wont get finished, you dont mind all the bugs and game crashes. And you dont care about gameplay.
Then you might want to get this game if its on sale for 5 euros or less.
Forever alpha... but who knows, maybe in future gonna be a fixed game. Glitches and laggy zeds breakin this game only.

Like many others have said, it is very difficult to review this game without ruining the experience.  All I'm going to say about the story is that you play as a human who falls into an underground world of monsters, and you have to make your way back to the surface.  What you decide to do for the rest of the game is entirely up to you.
Undertale is something unique and refreshing in a game industry where most developers seem like they're just trying to build the better wheel.  While it's clear that the game's graphics and HUD were inspired by Earthbound, it challenges JRPG conventions in mind-blowing ways that most players would not expect.  For example, if you've read other reviews, you may have heard about how you dodge enemy attacks in a manner similar to Bullet Hell, or how you have the option to become friends with the monsters you face duing battle in addition to killing them (which affects the story and therefore the ending).  However, these features are only the tip of the iceberg, and you'll experience plenty more unique twists as you play through the game yourself.  As tempted as I am to give advice on how to play through Undertale, I believe it really is best just to go in blind so that you can make your own decisions.  Instead, I'll only say that there's a VERY good reason why there are no achievements for this game, despite the fact that there are multiple endings.
Undertale also does an excellent job at blending humorous moments with the more dramatic/epic moments.  No game has ever managed to make me feel so emotionally attached to a bunch of pixels on my computer screen like this one has.  What's even more impressive is that this whole game was made almost entirely by one person (minus some of the graphics), and it's clear he poured his heart and soul into it.  Games like Undertale don't come around very often, so I'd definitely recommend buying it if you haven't already.

The game presents interesting dilemmas at first. Such as sparing monsters, whereas you would normally be expected to kill any random encounter in RPGs.

-Hamfisted writing
-Forced 'feelings' moments
-Humour so bad it isn't funny again from being bad
-Any attempt at puzzles were botched (Snowedin puzzles are laughably easy, the Hotland grid puzzle is not even challenging)
-The endings leave something to be desired.
-The characters and some of the game's traits are obviously inspired, but to this end they're essentially a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ization of what they're borrowing from.
5/10, I wouldn't recommend this game even if it were on sale, unless the cost was less than Bad Rats, considering that to be its quality.

The graphics are stylized but very well crafted so you will either love the look or hate it.  Similarly, the characters and stories are over the top, tongue in cheek and definitely do not take themselves to seriously which just adds to the charm of the game.  Tiny Tina is without a doubt my favorite.  As a whole, the game is a truly enjoyable experience if you like the genre.
In addition to the basic game, the DLC that adds additional gameplay is very good and I found that each one was better than the last culminating the role-playing spoof that was challenging, hilarious and surprisingly emotional in a game that is clearly anything but.

All I'm going to say about the story is that you play as a human who falls into an underground world of monsters, and you have to make your way back to the surface.  What you decide to do for the rest of the game is entirely up to you.
Undertale is something unique and refreshing in a game industry where most developers seem like they're just trying to build the better wheel.  While it's clear that the game's graphics and HUD were inspired by Earthbound, it challenges JRPG conventions in mind-blowing ways that most players would not expect.  For example, if you've read other reviews, you may have heard about how you dodge enemy attacks in a manner similar to Bullet Hell, or how you have the option to become friends with the monsters you face duing battle in addition to killing them (which affects the story and therefore the ending).  However, these features are only the tip of the iceberg, and you'll experience plenty more unique twists as you play through the game yourself.  As tempted as I am to give advice on how to play through Undertale, I believe it really is best just to go in blind so that you can make your own decisions.  Instead, I'll only say that there's a VERY good reason why there are no achievements for this game, despite the fact that there are multiple endings.
Undertale also does an excellent job at blending humorous moments with the more dramatic/epic moments.  No game has ever managed to make me feel so emotionally attached to a bunch of pixels on my computer screen like this one has.  What's even more impressive is that this whole game was made almost entirely by one person (minus some of the graphics), and it's clear he poured his heart and soul into it.  Games like Undertale don't come around very often, so I'd definitely recommend buying it if you haven't already.

5/10, I wouldn't recommend this game even if it were on sale, unless the cost was less than Bad Rats, considering that to be its quality.

A sequel that completely eclipses its predecessor.
Tons of varied environments ranging from icy mountains to futuristic cities and volcanic canyons and guns that are not just simple reskins of each other but also feel different for the most part with diverse and "funky" modifiers; they scream while firing, they may explode on reload, etc.
The PC version is also really well done this time arround with lots of options including FoV tweaking and UI placement/ resizement.
Matchmaking is handled throught Steam so dropping in and out of a game is a breeze.
Story and characters are also emphasized in comparison to the 1st one, with a likeable yet truly evil main bad guy, a completely insane little girl and characters from the 1st title making a triumphant return, with the game taking more time to showcase each one's  personality a little bit better.
This doesn't mean however that BL2 has become a story or character driven game.
It's still the same gun-toting, over the top violent loot fest as it was before, with quests just being an excuse for you to go buck wild on your enemies.
There are also raid bosses and tweaks since the game's release have made soloing them more difficult than before, just as it should be.
DLCs have also rebalanced the game's economy, especially Eridium that has other uses now than just inventory upgrades and Raid Boss fees.
The season pass is also highly recommended as it adds hours upon hours of new content to the game.
Recommended for solo, HIGHLY recommended for co-op.

I haven't written a review for any other games before this one but I have to say, this is one of my favorite games ever! I'll just hightlight some of my favorite components:
1. The soundtrack: Man the tracks were so infectious and appropiate. Everything from totally uplifting, to whimsical, to creepy, and eveyrything in between at exactly the right time! One of the few games I would buy the soundtrack for.
2. The characters: Memorable characters that always have something interesting/funny/quirky to say. Some are better than others but you really grow to love(or hate..?) the cast of the game.

So you can see the time I've spent, that I've done my fair share of playing Rust. It use to be great, but it is no longer worth paying nor playing.
Ironic how these Early Access games go. They become decent at first with a crap load of bugs, then approves later onward, and suddenly goes back to the crap hole. Rust is one of those games.
It use to be a struggle when Blueprints first existed, fighting to get the prints and praying to god to get that Bolt Action Rifle template or AK 47 template. Requiring one to get a bow and arrow to self defend ones self against other players till you research decent quality weapons. Oh, forget to mention it required a decent size amount of resources to create a Research Table (That had value) unless you're a risk taker to research in a nearby monumentum, which 9/10 is a battleground between solo's or clans. Wood use to be good (Till Flamethrower became a thing), then again why would you even go wood? You're silly to stick with wood over stone or metal, seeing that it takes 1 C4 or a Rocket to destroy the entire structure lol. But now days, it's easier to get that AK, that Bolt, That thompson, or any good weapon simply by farming boxes, crates, and airdrops throughout the Rust valley. Blueprints haven't existed for a while, and it's diffirculty has been banished, turning into a hand holding playthrough. Even soloing is now easier.
What broke the camels back to quitting Rust though is this new update: 158. Where one can build twig structures around a nearby base that has an active cupboard around it's radius. Cupboards officially have 0 use. It's defense is gone. Having external walls is now a waste of resources and time. One can easily build, upgrade, then build around it and conquer the domain easier rather than raiding it the old fashion way that requires X amount of C4's or Rockets. With this new update, it makes veterans like me turn away from Rust and say good bye.
Lastly of course are the aimbotters, but we all know aimbotting doesn't exist due to Rusts "Anti Cheat System" Pffft, right. This issue has been ongoing since Rust's existence, so I won't bother complaining. That complaint is on the bottom of my cry list, for every FPS shooter that is MMO have this issue. Move along.
If you enjoy hand holding, quick to play and conquer games, Rust is for you. If you're looking for an actual survival game that has real mechanics, a challenge, and requires the individual to work at it, Rust is not the game I would suggest.
I'll miss you Rust, but Facepunch can no longer polish your ugliness. The developers have officially ruined your beauty and existence. RIP, Jan 2016 - 5/14/2017.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

A sequel that completely eclipses its predecessor.
Tons of varied environments ranging from icy mountains to futuristic cities and volcanic canyons and guns that are not just simple reskins of each other but also feel different for the most part with diverse and "funky" modifiers; they scream while firing, they may explode on reload, etc.
The PC version is also really well done this time arround with lots of options including FoV tweaking and UI placement/ resizement.
Matchmaking is handled throught Steam so dropping in and out of a game is a breeze.
Story and characters are also emphasized in comparison to the 1st one, with a likeable yet truly evil main bad guy, a completely insane little girl and characters from the 1st title making a triumphant return, with the game taking more time to showcase each one's  personality a little bit better.
This doesn't mean however that BL2 has become a story or character driven game.
It's still the same gun-toting, over the top violent loot fest as it was before, with quests just being an excuse for you to go buck wild on your enemies.
There are also raid bosses and tweaks since the game's release have made soloing them more difficult than before, just as it should be.
DLCs have also rebalanced the game's economy, especially Eridium that has other uses now than just inventory upgrades and Raid Boss fees.
The season pass is also highly recommended as it adds hours upon hours of new content to the game.
Recommended for solo, HIGHLY recommended for co-op.

Of all the games I have ever played... this may be my favorite.  I've spent literally hundreds of hours on Pandora,  I have the script down pat, and I still keep coming back for more. It's clever, funny, and at times, heart-wrenching. The comic-book-esque artwork is a nice break from other styles. Nearly all of the voice acting is well done, and I enjoyed learning some of the characters' backstory as I played through the first time. Each DLC story expansion was well worth the money, except perhaps for Assault on Digistruct Peak - while I appreciate the extra levels immensely, the mission itself is a short snoozefest. The DLC packs shamelessly shower the player in good loot and cash. I even love the game so much, I picked up a bunch of paid-for skins, something I'm not usually prone to doing.
Playing with friends is even more fun, especially starting a new character and building them up together.  Each character can be built and rebuilt so many ways, each playthrough maintains its charm.
I didn't play the original until after this - and I couldn't do it. The UI improvements are vast and they spoiled me. I'm looking forward to the Pre-Sequel!

Like everyone else who is currently looking at reviews thinking about getting this game, I was drawn to it by the extreme hype spreading around the internet (mainly rule 34) but that aside I was geniunely interested to see if this game held up with all the hype.
Now I went into this game knowing there were multiple ways to play it so I read up and found out that being a pacifist was the best way. So I set off sparing the colorful (ironically black & white) monsters.
-
The only con I noticed within the first few hours is the fact that you run into the same mobs multiple times and the entertaining value of their encounters wears off after the first time. But this isn't even really a big deal.
-
And I nearly finished the game before finally realizing why this game is so hyped.
It's unique.
The developers used techniques which I can't recall ever seeing in any other games. It tracks how many times you've seen a cutscene regardless of your save data, which makes for some really cool easter eggs. They literally force crash your game at certain points which (again ironically) makes it very immersive.
And the game constantly breaks its own rules which (one more time, ironically) makes it extremely entertaining.
The Neutral - True Pacifist endings truly made my love for this game bloom. And just like that, I'm one of the cancerous fans.
I can't bring myself to start up the game ever again and do a genocide run. I literally do not want to ruin such a perfect ending.
I only played through half of the game and it's easily a gem that I would recommend to anyone.
The only real bad thing about this game is you WILL NOT get the soundtracks out of your head.
I give this game a solid 5/7.

Borderlands 2...what to say...I love the Borderlands series, not only because its a twist on the regular FPS clones that flood the game market, but because of its humor, art aesthetic, and pure insanity.
The original Borderlands will always be the best in the series, but Borderlands 2 is in no way a bad game (unlike some other Gearbox titles...cough, Duke Nukem Forever...cough, cough...Aliens: Colonial Marines...). It is a worthy successor to the original. Therefore, I recommend it.

To start, if you are one of the people who hates this game for the sole reason of its meme references, you are a massive ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and you need to swallow your pride because writing isn't the only part of a game.
Let's begin.
Writing - Bad. I'm not even talking about the meme references, it's just bad. The story is just as stupid as the first one, but small things like Claptrap's newfound annoying lines make everything worse. I ended up muting any mission that involved Claptrap because of how annoying he is, especially when compared to the first. Every character is unlikable because of their bad attempts at being witty.
Presentation - It's literally the exact same thing as the first game but with better models and textures and whatever. As per usual, the Unreal Engine 3 makes textures look like complete♥♥♥♥♥♥ but I still like the cel shading that they use. I barely hear any music because I'm either listening to music or I've muted the entire game because of annoying characters, so I can't really comment on the sound.
Gameplay - No different from the first, which is usually a good case if the first game is good, but with this game it's not. The reason I stopped playing the first Borderlands was because of how bored I got from it. The missions became stale and "endless looting" isn't an acceptable excuse to make me want to continue. So what did Borderlands 2 do? Absolutely nothing different. I seriously found almost nothing different from the first game aside from setting and graphics. I got bored of this game in probably a tenth of the time that it took for me to get bored of the first. I guess it's kinda fun, but not for very long.
And don't you dare tell me I need to play with friends to have fun. It made no difference at all.

Thankfully, BL 2 isn't just Borderlands: Again. Gearbox did a great job sticking to the simplistic yet fun gameplay (shoot mans, collect guns) from the original, all the while keeping it fresh. The character classes are fairly similar (2 new ones with DLC though), almost all the NPCs return, and if you enjoyed the humor of the first one you'll certainly keep laughing through your second romp in Pandora. There's still a lot of mindless fetch quests, but they've done a better job adding in more "set piece" moments to break the grind. As with the first one, it's best played with friends, although it's still a fine game to blow through solo.
Unfortunately, some of the problems in the original have migrated to the sequel. Once again, some skills are fairly worthless, especially later in the game, while others might as well be required. BL 1 was a ridiculously easy game, culminating in an embarrasing final boss battle. Rather than actually work on the AI (enemies will still largely rush you and occassionally use cover), they simply inflated health. Even with the best guns (golden key weapons), fights at your level will often take way too long. This is painfully obvious in the Big Game Hunt DLC. Level scaling is also awkward, you'll often outlevel quests, but the enemies in them will keep scaling, so quest marked trivial might still be hard, but will give awful rewards. As the game goes on fire and shock guns will be all but useless compared to corrosive and explosive, so good luck if you keep getting stuck with fire guns.
Still, Borderlands 2 is an easy game to recommend for anyone who enjoys fun, shooting and looting. The DLC quests are also well worth the purchase price, and provide some of the best content in the game.

In a nutshell, Borderlands 2 is essentially an OCD Looter's paradise, and hell all in one.
Loot:
They say there are a bajillion guns, and you can't exactly deny that, with weapons randomly generated from a variety of different parts, there are literally millions of combinations.
Specific gun manufacturers all have different traits that their weapons vary, such as Dahl guns fire in bursts when zoomed in, or Jakobs guns fire as fast as you can click, but have high recoil and high damage.
As you can imagine, you tend to come across a lot of crap weapons, and those are good just for selling. But are a double-edged sword in of themselves because of the very limited inventory space you have, both on your character, and the storage bank.
Storyline:
The first Borderlands certainly wasn't known for a storyline, and to be honest, you probably didn't even realize there was one there to begin with.
Borderlands 2 however, realized this issue, and really gave the storyline in spades. It still has that traditional dry sense of humor from the original, and then some. I don't think I've ever laughed so hard in a game from dialogue from characters bantering back and forth.
And the main villain, Handsome Jack... He's the very definition of "Love to Hate."
Misc:
Vehicles are still wonky as hell, same as in BL1. But they buffed the health by tons, so it's no longer a case of "You will live longer and take less damage if you get out of the vehicle." And there's a few varieties, but still, lackluster I'd say.
There is a much larger variety of enemies now, and environments. It is Pandora still however, so expect a lot of the same rocky rather desolate terrain.
All in all, It's an awesome game if you're into both FPS and RPG games. Cause it has a little something for everyone. It's got my two thumbs up for sure, and I can legitimately say that it is a GREAT improvement over it's predecessor.

As a long time player, and early adopter of both the Mod and now the Stand Alone, I have had a pretty long look at the life cycle of this game as it unfolds.
I enjoy many aspects of the gameplay, and I have a regular core of people that will hop on and try out new updates as they are released.
As the development time rolls on and the updates take longer and longer to push past the experimental stage, the conversations we have about DAYZ fall into the same areas.
What are the obstacles that are facing the team, and has anyone been trying to help them overcome them.
Do the developers have any idea how this cycle of slow updates effects the community?
Wouldn't a system of small, quick to release updates, including content changes keep development going and the masses happier ?
Is anyone applying pressure to the development team to perform, or have they been left to drift aimlessly as they please without oversight?
There is a lot to be said for proper management of a high performing team, and low performing teams can generally have the finger pointed right to the boss for the same reasons.
Until some reliable and meaningful changes are made I can't endorse what I have been waiting for, which is solid feedback and development of what is a potential blockbuster game.

Edit:
I have 2,760 hours in now.  Time to add some info
At the time I did this I had only played Zer0, with practice he is a force to be reckoned with.
Now, I gravitate to Gaige, the Mechromancer because, anarchy forever LOL  Early play her "pet" Deathtrap is killer and helps a lot, once I get the skill close enough and the skill Anarchy things get interesting
Maya, awesome support but a power house in her own right, cloud kill, baaahahahahahaa, phase lock.
Axton, well rounded out solder type, not my fave but he is balanced pretty well.
Krieg (Psycho class), for up close melee, this is on the edge of your seat fast paced action.  Once you unlock Release the beast, if you can work with it you can be a runway train.
Salvador, the Gunzerker.  If you manage to get the right guns, class mod and relic, he is pretty much a tank.  So much so that some find him boring, I think he is fun but not my fave (see Mechromance above).
If you get the GOTY + Ultimate Vault Hunter Upgrade pack 2 and the five head hunter packs you have it all, and I can honestly say hundreds of hours game play
Even my least favorite of the four main campaign DLC (NONE are in the main story, they have their own stories and maps) is good, my fave (Tiny Tina's Attack on Draggonkeep, an AD&D inspired story) is awesome.
The game has it's issues, but the good out weighs it by a lot.
PhysX is badly implemented and appears to work better on old NVIDIA cards (from 2011) than new ones.  PhysX if not on low causes loot to fall through the floor/ground in some places as well as poor frame rate.
If you are not trying to use PhysX the game can run on fairly low end hardware.
Borderlands, is was/is a good game, but this one (Borderlands 2) in spite of it's problems is just an amazing game.  If you like ARPGs and FPS then I think you should give this one a go.

To say any of the many reasons why I love Undertale would spoil the experience. Every individual aspect combines to make something greater, something that should be experienced with as little information as possible. That said, this review will try to convey the essence of Undertale with as little spoiling as possible.
Gameplay is largely a mixture of turn-based actions and bullet-hell dodging. Each turn, the player can choose to fight or perform a special, enemy-specific action, to respectively kill an enemy or convince them to end the fight peacefully. The enemy, meanwhile, will launch touhou-style attack patterns that must be dodged to avoid damage. Each enemy has unique, often entertaining patterns, and the mechanic stays fresh and interesting throughout the game. In particular, each boss has its own twist, affecting how the player moves, such that each new boss fight is something to look forward to.
The (at first glance) simplistic graphics disguise a powerful story that plays with the rules of the medium. The aforementioned bosses are among the most memorable characters seen in video games in a long time, and even side characters and enemies have charm and personality. Over the course of eight to ten hours, you'll grow to love the bizarre assortment of monsters found in the underground world; it's a testament to good writing how strongly the cast's hopes and dreams can affect the player.
The SNES RPG Earthbound is fondly remembered for blending the real and the surreal, the creepy and the comical, and Undertale proudly takes this influence and makes it its own.

Undertale has a whole lot going on.  It leans heavily on being both charming and whimsical, while simultaneously being a commentary on video games and players.  And to its credit, Undertale lives this double life quite well.  In my opinion, it’s able to do this so well by spending an incredible amount of effort was put into the characters and creatures throughout Undertale and in making them likable, and then making any commentary or fourth wall breaks be rooted in who these characters are.
It’s sort of a cousin to both Earthbound and the Stanley Parable that’s roommates with Abed from Community and Bat-Mite from The Brave and the Bold.  It may not be right for everyone, but I found it just right for me.  And I hope you do too.

Thankfully, BL 2 isn't just Borderlands: Again. Gearbox did a great job sticking to the simplistic yet fun gameplay (shoot mans, collect guns) from the original, all the while keeping it fresh. The character classes are fairly similar (2 new ones with DLC though), almost all the NPCs return, and if you enjoyed the humor of the first one you'll certainly keep laughing through your second romp in Pandora. There's still a lot of mindless fetch quests, but they've done a better job adding in more "set piece" moments to break the grind. As with the first one, it's best played with friends, although it's still a fine game to blow through solo.
Unfortunately, some of the problems in the original have migrated to the sequel. Once again, some skills are fairly worthless, especially later in the game, while others might as well be required. BL 1 was a ridiculously easy game, culminating in an embarrasing final boss battle. Rather than actually work on the AI (enemies will still largely rush you and occassionally use cover), they simply inflated health. Even with the best guns (golden key weapons), fights at your level will often take way too long. This is painfully obvious in the Big Game Hunt DLC. Level scaling is also awkward, you'll often outlevel quests, but the enemies in them will keep scaling, so quest marked trivial might still be hard, but will give awful rewards. As the game goes on fire and shock guns will be all but useless compared to corrosive and explosive, so good luck if you keep getting stuck with fire guns.
Still, Borderlands 2 is an easy game to recommend for anyone who enjoys fun, shooting and looting. The DLC quests are also well worth the purchase price, and provide some of the best content in the game.

In a nutshell, Borderlands 2 is essentially an OCD Looter's paradise, and hell all in one.
Loot:
They say there are a bajillion guns, and you can't exactly deny that, with weapons randomly generated from a variety of different parts, there are literally millions of combinations.
Specific gun manufacturers all have different traits that their weapons vary, such as Dahl guns fire in bursts when zoomed in, or Jakobs guns fire as fast as you can click, but have high recoil and high damage.
As you can imagine, you tend to come across a lot of crap weapons, and those are good just for selling. But are a double-edged sword in of themselves because of the very limited inventory space you have, both on your character, and the storage bank.
Storyline:
The first Borderlands certainly wasn't known for a storyline, and to be honest, you probably didn't even realize there was one there to begin with.
Borderlands 2 however, realized this issue, and really gave the storyline in spades. It still has that traditional dry sense of humor from the original, and then some. I don't think I've ever laughed so hard in a game from dialogue from characters bantering back and forth.
And the main villain, Handsome Jack... He's the very definition of "Love to Hate."
Misc:
Vehicles are still wonky as hell, same as in BL1. But they buffed the health by tons, so it's no longer a case of "You will live longer and take less damage if you get out of the vehicle." And there's a few varieties, but still, lackluster I'd say.
There is a much larger variety of enemies now, and environments. It is Pandora still however, so expect a lot of the same rocky rather desolate terrain.
All in all, It's an awesome game if you're into both FPS and RPG games. Cause it has a little something for everyone. It's got my two thumbs up for sure, and I can legitimately say that it is a GREAT improvement over it's predecessor.

Unfortunately, everything after Rust Legacy went downhill fast. Rust Legacy, though it was buggy and rough around the edges, was incredibly fun. The community was not nearly as bad as the new Rust. Some of the best times I've ever had in any multiplayer game were spent in Rust Legacy. I miss it.
The developers have added little new content to the game in its nearly 3 year Alpha development. Instead, they have highlighted and refined features in the new Rust that brings out the worst in its community. It's hard to pinpoint exactly why the new Rust that strips away many "survival" aspects and turns it into a cancerous FPS. With hackers and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s running wild, the game is nearly unplayable unless you play with a group. There is no cooperation. It's 100% KOS. You will die and lose everything as soon as you log out.
There isn't a clear direction for the game, either. Most of the dev updates are bug fixes here and there, new buyable in-game items and textures, and petty things. The anti-cheat system is practically useless. The optimization is terrible. The community is - saying it again because I cannot stress it enough - absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing horrendous.
There are a few good things to say about the game, though. For one, the graphics are quite nice if you have a high-end PC that manage to run it on high graphics settings. The building system is also pretty good, though Legacy's was better. The maps are huge and procedurally generated (if that's your thing - personally, I preferred Legacy's predetermined map much better).
I don't regret buying it because of the many wonderful hours (over 200 if you count the hours from my previous account) I spent in Rust Legacy. However, I cannot recommend the current version. This game is dead to me.

Undertale, when I heard about it I didn't think much of it. I thought that with my game preference being more serious and multiplayer oriented that a game like this would bore me to tears, but I was mistaken. Undertale opened a new genre of games for me and opened my eyes to many different avenues of thought. It is the only game to make me want to watch and look at fan art, comics and music. There are some who may say that the gameplay is repetitive and that the art is basic, but that is part of its character. The game is not about its gameplay or its graphics. (Not even its amazing soundtrack) It is about an experience, the story is one that will resonate for years to come. It's not cliché and overdone, though it isn't exactly the first of its kind. The story will also drastically change depending on your choices, even if the choices may not directly affect the story, they most definitely affect you. The music fits perfectly and adds to the personality of the game. It is one of the only games you can listen to and just by the sound remember the story. The minimalist 8Bit graphics are not ugly whatsoever and help drench the game in a style of its own. Through its basic graphics you can still understand your surroundings and characters personas. The gameplay if repetitive yes, is meant to be only part of the characters themselves. We are given characters through fights in which a characters persona will come out through its tactics and style. The characters are also some of the best I have ever seen in a game, even if they are not the first of their kind, they are most certainly one if the best of their kind. Toby Fox has made a masterpiece if I have ever seen one, the only thing I wish, is that there was more, however that is not a bad thing. Sorry for my rambling and bad grammar, but for a game like this, I've got to help spread the word.

At first look, this game doesn't seem like much. 8-bit atari styled graphics with a similarly styled song to match.  Players are given a cut scene that tells a basic backstory.  But things change very quickly in this game and it soon becomes apparent why it has become so popular.  As much as I'd like to go into specifics, if I say anymore I'll be entering spoiler territory.  Overall, I highly recomend the game.  A single playthrough took me about 10 hours to complete, but that can be easily broken into smaller chunks if you don't have a lot of time.
Pros: Music for one.  I know I said the music is very retro, but it opens up into more modern style compositions and has some excellent and memorable themes.  Charaters: There is a decent sized cast of memorable characters ranging from enemies to friends.  Choice: Player choice is heavily emphasized in this game and even the smallest choices can have large and lasting reprocutions.  This isn't a game you can just start over when you make a mistake either. The game remembers even when a file is reset.  Now, that isn't to say you can't do over an event and change your mind.  You can.  But character dialogue changes depending on choices you make during present and past runs.  Fun: Not only is this game fun to play, it has fun with itself.  It throws out a lot of jokes.  Depth: this game has a lot of it and can be very dramatic at times.
Cons: Puns.  There are a lot of them and most are covered in enough cheese to drown the main character.  While I had zero problem with this, if you aren't a fan of puns or cheese this can be a real turn off.  8-bit style:  It isn't the best looking game around, although it does have its moments.  Backtracking:  Boy did I do a lot.  While not necassary, the backtracking can be a flipping pain in the rear.  There are three "fast travel" points but even those are slow and not readily accesable.  Griding: Depending on how you play, you may be foreced to do a lot of grinding.  Again, avoidable.
This game made me feel like a kid again.

It's hard to try to figure out what I'm trying to say here. Essentially, I picked up this game months ago with the expectation that it was either going to fall just short of the hype, or not come close at all. That usually tends to be the case with overhyped games these days. So when I opened the game and found cute, retro-styled graphics and an overly simple control system, and the introduction to what felt like a typical rpg story, I felt like I was going to be immensely disappointed through the rest of it.
Instead, I was pleasantly surprised with the mechanics for both types of battling, and also heard that there were two main ways to play this game: Pacifist or Genocide. The option for not killing a single thing had never been presented to me before, so I thought if I was going to endure a game I wasn't confident about, it'd at least make it interesting.
The further I went into the game, the more I found myself getting attached to the characters, the writing style, the music and the world itself. Everything was so well done and surprisingly in depth from having the chance to befriend a character on a deeper level than is usually afforded in rpgs like this to even small hints of character in the programming, like the desperate nice cream punch card.
And the more I got attached, the easier it was to remain a pacifist and the more I got stuck on one fight, and the closer I came to just attacking, the more I found myself valuing the life of the monster and questioning what kind of consequences attacking it would have.
This is more of a game of choice than any other, because the option to choose is hardly presented to you. It's never a pick this or pick that game. The concept is offered, not required. There's no karmic scale, or path of good and evil. And it's up to you to play how you so choose and to accept the consequences therein.
It's hard to figure that there's no one who wouldn't enjoy the game. I'm finding it genuinely difficult to finish a genocide run.
(It's gonna get just a little personal)
The time I had to play this has come through one of the darkest and scariest points in my life, while being stuck in a situation where no decision I made mattered and I barely had choices in anything. And to be able to love something so deeply as I did the entirety of this game is a great and important thing to me. This isn't only a game that lets you make your own decisions, it asks you why you made them and if they were worthwhile. And through each play, I find myself learning just a little more that I hadn't figured before.
Every choice you make has a reason, is vital, and valuable.This game totes the idea of hope, and certainly helps to pass it along.

This is one of those rare games, that fits a lot of catagories. Its really good, but rather then take my workd for it:
The base game itself is good for those who like shooting things and comparing loot, always searching for the better gun that fits your playstyle. Sure, some may dislike this feature, and the bugs in the menus and item retrevial get in the way sometimes, but the base consept is awesome. The story is where it that awesome wit and great writing come in. Handsome Jack may be a well written ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but he's my least favorite villian ever. Not because he is a badly written character or anything like that, quite the contrary: he is a perfectly acted, perfectly delusional ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of an antoanogist, but he does his job so well that Its hard to like him at all. I won't spoil it, but I think when you play through, you will find that moment of obvious ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥gery.
If you plan on getting the DLC, do so. Even if you aren't, get the DLC. The expansion on the story is funny and awesome, even if some characters (like the badass savages/Witch Doctors from Hammerlock's Big Game Hunt) can be nutty with the ammount of bullets they cane take, but they are all well written and worth it. AT the time of writing, Tiny Tina's Assault just came out, but I am hoping they are not stopping at 4 DLC campaigns.
Other DLC's like the Psycho and Mechromancer are good too, as well as the UVHM; as they bring a fresh new face to the same story. The only DLC i would pass on is the costume packs, as microtransactions are not my thing for something so simple. That would change if they release "weapon" DLCs where you could get different brand of weapons (like atlas or some other company), but again, thats a wishlist thing.
Having never played the original borderlands, I was swept away with how awesome the second was and wanted to try the first, even if my friends say "its not as good as the sequel". Still, with how awesome BL2 is, the only way BL1 could be bad is if the wit, the charm, and everything was completely removed from its predocessor.
TLDR: Boderlands 2 is aweosme, it has some flaws, but that make it more awesome. What are you waiting for, buy the game, and GO KILL HANDSOME JACK (But call him Ugly Jack, he is in no way handsome).

At first look, this game doesn't seem like much. 8-bit atari styled graphics with a similarly styled song to match.  Players are given a cut scene that tells a basic backstory.  But things change very quickly in this game and it soon becomes apparent why it has become so popular.  As much as I'd like to go into specifics, if I say anymore I'll be entering spoiler territory.  Overall, I highly recomend the game.  A single playthrough took me about 10 hours to complete, but that can be easily broken into smaller chunks if you don't have a lot of time.
Pros: Music for one.  I know I said the music is very retro, but it opens up into more modern style compositions and has some excellent and memorable themes.  Charaters: There is a decent sized cast of memorable characters ranging from enemies to friends.  Choice: Player choice is heavily emphasized in this game and even the smallest choices can have large and lasting reprocutions.  This isn't a game you can just start over when you make a mistake either. The game remembers even when a file is reset.  Now, that isn't to say you can't do over an event and change your mind.  You can.  But character dialogue changes depending on choices you make during present and past runs.  Fun: Not only is this game fun to play, it has fun with itself.  It throws out a lot of jokes.  Depth: this game has a lot of it and can be very dramatic at times.
Cons: Puns.  There are a lot of them and most are covered in enough cheese to drown the main character.  While I had zero problem with this, if you aren't a fan of puns or cheese this can be a real turn off.  8-bit style:  It isn't the best looking game around, although it does have its moments.  Backtracking:  Boy did I do a lot.  While not necassary, the backtracking can be a flipping pain in the rear.  There are three "fast travel" points but even those are slow and not readily accesable.  Griding: Depending on how you play, you may be foreced to do a lot of grinding.  Again, avoidable.
This game made me feel like a kid again.

"Entertainment gives you a predictable pleasure… Art leads to transformation." -Makoto Fujimura
I'm constantly debating others on whether or not video games can be considered an art form, and this game has given me all the fodder I need to say without a doubt that video games CAN indeed be art. While it doesn't have the technical prowess of AAA games, this game has achieved something that photo-realistic graphics and fully orchestrated soundtracks can't -- a transformation. Expanding on the Fujimura quote above, art should lead to a transformation in the people who experience it. Art should surprise us, wound us, change us, and not be predictable and comfortable like our entertainment so often is.
Through its masterful mechanics and excellent writing and character develpment, Undertale achieves all three of these goals, while simultaniously remaining engrossing, funny, and downright touching. Furthermore, it touches (briefly) on various social issues plauging our world today, and reframes them in new ways I've never seen before.
While this review has seemed super general, I'm sure, that's on purpose.
The best way to play this game is by knowing as little about it as possible going in, don't use a guide, don't do any research. You're going to make a few mistakes and that's okay.
Just trust me, and buy the game. You won't regret it!

It's hard to try to figure out what I'm trying to say here. Essentially, I picked up this game months ago with the expectation that it was either going to fall just short of the hype, or not come close at all. That usually tends to be the case with overhyped games these days. So when I opened the game and found cute, retro-styled graphics and an overly simple control system, and the introduction to what felt like a typical rpg story, I felt like I was going to be immensely disappointed through the rest of it.
Instead, I was pleasantly surprised with the mechanics for both types of battling, and also heard that there were two main ways to play this game: Pacifist or Genocide. The option for not killing a single thing had never been presented to me before, so I thought if I was going to endure a game I wasn't confident about, it'd at least make it interesting.
The further I went into the game, the more I found myself getting attached to the characters, the writing style, the music and the world itself. Everything was so well done and surprisingly in depth from having the chance to befriend a character on a deeper level than is usually afforded in rpgs like this to even small hints of character in the programming, like the desperate nice cream punch card.
And the more I got attached, the easier it was to remain a pacifist and the more I got stuck on one fight, and the closer I came to just attacking, the more I found myself valuing the life of the monster and questioning what kind of consequences attacking it would have.
This is more of a game of choice than any other, because the option to choose is hardly presented to you. It's never a pick this or pick that game. The concept is offered, not required. There's no karmic scale, or path of good and evil. And it's up to you to play how you so choose and to accept the consequences therein.
It's hard to figure that there's no one who wouldn't enjoy the game. I'm finding it genuinely difficult to finish a genocide run.
(It's gonna get just a little personal)
The time I had to play this has come through one of the darkest and scariest points in my life, while being stuck in a situation where no decision I made mattered and I barely had choices in anything. And to be able to love something so deeply as I did the entirety of this game is a great and important thing to me. This isn't only a game that lets you make your own decisions, it asks you why you made them and if they were worthwhile. And through each play, I find myself learning just a little more that I hadn't figured before.
Every choice you make has a reason, is vital, and valuable.This game totes the idea of hope, and certainly helps to pass it along.

"Entertainment gives you a predictable pleasure… Art leads to transformation." -Makoto Fujimura
I'm constantly debating others on whether or not video games can be considered an art form, and this game has given me all the fodder I need to say without a doubt that video games CAN indeed be art. While it doesn't have the technical prowess of AAA games, this game has achieved something that photo-realistic graphics and fully orchestrated soundtracks can't -- a transformation. Expanding on the Fujimura quote above, art should lead to a transformation in the people who experience it. Art should surprise us, wound us, change us, and not be predictable and comfortable like our entertainment so often is.
Through its masterful mechanics and excellent writing and character develpment, Undertale achieves all three of these goals, while simultaniously remaining engrossing, funny, and downright touching. Furthermore, it touches (briefly) on various social issues plauging our world today, and reframes them in new ways I've never seen before.
While this review has seemed super general, I'm sure, that's on purpose.

Do I recommend this game in it's current state? No. As a friend of mine warned me, with all the bugs, wonky combat and general lag, it's nearly unplayable. This game has been in Alpha for how long? Every time they seem to fix something, something else goes wrong or they bring back a bug that they had already fixed. Global sound bugs like bandaging, drinking or reloading are still a pain in the neck. Only in this game can you shoot someone with a pristine gun from mere feet away, aiming center mass and miss every shot while they stand still. They STILL have issues with loot and persistence, literally whole cities will have not one lootable item after a server restart. Loot tables are still jacked up. You can find clothes for days but end up starving to death becuase you can't find any food items, animals to hunt or plants to forage. Spend hours looting up when you do find weapons and equipment only to instantly lose it in a player encounter not due to PvP but rather lag. They have ONE vehicle so far and it's a pain in the neck to drive. Hit some lag and you're wrecked. A large number of bugs that affect play seem to get fixed and keep cropping back up. Rather than build something similar to the Mod, which I haven't heard many people say was bad, they add in ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t equipment like a medical thermometer and medical scrubs. They do keep tossing in the additional firearm or melee weapon which only adds to the PvP fervor. FF is a big issue because they have no real friend or foe identification except for colored  armbands (yay!), so you'll still hear lots of "who is this? is that you?" in TS which is exacerbated by the fact that people all have identical gear.
I really loved this game in the Mod. I was really digging it on the SA, but nearly two years in Alpha and they still can't put more than 4 zombies in a city? This isn't a zombie game, it's another PvP deathmatch with a lot of cross country run simulator tossed in.
Maybe in a year or two when they've finally come out of Alpha this game might be more interesting to play. If you're into wonky PvP combat FPS drop gunfights, this might be for you. If you're an RPer or a survivalist-type, look elsewhere.

This is easily one of the best games ever made. It's not merely an excellent piece of "art" (whatever that means).  It's also fun, engaging, and replayable.  Undertale is a singular achievement, one that could not possibly have emerged from the minds of studio executives and focus groups and middle managers.  Millions of dollars have been poured into lesser games which feebly attempt to communicate some sort of feeling or idea to the player, which invent new rendering technologies to bring you vast continents to run around and shoot/slice/stab everyone you encounter, and all of them come up short compared to Undertale.  Made by Toby Fox and his cohorts, probably in their spare time, probably with a $30 copy of RPGMaker or something, tells a deeply moving story, not merely through cutscenes or dialogue, but through the manner in which the player chooses to play the game.  Undertale is not "challenging" (although it can certainly be difficult), and it is not "epic" (although its world is fully realized and is a delight to dwell in it for a few hours).  But it is, probably, the best game I have played in years.  Buy five copies and gift them to friends.  They will thank you for it.

I can very easily say that this is the finest game that I have ever played.  Borderlands 2 is an improvement (for the better) in nearly every aspect of the original game.  Borderlands 2 comes with a much better story, much more varied environments and enemies, better user interface and more variety in the way the gear behaves.
The cooperative system is also very much improved in Borderlands 2.  The game moved away from using Gamespy for an online lobby and now uses full Steam integration with drop-in and out cooperative play.
The game features 4 new classes (Soldier, Siren, Gunzerker and Assassin) with 2 others available for purchase via DLC (Mechromancer and Psycho).  Each class features all-new skill trees that have been mostly well designed and appear to work well for both solo and team play.
Most of the original cast of NPC characters have returned along with a few new ones.  The story is very well written this time with an extremely interesting villain in Handsom Jack.  The story for Borderlands 2 does attempt to be a continuation of the original game and miraculously improves the previously lackluster story to a point where it now actually makes some sense.  The game also includes a TON of sidequests and activities so you can expect to have about 30 hours of gameplay with the main questline and roughly 50+ hours if you include most of the side activities.  There are 4 large campaign DLC and a variety of smaller DLC packs which will add significantly to an already huge amount of content.
The only few negative things that I have found in the game include:
1)  Less storage space than you had in the original game.
2)  Inability to replay echo logs like you could in the original.
3)  There is much more dialog (good) but too easy to interrupt (bad) with no way to replay as mentioned in my second point above.
Overall I feel that Borderlands 2 is a huge improvement over the original in most aspects and the many improvements definitely outweigh the few negatives.  I have newer games in my library but this one always keeps drawing me back.
