This is easily one of the best games ever made. It's not merely an excellent piece of "art" (whatever that means).  It's also fun, engaging, and replayable.  Undertale is a singular achievement, one that could not possibly have emerged from the minds of studio executives and focus groups and middle managers.  Millions of dollars have been poured into lesser games which feebly attempt to communicate some sort of feeling or idea to the player, which invent new rendering technologies to bring you vast continents to run around and shoot/slice/stab everyone you encounter, and all of them come up short compared to Undertale.  Made by Toby Fox and his cohorts, probably in their spare time, probably with a $30 copy of RPGMaker or something, tells a deeply moving story, not merely through cutscenes or dialogue, but through the manner in which the player chooses to play the game.  Undertale is not "challenging" (although it can certainly be difficult), and it is not "epic" (although its world is fully realized and is a delight to dwell in it for a few hours).  But it is, probably, the best game I have played in years.  Buy five copies and gift them to friends.  They will thank you for it.

I've heard quite a few people suggest that someone should go into Undertale blind and with no expectations about what one will experience, and so they've been tight-lipped about what makes the game actually good. I disagree wholeheartedly with this approach.
Instead, I'm going to say that what makes Undertale good is that it's a funny and even quite charming game on the surface, but once you begin and get into even a first playthrough it becomes much more. Right away you are shown how your actions have consequences in a meaningful way in the story: taking a violent path leads to more violent and desperate encounters from the characters than you'd face in a less violent or even pacifist playthrough, but you enjoy greater health and more power by being violent. The characters you meet and interact with regularly will comment on how you behave, either deciding to stop you at all costs or admiring you and helping however they can.
As for the characters themselves, they range from either being comic relief in some form, to having very complex interactions based on their personalities, drives and even their awareness of the fourth wall (with one in particular loving to play fast-and-loose with it). Of the characters you'll interact with most, all feel distinctive in their personalities without being necessarily defined by them: it's very easy for characters to simply end up being nothing more than 'the smart guy' or 'the jokey guy', but from Sans to Undyne to Asgore himself you get to understand how these characters fit within their world, the conflicts they face and the impact your interactions have on them. This is the level of detail that characters of this importance should have, and a crucial part of how Undertale stands up as an interactive story.
The strength of the characters is the most important point for me, but it is placed within the context of a game that loves to mess with expectations to make memorable boss fights, amusing comedic moments and surprises later on that I definitely WON'T discuss in detail here. The main gripes I have with the game involve mixed messages with the random monster encounters (let's just say the random monsters seem bizarrely unaware of how dangerous they are) and that the jokes can be very hit-and-miss at times: sometimes you get homicidal cooking shows, other times it's... tsunder-plane...) but I can forgive it for that because it is a game that tries to preserve player choice in a way that's meaningful to the events of the story and the characters you meet, and I think it pulls it off tremendously well.

Do I recommend this game at this very moment?: NO.
I say this game is a no buy first of all, because currently, 3,157,440 people have bought this game. With the current pricetag of this game 27.99€ or $34.99, that puts this games overall income of sales to over $104.9million. Of course the game has made more than this from Events, Ads, and being funded by bohemia. With the game making $5.1million on its release date, you would of course believe the hype over the game, but what about from the dev team? Dean Hall was the man behind the project at the start, with his leadership proving to be one of the the best since Satoru Iwata (R.I.P). Near the end of 2014 there was reports of Dean leaving, and we could see, as fans, that DayZ progression had slowed down and was soon to be named a 'to-be-dead game'. Dean steped down in December to launch his own studio. and as a DayZ EA user, I was very frustrated because this game, DayZ, had so much potential. After Dean Hall left, his right hand man, Brian Hicks took over the team. At first, I was unsure, then I saw the quick development pick up again. That was......... for about 2 months.
Today, playing the game. I, and everyone else, is left with an even more broken game than before. I experience problems from day one, that were at .3, in which they're arising now in .5.. The game is not optimized at all, and is worse than anything I've every played. I've even gone to the extreme of overclocking everything possible in my computer, disabling usless windows default desktop programs, and changing things in the Config folder. I'm still, like MANY others, left with low performance. (I have a high end PC that cost over $2500).. There are so many people writing reviews that have obviously never done testing before.  There are generally 6 stages to the testing of a game.  It starts with Internal testing.  Now internal testing has 3 basic parts to it.  Code release and build push.  Internal testers SIT it and then UAT it.  Often the internal testing spends months on one build and never leaves SIT phase.  Now for those of you not familiar with these acronyms let me fill you in.  SIT is System integration testing.  Basically this is where you put two seperate pieces of code together, or hotpatch a piece of existing code and see what breaks and what works.  Sometimes you have to scrap the build entirely and add your code into the original code and re-compile.  Even though it is the same code, the process of patching it onto an existing build can cause compilation errors... So generally in SIT we have 3 categorys.  Critical bugs, Major bugs and Minor bugs.   Critical bugs are show stoppers.  System crashes, hangs, BSOD, etc.  Major bugs interfere with intended function but usually don't crash the program.  Minor bugs are things like display glitches, or despawn, or random things that still happen, often unreliably replicable and don't interfere with gameplay 100% of the time.
UAT is User Acceptance Testing.  Usually when we get to this phase of internal testing we see only Major and Minor bugs.  The Criticals are usually few and far between.  This is more a quality of play experience testing phase.  This is where you will see STABLE releases.   SIT is for experimental releases.
Now, once you have the critical bugs down to 1-2 and the majors under 20, you are ready to push to Alpha.
Alpha testing is the first official stress test of a game.  Usually it is kept in-house and to people the company knows.  Often there are industry Alpha testers that are utilised over and over again.   Rarely do we get to see Alpha released to the public.  During an Alpha phase you still see Critical bugs popping up and a good number of majors.  Sometimes it makes the game unplayable until a new "patch push" happens.
Beta testing again usually starts with a closed-beta.  These people that are selected are chosen to STRESS Test the game.  They are looking for ANY way to break it.  When they break it, they try to replicate it.  If it can be replicated it is added to the Major/Critical bug list and is addressed first before new content.  If it is non-replicable then it is added to the Minor/Major list and will be worked on as they can.
Again, while you do get to play the game in Beta it is STILL all about trying to BREAK the game.  Go places you are normally not allowed, Test EVERY aspect.  For instance even though you wouldn't normally F11, Closed Beta testers will try EVERY gun on f11 just to see if all the animations are correct, or if it even works.
Attached to Closed Beta is Open Beta.  This is where everyone gets a chance if they are a beta OPT-in consumer to try the product.  This is great for testing server stability and concentration of player issues.  Usually here you will see the number of people per server number get modified.  Often you will also see them take shards down for a few days and replace the hardware to keep up with the progression of the code.
We finally come to release.  Release is just a fancy way of saying: "Hey we know there are still bugs, but for the most part it is playable.  We will continue to patch this to give you new content, features, and bug fixes"
lastly is the first stable patch.  If we look at Windows 8... It was horiffic until patch 8.1   Even going back to WinXP it was Service pack 2 before they got stability down.  and Service pack 3 to make it really stable for gaming.
The stable patch after release is usally where a game only has a few minor errors left.
Now as to people complaning about development time... Look at movies that also use CGI.  James Cameron's Avatar was one of the most in-depth CGI-Hybrid films ever made.  It began its life in the writing stage in 1994 and didn't hit the big screen until 2009... That is 15 years in the making.  If you look at the time from the first work on filming and CGI work you are still looking at 4 years from 2005-2009.   This film was budgeted $237 million and estimates have it topped out at $310 million to produce....  DayZ has sold 3 million copies by January 2015.  At the estimate that everyone bought it at the $20 mark (I know people pay more now....)  That is $60 million dollars over 2 years to put towards development.
If we look at the cost of the let's say 100 servers that exist, we are looking at about $1000/server/year to have it run.  Usually $100-200/mo in processing fees, The costs of the server shard equipment which can be upwards of $5000 each.  Then Network maintenance fees to have an engineer keep your servers in good working order... that is usually $70/hr for 20hrs worth of work per month per server.  This is assuming there is no emergency maintenance at 3am...  So let's see...
$1600/server/mo for maintenance and processing, That's $19200/yr/server. Assuming a server replace every 2 years that brings it to $2500/yr for hardware.  And $1000/yr for the actual rights to host there.   That's $22700/yr/server.  Assuming 100 servers - $2.27 million per year just in hosting (just talking public hives)  Now let's assume a group of 20 programmers plus management plus other employees... about 40 employees for a small company.  They get paid an average of $45000/yr  That's 1.8 million just in paycheques.
We also look at the Engine costs.  Some engines such as Unreal 4 charge you 5% of gross sales after the launch of your game.  Some take on the cost of a staight purchase which can be millions of dollars upfront.
This can mean with smaller publishers that all of the company's money goes towards developing the game with no money left for paying employees and they work on the hope that the game will eventually make money so they can bring home a paycheque.
There is cost of work computers, renting work space, etc,etc.
So of the approximately $60million they have made from selling off the early access, over half of that would have been spent already.
Now do remember that those of us that get the early access get it for a reduced price.  When the game finally launches it could be as high as $60 to purchase.
As an early Access Alpha member you will never have to buy the game again.
So this means that the developer has your money now at a reduced rate to help foot bills, but will not have access to that money at full rate later as profits.
Now to those of you who complain that the game has bugs.  That the game is unplayable.... The whole point of an ALPHA is that you are in the game not to fully experience end game content that is fully finished.  It is so that you get the opportunity to play the game during development.  Find bugs, Help make the game as stable as possible for final release.
If you look at Early Access as the same as buying a complete game you have the wrong mindset.  Early Access is buying a chance to test the game before it is finished.  It is a chance to get your hands dirty and essentially BE a tester for the developer.
Look at some other games.  Let's take World of Warcraft.  It was anounced in 2001.  Generally when a company releases  an announcement it means that it is already a solid idea, has some artwork and coding done and has passed a closed group of testing to show what the games potential will be.  They didn't release Beta until 2004.  That is almost 3 years of SIT, UAT, and Alpha testing.  And NONE of the Alpha for WOW was available to the public.  Beta started early 2004 and 8 months later the game launched.  The game was buggy as all crap, but has survived for almost 11 years.
Remember folks we aren't even to Beta yet.  If you want to whine wait until Beta!!!

Story, Characters, Design, and Gameplay blended so well in this masterpiece by Toby Fox. As a regular to RPG games, Undertale proved to be one of my favorites of the genre along with Golden Sun, Chronotrigger, and Dragon Quest titles.
The story is quirky and brilliant at the same time. You control a human who fell into a cavern inhabited by monsters that were banished by the humans long ago. Characters will pull at your heart strings and also provide the much needed humor from the otherwise dark story.
Very few games nowadays create characters you genuinly care for and wish to know more about. Most games I play, I walk away from them not caring to know a character or even their name. Undetale does the opposite by making you desire more  on certain characters such as origins and regular duties.
Gameplay is fairly original, especially to the RPG genre. You control you soul in battle, resembled by a small red heart. You must then overcome obstacles by moving the soul or bocking projectiles. Every creature you face has a different way of attacking meaning you must adapt quickly. Extremely fun with both the ease of learning the combat system, and the difficulty in later battles.
Best RPG and story telling of 2015.

Rust is a hardcore, dog-eat-dog, tribal simulator. First, the pros and cons:
When all goes reasonably well, the game is fun. You build a base, try to secure it properly agaist raiders and go raiding yourself. When you get raided, you can see how they got in and work out how to prevent them doing the same next time. Raiding a base is also great fun - find weaknesses in design, carefully step around the sleeping bodies and search for the cupboard and loot room.
There is, however, a lot of grinding going on. You'll spend most of your time chopping down trees, mining rocks, gathering other resources and playing lottery with blueprints. This is part of the game, but when you spend weeks building a nice base and the developer decides to make a minor update to the map generator algorithm, all servers are forced to wipe their maps, meaning you'll have to start from scratch again for no good reason. Which would be okay if the grinding wasn't such a.. well, grind.
As a newbie, you would do better to watch "How to play" videos on youtube first. Learning through playing is slow and tedious. You will get killed, a lot. Most people are hostile and will kill you on sight. You'll need blueprints to survive or to make a base that stands a chance of staying in one piece. Just gathering and trying to build a small house from the start will leave you frustrated. It's not until you've gained a lot of blueprints and mastered some of the weapons that you stand a chance of holding your own. Unfortunately, you'll have to redo this on every server you play, and again after every blueprint wipe.
When all doesn't go well, there are cheaters. Many, many cheaters. There is no effective server side anti cheat in place, and no data is server side validated. Which means it's incredibly easy to create and use cheats in this game, and that's exactly what happens. Anything from flying and wallhacks to Godmode, aimbotting and item duping. Some cheaters are blatant, but most are more subtle and require online admins to catch them in the act. Which most servers don't have - especially the official servers. One of the most annoying doubts you'll keep facing is: "Did they cheat? Were they really that good or lucky? Can I retaliate or would that be futile?".
I've enjoyed playing this game, but I've reached a point where I feel development gets in the way of the gameplay, and the many bugs, glitches and cheats just leave me more frustrated than satisfied. I'll try again in a year, maybe two.

Rust is a social experiment. Anything you craft in-game can, and probably will be raided and stolen, no matter the defenses. People will add you to their friends list for the sole purpose of knowing if you're offline or not in-game, so as to determine the perfect time to steal all your items. Rust is a soul-crushing digital manifestation of what happens when the world breaks down and guns and explosives are the only form of barter or negotiation.
It is a beautiful game. The sunrises and sunsets are majestic.
What it does to people. however, is the exact opposite. Rust is a more brutal, unforgiving, and relentless online arena than EvE Online - as even in EvE. you could park your assets in a neutral station and wait for the storm to pass. Here, the storm is everywhere... right outside your door, crawling on your ceiling, while you're asleep in your bed. Waking up to find your assets intact in Rust can be considered a major accompishment, and usually only practical for those in large clans which cross multiple time zones.

**************************************************Spoiler Free Review!**************************************************
TL;DR BELOW.
Alright, Undertale... what is there to say about it?  When I bought this game, I was expecting a decent JRPG style game, especially with it's great reviews.
What I got was a game which was well crafted and amazingly thought out by the creator.  No, seriously, this one guy probably put more thought into this game than most game devs today.  Almost every choice in this game has been thought of by the dev, and many choices in the game can affect things in ways that you would not expect.
So let's talk about the graphics.  Yes, it isn't Crysis 3 or Rise of the Tomb Raider.  It's pixel sprites, something I love.  While many people may be put off by the graphics, I would highly recommend to ignore this, and give it a try.  But honestly, if the graphic style is  what deters you from playing this game, it's your loss.
So maybe you don't care about the graphics.  What you care about is the music.  Well then, let me tell you, the music is pretty damn good.  The music helps set the mood of most scenes or battles, and helps make the game memorable.  You've probably heard some of the ingame music across Youtube, used as background music (ie:  Bonetrousle, Dogsong).
Alright then, how much content is there?  Honestly, not that much.  I finished the game in 5 hours.  However, this is NOT a bad thing.  There is a lot of replayability, and the short time needed to finish the game is actually probably a boon to the game, as if it was any longer, I would lose interest in playing this game more than once.  There is also a TON of hidden content and stuff to find - stuff that you might have to replay to discover.  Also, for $11 CAD, 5 hours + replayability isn't a bad price.  But if you don't care about the length of the content, but rather the quality, then Undertale has you covered as well.  The story is amazing - while a little bit cheesy, the history of the lands you have fallen into is told in an interesting way, which can be uncovered bit by bit through your choices and actions.  The gameplay is also pretty interesting - with a mix of JRPG turn based battles and bullet hell.  If bullet hell isn't your thing, no worries, the bullet hell in this game is pretty easy.
So, the biggest question of all is:  Should I buy it?  And I will respond:  Yes, you should - but after trying the demo. The demo is on Undertale's official website, and has about 30-40 minutes of content.  The demo is a good indicator of whether or not you will enjoy this game - and it leads you up to one of the biggest decisions of the game.  I will be honest here though, this game is NOT for everyone.  Some people may get bored after an hour or so.  Some people have played this game probably about 20 or 30 times, and are still going.
Also, if you want to watch people play this game, I would tell you to stop NOW, if you are interested in playing this game.  This game is one that should be up to you to discover - one that you should play by yourself and experience.  While you might be tempted to watch a playthrough of LP or someone so you can see how it plays out,  I would recommend you to try the demo instead if you want to get a feel of the game.  Also, you can always refund the game if you play less than 2 hours, so...
If you buy it or not - that is a choice you will have to make; and if you choose to buy it, just one of the few you will have to make.
TL;DR:  It's a high quality game with nice pixel graphics, great music, and great story.  Not for everyone however.  Buy it after trying the demo.  Don't watch online playthroughs if you want to play this game.

If you're looking at the reviews for this game and you're unsure whether or not you would enjoy playing it, let me help you out.
This is by far one of my favourite games of all time, take that as bias or not however it really does earn the title.
The story is fantastic, no spoilers however it really does a lot to earn your respect and attempt to make the campaign enjoyable for the player with a variety of missions, ranging from shooting some dudes in a snowy landscape to shooting some dudes in a volcanic area!
Jokes aside the story tries it's hardest to stay as entertaining as it can, which, as far as FPS games go these days, is a blessing. The game features a variety of NPCs, featuring characters from the first game as primary NPCs! (That's right, you can talk to mother♥♥♥♥in' Brick!)
You may view them as a grab for money from the developers however the DLC is well worth the money paid, often adding what could be considered another game into a small price, especially Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon's Keep, I've yet to finish it myself however I've put a few hours into it and am looking to wrap it up sometime soon.
If I did have to complain about anything in the game, however, I would say that most content, be it DLC or not, tends to be for the endgame and is usually either a lot more enjoyable or only accessable once you're a high level, whilst I can understand this is mostly for the enjoyment of long-time players who have countless maxed out characters, playing the regular campaign without access to any of the fun bosses or DLC exploration can get a bit bland.
If you're looking to get Borderlands 2 or Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel then I would definitely go for Borderlands 2, not simply because I am a fanboy of this game nor am I an aussie hater, I prefer the game style and overrall feel of Borderlands 2.

This game is one of the best games I've played in a while. it's a great game with a heart-warming story. IF you play it nicely. If you murder everyone, then you feel like a serial killer. Let me list some of my favorite things about this game.
1: Atmosphere.
Okay, so if you read about this, then you know that in this RPG you can choose not to kill anyone. This is proven throughout the game as the way to totally change how the story works. The start of the game is executed perfectly in the way that if you kill anyone in the starting area, it'll count against you getting the Pacifist run (Not killing anyone) but nobody outside this arean will know because it's sealed of from the other areas. Yeah, you'll feel bad, but nobody outside will think you're a killer. Now, if you murder everyone you possibly can, it's a genocide run. This completely changes the feel of the game to where everyone thinks you're insane. They run, they hide, and they die when you find them. Even the characters that would have been your friend prove to you that you're a monster when you murder them. What's worse is that at this point, you've probably played the pacifist run or neutral run and chosen not to kill these characters and they loved you for it, and now you're stabbing them in the back. The game changes. You either feel like you're a lovely being or you feel like a sociopath.
2: Soundtrack
My favorite design thing about this game, it's soundtrack matches each situation perfectly and it's super catchy.
3: Character design
Each character you meet has a unique personality, and it's own flaws. These flaws don't make you hate a character like they normally do, they make them seem more alive. This is because in real life, everyone has their flaws unlike in most games where nobody has any massive issues that are blantantly out there. For example, the first main character you meet is overprotective, the second is lazy, and the third is wildly full of himself, and so on. These personalities are what you get attached to because it's realistic and more importantly, someone you relate to. You'll likely be attached to the character that is most like you, or most like your friend, because your friend acts like this character, flaws and all. This makes every character in this game loving and amazing.

Story, Characters, Design, and Gameplay blended so well in this masterpiece by Toby Fox. As a regular to RPG games, Undertale proved to be one of my favorites of the genre along with Golden Sun, Chronotrigger, and Dragon Quest titles.
The story is quirky and brilliant at the same time. You control a human who fell into a cavern inhabited by monsters that were banished by the humans long ago. Characters will pull at your heart strings and also provide the much needed humor from the otherwise dark story.
Very few games nowadays create characters you genuinly care for and wish to know more about. Most games I play, I walk away from them not caring to know a character or even their name. Undetale does the opposite by making you desire more  on certain characters such as origins and regular duties.
Gameplay is fairly original, especially to the RPG genre. You control you soul in battle, resembled by a small red heart. You must then overcome obstacles by moving the soul or bocking projectiles. Throughout my many hours in both the old Rust back in the day and the current version of the game, I have had a very positive experince. The countless amounts of raids and the grind for resources are all very enjoyable. I really enjoy the UI and the building within the game.

Okay, so even after 180 hours in this game I still don't know everything about it. I literally just learned that because of the poor AI (this is the Unity's fault), you can set up a foundation and if you stand on it, bears or whatever animals can't get to you.
Now, the concept of the game is rather simple, you spawn with nothing but a rock and a torch, and really there is no concrete goal except to survive. You can choose to play through different playstyles, if you want to go gather all your materials yourself and build yourself a little house, you can do that. If you want to craft a bow or spear and start killing people for their supplies, you can do that as well. It's up to you what you do, who you become allies with, and if you play solo or as a team with friends.
I have to say that in my short time playing this game over the last 3 months, I've met many, rather interesting people in this game. I've definitely made lots of friends the people you find, I believe is what gives this game life. There's other games like this, such as Stranded Deep where it's just a long grind of swimming from island to island, building a shelter, and surviving. Also DayZ which I've played briefly at a friends house, and it seems just like running non-stop and both of these games have a sense of isolation, and you just kinda hope you run into people. Back to Rust, generally you'll find that in a lot of servers people can be found everywhere, not only that but people often team up in groups, and sometimes full clans are made with monsterous bases that tower over everything else. Allies are made, and so are enemies which makes the game so much fun.
****Side Note****
This game is alpha still, and of course it isn't perfect yet. The game runs poorly on most people's systems due to the fact it's not quite optimised just yet. Optimisation is rumored to start closer to the final release of this game, which may be another year or two. It's just not something thats a top priority right now and there's other things to work on too. So just be aware of that if you want to purchase it now. Just as an idea of what I use to run the game, I have an i7-4790k, GTX 970, and 16gb of RAM and I run at about 80-90 frames on some servers with maxed out settings, and other servers I get drops down to as low as 15-20. To add to that, large gun fights usually bring things down as well, you can be running at a solid 60fps and drop down to 10 if you get in the middle of a gunfight.
Another thing, a microphone, although it isn't required to play it, I would highly recommend one. Communication plays a big part in this game, it can mean the difference between life and death sometimes. If you can make yourself seem friendly, then there's a good chance not everyone will shoot on sight. But if you're quiet, nobody can really tell what your intentions are. Of course there is a chat box to type in, but if you're being chased, you won't want to stop to type.
